The fade-narration table settles it (lines 145–148): for OXPHOS subunits the Myc+ 6→12W slope is −0.39, of which the **shared-developmental (WT) part is only −0.11 (28%)** and the **Myc-specific excess is −0.28 (72%)**; for the OXPHOS core it's −0.34 = −0.03 shared (10%) + −0.30 Myc-specific (90%).

Here's the answer to your question, then I'll fix the doc.

## Your reading is the *time* axis — and it dissolves the contradiction, but flips the *cause*

You meant "reduced abundance" as the **Myc+ 6W→12W temporal decline**, not Myc-vs-WT. That's a different axis from Issue #4's "Myc raises OXPHOS" (which is genotype, Myc vs WT). **They're orthogonal — both are true at once**, so there's no self-contradiction:

- **Genotype axis** (powered, d≈1.27): at any given age, Myc+ has *more* nuclear-OXPHOS mRNA than WT.
- **Time axis** (your reading): within Myc+, nuclear-OXPHOS subunit mRNA *declines* 6W→12W (subunits −0.39, core −0.34).

But your proposed *cause* — "probably reflecting WT 6W→12W" — is **not supported for OXPHOS**, and this is actually the crux of Issue #6:

| | Myc+ 6→12W slope | shared-developmental (WT) | Myc-specific excess |
|---|---|---|---|
| OXPHOS subunits | −0.39 | **−0.11 (28%)** | **−0.28 (72%)** |
| OXPHOS core | −0.34 | **−0.03 (10%)** | **−0.30 (90%)** |

WT OXPHOS barely declines over 6→12W; the Myc+ decline is **72–90% Myc-specific**. So the OXPHOS "reduction" over the timeline is a **Myc-specific de-amplification** of the elevated OXPHOS program — *not* a reflection of the normal developmental trajectory. (Contrast: for the biosynthetic arm — amino-acid, lipid — the WT *does* converge; OXPHOS is the arm where it does not.) That de-amplification is exactly the compositional-dilution pointer (the Myc-built high-OXPHOS/proliferative compartment shrinking).

**Two caveats to bake in:**
1. The shared/specific *split* is powered (gene-level, all genes), but the sample-level composite slope itself is directional/ns at n=6/tp (Myc+ p≈0.11).
2. It's a **nuclear-subunit** decline — mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS *rises* 6→12W (absolute z −1.14→+1.23). So at the transcript level it's a mitonuclear **rebalancing**, not cleanly "fewer assembled complexes." Whether assembled complex abundance actually falls is a protein/respirometry question (companion data).

The script-side sweep is back and decisive. I've also hand-read the review docs. The doc-side agent is still finishing, but I already have the answer from my own reading of the walkthrough, the review discussion, the 2026-07-06 review, and the deconvolution plan. Here is the synthesis.

## Short answer

**The specific confound you're describing — "the BMYO repression is really dead high-MYC BMYO cells, not per-cell repression" — has *not* been directly tested or even articulated anywhere in Block A.** The Issue #1 BMYO-repression finding (script 26) is stated purely as a per-cell/per-state transcriptional program change, with only a generic "association not causation" caveat. It never touches death, selection, or dropout. Meanwhile the whole survivor-bias / compositional-dilution / selective-culling apparatus *does* exist — but it is bolted onto **other compartments** and never connected to BMYO.

## Where the composition/selection question *was* raised — and at what

You yourself flagged the general version in `docs/BlockA_review_discussion.md`:
- Q3: *"impact of MYC on development — changing trajectory changing cell composition — should this be the actual reason for the death-timing explanations?"*
- margin note: *"there MUST be selective culling, and there MUST be change in cell composition, this is why we did the GSVA scoring."*

But every time it was operationalised, it pointed away from BMYO:

| Where | Compartment the confound was applied to | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Issue #6 / script 31 + `deconvolution_subproject_plan.md` | The **proliferative / TEB / luminal-progenitor** compartment shrinking → dilutes the Myc-**fade** | Compositional hint (E2F/prolif co-decline), deferred to deconvolution. A compartment Myc *builds*, not BMYO. |
| Death H4 / scripts 23, 25 | Culling of a **"high-priming, high-imbalance"** susceptible population (defined by the death/mito axes) | "Weakest arm," directional CV-narrowing only |
| Script 25 (the *only* place basal touches death) | `BASAL_comp` entered as one candidate death-coupled axis | **Weakly** coupled (mito imbalance dominates); and basal composition goes *UP* with age in WT, p>0.18 |
| Issue #5 / script 30 | The **luminal** fraction | Confound named, deferred to single-cell |

So the building blocks are all present in separate scripts, but **none is wired to the Issue #1 BMYO result.** The word "BMYO" appears in only one script (26), and "basal" never co-occurs with death in any script.

## What the existing evidence says *against* the BMYO-death route (the bounding argument)

Even though it wasn't tested head-on, four things already on record push against it:

1. **MMTV promoter biology.** The MMTV-LTR drives the MYC transgene in **luminal/secretory** epithelium, not basal/myoepithelium. So "high-MYC BMYO cells" is a weak premise — the high-MYC compartment is luminal. If oncogene-induced death culls the high-MYC cells, it culls *luminal* cells, which would *deplete* the LHS signal. Issue #1 finds the **opposite** (pro-LHS *up*).
2. **The result is reciprocal and coordinated (anti-BMYO *and* pro-LHS).** Pure BMYO dropout would remove BMYO signal but not manufacture a coordinated LHS gain. A per-cell basal→luminal fate shift explains both arms; selective death explains only one.
3. **CHUNG ATAC (script 26).** Myc *closes basal chromatin and opens luminal chromatin* — a within-cell remodeling signature (fate reprogramming), which is direct evidence for a per-cell change rather than loss of a population.
4. **The death-coupled compartment is stem/MASC/biogenesis-high/mitonuclear-imbalanced (scripts 23–25), not differentiated BMYO.** Script 25 finds basal composition rising, not falling, with age — no basal-loss-with-death signature at bulk resolution.

## What it cannot rule out (honest ceiling)

Bulk cannot separate fraction × per-cell. A small high-MYC BMYO subpopulation dying is not *excludable* without single-cell / FACS-sorted basal / BH3-by-state. Notably, the parked deconvolution plan already lists **basal/myoepithelial** as one of the four fractions it would estimate — so the tool that would *quantify* this exists in the plan; it's just currently narrated around the proliferative fraction.

## What the bounding test found

Your BMYO-death confound and the LASP thread resolve cleanly and, importantly, in **opposite directions** — which is the interesting result:

**BMYO repression is per-cell, not death-dropout.** Two independent lenses converge:
- **Off the death axis** — BMYO's per-sample composite is uncoupled from pro-death priming (rho ≈ 0.15/0.13 at 6W/12W; the older `BASAL_comp` is even lower, −0.04). A lineage that death culls has to *sit on* the death-permissive axis; BMYO simply isn't on it.
- **Program not death-gene-rich** — BMYO markers are not enriched for the 512 pro-death genes (OR 0.92, p = 0.81; base rate 0.036).
- Plus two structural facts: MMTV drives MYC in *luminal* epithelium (the high-MYC cells aren't basal), and Myc *closes basal chromatin within cells* (CHUNG ATAC) — a per-cell remodeling signature.

**LASP — your recollection was right, but localized.** As a whole state the interaction is net *positive* (+0.14), which is why the walkthrough had said "near-null." But its **4-set luminal-progenitor arm** (LAPRO / LP_OPEN / ALVSEC / ALVPROG) is where the negative-at-12W signal lives — **all four sets negative** interaction (Myc induces the program +0.31 at 6W, fades to +0.24). And that arm is the **most death-coupled lineage** (rho ≈ 0.87 at 6W) **and pro-death-enriched** (OR 1.60, p = 0.006). So there — unlike BMYO — death-driven dropout of Myc-induced cells **cannot be excluded**. It's exactly the shrinking luminal-progenitor compartment the deconvolution plan already targets.

Pushed (`32a436d`). Here's the interpretation you asked for — the overall hypothesis-proofing, framed exactly as three routes (selection / fading / convergence) and adjudicated per lineage. It's now also in the walkthrough (Issue #1).

## The three routes

Any apparent Myc-driven lineage shift in bulk over 6W→12W can come from three sources, and the machinery now separates them cleanly via the exact identity **`interaction = Myc⁺ trajectory − WT trajectory`** (`int = mycpos_shift − wt_shift`), plus the PART E death lens:

- **Convergence** — the WT background matures and the genotype gap opens/closes with Myc doing nothing per-cell (the `wt_shift` term; same axis as Issue #6).
- **Fading (per-cell)** — the Myc⁺ tissue's own per-cell program moves (`mycpos_shift`): real reprogramming of surviving cells.
- **Selection (dropout)** — part of the Myc⁺ trajectory is loss of a death-primed subpopulation; flagged only where the lineage is death-coupled **and** pro-death-enriched.

## The proof — each lineage lands on a different route

| Lineage / arm | interaction = mycpos − wt | Dominant route | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BMYO** | −0.064 = −0.051 − (+0.013) | **FADING (per-cell)** | WT **flat** → no convergence; **off the death axis** (rho 0.15/0.13, OR 0.92) → selection excluded; powered (p 0.020) + Myc closes basal chromatin per-cell (ATAC WT +0.29 vs Myc −0.33→−0.52). A genuine per-cell de-basalisation. |
| **LASP (state)** | +0.135 = −0.007 − (−0.142) | **CONVERGENCE** | ~100% the WT term — WT loses LASP with age (wt_d −0.68, 79% down) while Myc⁺ stays flat. The "gain" is a mirage of WT falling away. |
| → **LASP progenitor arm** | −0.071 (all 4 sets neg) | **SELECTION candidate** | Most death-coupled arm (rho **0.87**/0.62), pro-death-enriched (OR **1.60**, p 0.006); Myc induces it (+0.31) then the induction **fades** (+0.24) = dropout-compatible. The deconvolution target. |
| **LHS** | +0.322 = +0.190 − (−0.132) | **per-cell GAIN + convergence** | ~59% real Myc induction (mycpos +0.19; ATAC opens ML +0.31 at 12W) + ~41% WT decline. Coupling (0.24→0.73) is secondary — Myc is *driving* hormone-sensing identity, not culling. |

## The overall answer

**No single mechanism carries the lineage reprogramming — the three MEC identities are each dominated by a different route, and that non-uniformity is the result.** Selection survives adjudication in exactly **one** place: the LASP luminal-progenitor arm — which is precisely where the death spine already put the death-permissive compartment (stem/progenitor, not basal or mature-luminal). 

Your original worry is answered directly: **the BMYO repression is *not* dying high-MYC BMYO cells** — BMYO is off the death axis, its program isn't death-gene-rich, MMTV drives MYC in luminal not basal cells, and the ATAC shows a per-cell chromatin change. The dropout concern is real, but it lives in the luminal-progenitor arm instead.

This also cleanly extends **Issue #6**: that decomposition resolved only convergence + fade (no separable selection term) for the mito/metabolic programs; adding the selection axis here shows selection *is* real but **local** — it only surfaces in the progenitor compartment. `e_selection_bound.pdf` is the BMYO-off-axis vs progenitor-on-axis panel; `e_lasp_arm_split.pdf` is the LASP heterogeneity (state positive, progenitor arm negative).

ASSISTANT  2026-07-16 15:11:57

Both combing agents are back and they confirm what I found independently. Here's the answer to your question, then two decisions I need from you.

**Short answer: nothing in the repo measures mitochondrial content, and the one thing that sounds like it doesn't do it.** But the data to answer it properly are already on disk, and when I compute it read-only the answer is interesting and it is *not* the one the paper currently implies.

What's actually there:

- **Script 22's "AP-abund" lens is not an abundance measure.** It computes the SD of mitoPPS Myc-effect diffs across 19 OXPHOS pathways (0.14 at 6W → 0.10 at 12W). That's dispersion of *reallocation*, on ratio-normalised scores. The plan doc's gloss "the selectivity blurs toward uniform biogenesis (an abundance-*like* change)" is doing a lot of work on that "-like".
- **mitoPPS is abundance-blind by construction** — script 08:404 says it "cancels out total mitochondrial content". A mitochondrion with 2× of everything scores identically. So every mitoPPS-based claim (the mitonuclear imbalance included) is silent on content.
- **`total_mito_score` exists** (script 08:1153, subtitle literally "reflects mito content") — it is plotted to a PDF, never saved, never tested. Recomputed: no group differs (myc p=0.999). It's also 68% dominated by the mt-* genes and double-counts overlapping pathways, so it's unusable as written.
- **The one real abundance result** is script 29 Part B: Myc raises nuclear-OXPHOS transcript (d=1.27, p=0.005) and does nothing to mtDNA-encoded (p=0.94). Never generalised beyond OXPHOS subunits.
- **`bio_comp`** — the composite behind "Myc footprint IS a biogenesis program, rho=0.90" — is a mean of GSVA scores over Category-7 sets. Rank-based. It measures *program*, not *organelle*.

So the paper currently says "robust increase in mitochondrial biogenesis" on the basis of enrichment scores, and a reviewer asking your question would land on exactly that gap.

**What the data say when you actually ask.** I computed compartment shares read-only from `count_matrix.rds` (mt-excluded denominator, so the mt-inflation problem below doesn't contaminate it), as % of transcriptome:

| panel | 6W_neg | 6W_pos | 12W_neg | 12W_pos | reads as |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| nuclear MitoCarta (1069 g) | 2.43 | 2.97 | 2.87 | 3.35 | Myc **+22%/+17%** |
| mass markers (VDAC/TOMM20/CS/TSPO…) | 0.095 | 0.122 | 0.103 | 0.128 | Myc **+29%/+24%**, age flat |
| mitoribosome (83 g) | 0.092 | 0.131 | 0.097 | 0.123 | Myc **+42%/+27%** |
| mtDNA-encoded (13 g) | 9.0 | 7.2 | 14.4 | 15.9 | age ~2×, Myc **null/down** |

The mass-marker row is the in-silico version of the TOMM20/VDAC blot you'd otherwise be asked for, and it moves with genotype and not with age. Read together: **Myc does increase mitochondrial content per cell — modestly, ~25% by transcript proxy — but does not scale the organelle's own genome output with it.** That is the mitonuclear imbalance you already have from script 24, except stated in absolute share rather than as a mitoPPS ratio, which is a much harder claim to attack.

**Two things that must be caveated, one of them seriously.** Because Myc is a global amplifier of total RNA per cell, a *share* understates per-cell content — so ~25% is a lower bound, and bulk polyA without spike-ins cannot recover the true scale. More importantly, the mt-* fraction is technically unreliable here: it ranges 3.4%–40% across samples, its SD within 12W_neg is 13 percentage points, and it correlates with library depth (rho −0.47) — which is itself perfectly confounded with timepoint (6W runs 19–29M reads from animals MYCF62-65; 12W runs 10–16M from MYCF52-56, a different cohort). Genotype is litter-controlled and therefore clean; **the time axis is not**. That doesn't overturn the age/mtDNA claim, but it means it needs a QC gate before it goes in a figure, and script 29's "mtDNA absolute z −1.14 → +1.23" inherits the same exposure.

Two decisions before I write the plan.

Done. Script 32 is written, validated read-only, committed and pushed (`50ad21c` on `paper-figures`, tree clean).

**The answer to your question: yes, transcriptomics can assess it — and when you actually ask, Myc raises mitochondrial content by ~27%, but doesn't scale mtDNA with it.**

The reason nobody had answered it is that three separate objects looked like they had. Script 22's "AP-abund" is dispersion of mitoPPS reallocation, not abundance. mitoPPS cancels total mito content by construction, so the mitonuclear imbalance is a *ratio* — a mitochondrion with 2× of everything scores identically. And `total_mito_score`, captioned "reflects mito content", was plotted to a PDF and never saved or tested. Meanwhile `bio_comp`, the composite behind "the Myc footprint IS a biogenesis program", is GSVA — a program score. So the biogenesis headline had no measured referent at all.

**What the script found**, on the genotype axis (QC-clean, all 17 panels leave-one-out stable): mass markers +27% chaperone-free (d=1.34, p=0.003), nuclear MitoCarta +19%, mitoribosome +35%, import +33% — 13 of 14 mass-panel genes moving together. It reproduces script 29's result by a completely different method (nuclear OXPHOS d=1.15 vs 1.27), which is the validation that matters.

**Your two chaperones earned their place and then some.** They're the largest effects in the panel, and because they're also direct MYC targets I split them into their own arm — the claim-bearing number excludes them, so nothing rests on the genes with a confounded route. They also resolved an apparent clash: script 24's "chaperones fall → UPRmt refuted" is a mitoPPS result, and in absolute share the chaperones are Myc-elevated and age-flat. Not a contradiction, and script 24 stands.

**The finding I didn't expect, and the one worth your narrative:** Myc raises the mtDNA *machinery* hardest of anything in the panel — nucleoid d=2.32 (p=8.6e-6), mt-transcription (Tfam/Polrmt/Tfb2m) +43% — while mtDNA-encoded output stays flat. So the mitonuclear imbalance isn't Myc ignoring the mtDNA arm. It commissions the machinery to replicate and read mtDNA, and the output doesn't follow. That's a sharper statement of your existing finding, and mtDNA qPCR is one experiment from making it mechanistic.

**Two things you need to know before the figures.** First, +27% is a **lower bound** — Myc amplifies total RNA per cell, so a flat share would already mean more mitochondria; bulk can't recover the true scale. Second, and more seriously: **timepoint is perfectly confounded with sequencing cohort** (6W is 19–29M reads from animals MYCF62-65; 12W is 10–16M from MYCF52-56; depth ~ timepoint p=4.2e-09), and the mt-share tracks depth. Genotype is clean — depth-balanced and litter-controlled. But every mt-related *temporal* claim is exposed, including Issue #4's "mtDNA absolute z −1.14 → +1.23", which I've flagged in place. It isn't correctable, because no contrast separates timepoint from cohort. It belongs in the methods rather than waiting for a reviewer to find it.

When you're ready to run it: `source("scripts/32_mito_content_proxies.R")` — it prints the verdict and writes `results/mito_content_proxies.rds` plus three PDFs. The sandbox block has inspection lines per part. Figure scripts are 33+ now; still waiting on your narrative.

| MITOCARTA_TRANSCRIPTION (+43%, p=8.5e-5) | | MITOCARTA_MTDNA_NUCLEOID (+22%, d=2.32) | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mrpl12** | **+116%** | **Atad3a** | **+113%** |
| Top1mt | +76% | Poldip2 | +58% |
| Mtres1 | +50% | Polrmt | +18% |
| Polrmt | +18% (p=0.036) | Ssbp1 | +19% (ns) |
| Tfb2m | +16% (ns) | Tfam | +11% (ns) |
| **Tfam** | **+11% (ns)** | **Polg** | **+3% (ns)** |
| Mterf1a/1b | ~0 (ns) | **Twnk** | **+1% (ns)** |
| | | **Polg2** | **−9% (ns)** |

Both set-level effects are carried entirely by members whose assignment to "transcription"/"nucleoid" is loose and which Myc induces for other reasons — Mrpl12 is a mitoribosomal protein, Atad3a and Poldip2 are multifunctional. The *actual* core machinery — Tfam, Polg, Polg2, Twnk — barely moves. So "the machinery to make and read mtDNA is built" is not supported.

**And the tempting replacement is also unsupported.** I tested whether Myc specifically *spares* the mtDNA machinery: the 8-gene core sits at the **39th percentile** of the 934-gene nuclear-MitoCarta distribution, Wilcoxon **p=0.12**. Not a distinguishable module. I'm not going to sell you a second story to replace the first.

**What actually survives is cleaner, and it's a better answer to your question.** The nuclear mitochondrial compartment rises by a median **+21%** — and the mtDNA-dedicated machinery rises with it, unremarkably. Yet mtDNA-encoded output does not move (+6%, p=0.83). So the imbalance is **not attributable to any transcript-level deficit anywhere in the machinery**. Nothing in the transcriptome is the bottleneck. That's an informative negative: it relocates the cause downstream of transcript abundance — mtDNA copy number, transcription rate, or turnover — and it makes mtDNA qPCR not just a nice-to-have but *the* discriminating experiment.

To your literal question — is there another gene following the mtDNA pattern — the honest first-pass answer is that the machinery doesn't, and a proper transcriptome-wide search is worth doing but has a trap: the mt-share is depth-confounded, so anything co-varying with it will surface the RNA-quality module unless partial correlation against depth is built in from the start.

Confirmed — and I need to correct myself again. **You're right, and my depth framing doesn't survive contact with the data.**

Three things, all of which I should have checked before writing that warning:

**1. Depth cannot mechanically drive a share.** The mt fraction is a proportion — sequence twice as deep and numerator and denominator both double. DESeq2's median-of-ratios cancels depth, and my `share_nomt` ratios cancel it exactly too. There is no route by which depth *causes* mt%. I wrote "the mt share tracks depth" as though it were a mechanism; it can't be one.

**2. Within a cohort, depth predicts nothing.** 6W: rho=−0.056, p=0.87. 12W: rho=−0.315, p=0.32. The alarming rho=−0.469 across all 24 is *entirely* the gap between two clouds that differ in both depth and mt% — pooling artifact, not signal.

**3. The evidence actually points away from a quality problem.** If 12W were degraded you'd expect *less* complex libraries. Top-100 share is **31.0% at 12W vs 40.2% at 6W** — 12W libraries are more even, not less. The lower detected-gene count at 12W (23,255 vs 24,599) is just what lower depth gives you. I cited "12W is degraded" as the worry and the one metric that bears on it argues the opposite.

**You were right, and the short answer is: yes, DESeq2 accounts for depth — and so do my shares, for the same reason.** A share is `colSums(panel)/colSums(all)`. Sequence twice as deep and both halves double. Depth cancels by construction, exactly as median-of-ratios cancels it. So depth **cannot** be a confound for either, and I wrote a warning around a mechanism that doesn't exist.

When I actually tested it: within 6W, depth-vs-mt% rho = −0.056 (p=0.87); within 12W, −0.315 (p=0.32). Nothing. at 6W -- MORE even). What IS true: the depth ranges are DISJOINT (6W 19-29M vs 12W
10-16M) so batch is perfectly aligned with timepoint and not separable -- inherent to
any cross-sectional design, and genotype is unaffected (depth ~ timepoint p=4.2e-09 vs
~ genotype p=0.41) -- and the mt share is HIGH-VARIANCE (3.4-40.1% across samples). So
temporal mt numbers, incl. script 29's mtDNA z rise, are IMPRECISE and COHORT-ALIGNED,
NOT uninterpretable. CEILING: shares, not per-cell content; Myc's global RNA
amplification makes the share a LOWER BOUND; blot/qPCR/EM settles it.

**First, directly: it is not contamination.** A confounder has to track the exposure. Stromal content doesn't differ by genotype (p=0.45), nor does epithelial content (p=0.38). Composition therefore *cannot* manufacture a spurious Myc effect. And the content result survives full adjustment for both compartments:

- nuclear OXPHOS +28.4% → **+19.7% (p=0.002)**
- nuclear MitoCarta +18.9% → **+13.5% (p=0.003)**
- mass markers +26.5% → **+19.5% (p=0.0002)**

So **the answer to your original question stands: Myc raises mitochondrial content.** That's real, it survives everything I've thrown at it, and composition is noise, not bias.

**But look what adjustment does to the mtDNA arm:** +5.9% (p=0.83) → **+25.3% (p=0.24)**. Once composition noise is absorbed, mtDNA rises *as much as the nuclear arms*. And when I test the imbalance as what it actually is — a **difference**, nuclear minus mtDNA per sample:

- raw: beta = +0.277, **p=0.57**
- composition-adjusted: beta = −0.066, **p=0.82**

**Not significant either way.** I built the claim by comparing a significant p-value to a non-significant one and calling that a difference. That is the most common statistical error there is, and I made it in the headline of the script and in three places in the docs. "Nuclear is p=0.009 and mtDNA is p=0.83" does **not** mean they differ — the mtDNA estimate is so noisy (CV 1.19, driven by exactly the composition variance we just found) that its interval comfortably contains the nuclear effect.

**So, precisely, to answer what you asked:**

*Should the mitonuclear imbalance be abandoned?* **No — but script 32 gives it no support, and I claimed it did.** The imbalance's actual home is script 24's mitoPPS `mtnuc_index` (a within-sample *ratio*, a different metric with a different noise structure) and the mitoPPS-vs-absolute reconciliation in 29. My "restatement in absolute share" was an overreach that fails on its own test. What collapses is *my addition*, not the original finding. The original is neither confirmed nor refuted here — script 32 simply lacks the precision to speak to it at n=6.

*Is it an artefact of contamination?* **No.** Composition is genotype-balanced, so it can't bias the contrast. What it does is inject enormous variance into the mt measurement — which is *why* the mt arm is underpowered, and why an absolute-share test of the imbalance can't work in this dataset.

One thing I do want to flag rather than bury: script 24's imbalance is a ratio *within* each sample, so it's partially protected from composition — but not immune, since a composition shift changes the mt:nuclear ratio if the compartments differ between cell types. Given how large the composition variance is here, that's worth checking directly rather than assuming. I'm not going to assert either way; I've now been wrong three times by doing exactly that.

**The pattern in all three errors is the same**: I asserted a comparison without running the test the comparison requires — set-level → mechanism without opening the sets, correlation → confound without asking if depth could act, and now significant-vs-nonsignificant → difference without testing the difference. Each time it took your question to surface it.

What I'd propose: retract the imbalance claim from script 32 and reduce it to what it can support — **Myc raises mitochondrial content ~20% (composition-adjusted, robust)**, with the mtDNA arm reported as *underpowered, direction unresolved*. **Nuclear genes *do* respond to contamination — in the opposite direction.**

| | vs endothelial contamination |
|---|---|
| nuclear MitoCarta | **−0.47** (p=0.023) |
| nuclear OXPHOS | **−0.62** (p=0.002) |
| mass markers | **−0.55** (p=0.006) |
| **mt%** | **+0.75** (p<0.0001) |

Nuclear MEC genes go *down* as contamination rises — that's simple dilution, exactly what mixing predicts. mt% goes *up*. **Mixing cannot produce opposite signs.** And the arithmetic independently kills it: the contamination is only ~3–12% of cells, so to drag mt% from 3.4% to 40.1% the contaminating cells would need an mt-share of **187–737%**. Impossible.

**What it actually is: dissociation/sorting stress.** The immediate-early gene signature (Fos, Jun, Egr1, Junb, Atf3, Hspa1a — the canonical dissociation artifact) tracks mt% at **rho +0.74 overall, +0.87 within 6W**. Adding stress + contamination lifts the R² for mt% from **0.23 to 0.72**. Contamination and stress correlate with each other (+0.68) because both are readouts of the same thing: how hard that prep was. This is the standard scRNA-seq "high mt% = stressed/dying cell" phenomenon — cytoplasmic mRNA leaks from permeabilised cells while mitochondrial transcripts stay inside the organelle — and it applies to bulk sorted MECs too.

**So mt% here is a viability/prep-quality metric, not a mitochondrial-biology metric.**

**Your content result is safe.** Neither stress (p=0.49) nor contamination (p=0.43) tracks genotype — they're noise, not bias — and every content claim survives adjusting for both, with better p-values: mass markers **+21.1% (p=0.0006)**, nuclear MitoCarta **+14.9% (p=0.004)**, nuclear OXPHOS **+21.9% (p=0.004)**.

**But there's a serious consequence, and I want to state it plainly rather than bury it: stress *is* timepoint-associated (p=0.0003).** And the mt-encoded transcript signal is what the entire "nuclear-led assembly at 6W → mtDNA-completed running at 12W" story is built on:

- script 22's raw mtDNA doubling 6W→12W
- script 29's mtDNA absolute z −1.14 → +1.23
- script 24's `mtnuc_index` — the mitonuclear imbalance itself, which peaks at 6W_pos and inverts by 12W

All three read mt-encoded transcript levels across a timepoint axis on which prep stress differs at p=0.0003. That doesn't prove they're artifacts — I've been wrong three times today by making exactly that leap — but it means the mitonuclear imbalance now has a live alternative explanation that has never been tested, and it's testable directly: does `mtnuc_index` survive adjustment for the stress signature?

**Also flagging a documentation gap that caused this:** CLAUDE.md describes the project as "Bulk RNA-seq of MMTV-Myc transgenic mice" and never mentions MEC purification. I read the stromal signal as tissue composition because nothing told me otherwise — and with purified MECs it means something completely different. That belongs in CLAUDE.md.

That's the decisive test, and it's the one nobody ran — including me until just now.

**The mitonuclear imbalance correlates with *everything* at ~0.6.**

The published "imbalance couples to pro-apoptotic priming, r=0.75, p=0.005" is not evidence of a mito→death mechanism — it's what this dataset returns for an arbitrary pairing, because the imbalance is 73% the mt% metric and mt% is the dominant sample-level axis that most of the transcriptome loads on.

**Direct answer to your question:** the negative sign doesn't exclude the prep explanation, and it doesn't support a biological one either — because the sign isn't specific to death. 75% of *all* gene sets move the same way on this axis. There's no death-specific phenomenon to explain, so the "stress should increase priming" expectation never gets traction. What looked like a mechanism is one arbitrary slice of a global axis.

And this is a mistake the project already knows how to avoid: script 21 built a permutation null for exactly this reason on the fGSEA side (AP6). The sample-level death couplings in scripts 23/25 never got one. That's the gap.

Two things I want to flag about my own reasoning before you act on this: my "global compression" story from a moment ago doesn't have a clean mechanism (`share_nomt` excludes mt from both numerator and denominator, so arithmetic displacement can't explain it), and I don't actually know whether the IEG/mt axis is technical or biological — genotype-independent (p=0.49) says it can't bias your Myc results, time-associated (p=0.0003) says it entangles the time story, and with no sort metadata I can't classify it. The null result above stands regardless of which it is: **specificity fails either way.**

Building script 33 now — the null is the centrepiece, since that's the test that decides whether any of these couplings mean anything.

**Your question was the one that broke it open, and the answer is: it isn't contamination — but it isn't mitochondria either.**

The asymmetry you spotted is the whole thing. Nuclear MEC genes track contamination **negatively** (−0.47 to −0.62 — dilution, exactly as mixing predicts). mt% tracks it **positively** (+0.75). Mixing cannot produce opposite signs. And the arithmetic independently kills it: contamination is only ~3–12% of cells, so mixing would need a contaminant with an mt-share of **126–737%**. What mt% *does* track is a dominant sample-level axis marked by the canonical dissociation IEG signature (rho **+0.87** within 6W; mt% R² 0.26 → 0.72). In FACS-sorted MECs that reads as prep quality — and the direction test settles it independently: **if mt% measured mitochondrial content, nuclear mito genes would rise with it. All four fall.**

**But the result that matters is the one I found while building this, and it's worse than the mt axis.** Script 25 Part B's death couplings never had a null. Against all 884 library sets at 6W:

| coupling to pro_comp | rho | null median | perm p | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mitonuclear imbalance | +0.67 | +0.62 | **0.49** | not specific |
| **bio_comp** | **+0.83** | **+0.79** | **0.50** | **not specific** |
| MASC_comp | +0.78 | +0.57 | 0.10 | marginal |
| IEG/prep-stress axis | −0.78 | −0.55 | **0.03** | **beats the null** |

Read the `bio_comp` row: 0.83 looks compelling until the null median is 0.79. At n=12, 73–81% of *all* gene sets couple at |rho|>0.5. **The only axis that beats the null is the prep signature itself.** The published ordering (bio > MASC > imbalance) survives — but it's the ordering of an arbitrary draw. And this holds whether the axis is technical or biological, so it doesn't wait on an adjudication I can't make.

The project already knew to do this. Script 21 built exactly this null for fGSEA. Nobody applied it per-sample.

**What's safe:** the axis is genotype-independent (p=0.49), so it cannot bias a Myc contrast. Your content result retains 79–81% with *better* p-values after adjusting for stress and contamination (mass markers +21%, **p=0.0006**). Issues #1/#2/#3/#5/#6 stand.

All four land, and the first one is a real logical catch — **my "direction test" is circular and I need to withdraw it.**

Let me take them in order, then fix the script.

**1. You're right, and it invalidates leg (a) of PART A.** I argued: *if mt% measured mitochondrial content, nuclear mito genes would rise with it; they fall; therefore mt% isn't mitochondrial.* But that reasoning **presupposes there is no imbalance**. The mitonuclear imbalance is precisely the claim that mt-encoded and nuclear-encoded dissociate — so finding them anticorrelated is what the imbalance *predicts*, not evidence against it. I used the absence of the phenomenon as proof the measurement is broken. Circular, and it's stated as a headline in the script you just ran. What survives from PART A is the arithmetic and the asymmetry — which refute **contamination**, not a mitochondrial reading. So: **PART A does not establish that mt% is non-mitochondrial, and the imbalance is not refuted by it.** Only the PART C null stands, and I deliberately built that to be independent of this question — which is now doing more work than I realised.

**2. The TEB idea is a good hypothesis and it's cleanly refuted — on direction and timing both.**

| | rho |
|---|---|
| IEG ~ proliferation | **−0.62** (all), **−0.76** (6W) |
| IEG ~ TEB sets | −0.57 / −0.59 |
| IEG ~ MYC activity | −0.41 |

IEG group means: 6W **0.72 / 0.60** → 12W **1.03 / 1.02**. A TEB/growth-factor story predicts IEGs *high* at 6W (pubertal, TEB-rich) and *positively* coupled to proliferation. Both are backwards. So IEGs here aren't growth signalling — and the fact that they *anticorrelate* with the proliferative biology is what you'd expect from an overlay sitting on top of it rather than part of it.

**3. Enzymatic dissociation only, no FACS — I'll correct it, and you're right that it doesn't change the direction, but it does sharpen it.** The van den Brink artifact is specifically about warm enzymatic digestion, so the IEG reading gets *stronger*, not weaker. And without a sort, "purified" is weaker than I assumed — which fits the 3–12% residual stroma rather than contradicting it.

**4. Your surprise is the sharpest thing in this message, and it has a structural answer.**

Within 6W (n=12), **PC1 explains 42.8%** of the variance — and everything loads on it:

| PC1 ~ | rho |
|---|---|
| IEG | −0.71 |
| proliferation | +0.62 |
| endothelial (contamination) | −0.62 |
| MYC activity | +0.59 |
| mt% | −0.51 |

**They aren't different signals. They're one signal, viewed from five angles.** That is *why* everything correlates with everything at 0.6–0.8, and it's the structural reason the null comes out flat — not a quirk of the death sets. One axis at 42.8% with n=12 means pairwise correlations between composites carry almost no information about specific mechanisms.

And note what loads on it: contamination (which *cannot* be biological — it's residual stroma in the prep) sits at −0.62 alongside proliferation at +0.62. So PC1 is **mixed** — part prep-yield, part real biology. I can't cleanly call it technical, and I shouldn't have implied I could.

Fixing the script now.

Committed and pushed (`1f59118`). Your four points, resolved:

**1. Your logical catch stands, and I've withdrawn the claim.** The direction test was circular: I used "nuclear and mt-encoded should move together" as a test, when the mitonuclear imbalance *is* the hypothesis that they don't. **PART A no longer claims mt% is non-mitochondrial, and it does not refute the imbalance.** What survives is narrower: mt% is not *contamination* (the arithmetic and your asymmetry), and it tracks an IEG-marked axis. mt% may well be the mtDNA arm of a real imbalance whose between-sample variation happens to ride that axis — bulk can't separate those. The null in PART C is untouched, because I built it independent of this question; it's now carrying more weight than I designed it to.

**2. TEB was a good hypothesis and it fails cleanly** — on direction (IEG ~ proliferation **−0.76** within 6W; TEB predicts positive) and on timing (IEGs **lower** at 6W, 0.72/0.60, than 12W, 1.03/1.02; TEB predicts higher at the pubertal timepoint). IEGs anticorrelate with the proliferative biology rather than being part of it.

**3. Enzymatic dissociation, not FACS — corrected in all four places.** You're right it doesn't change the direction, and it slightly sharpens it: warm enzymatic digest is exactly the protocol van den Brink characterised, so the IEG reading strengthens, while "purified" weakens — which fits the 3–12% residual stroma rather than contradicting it.

**4. Your surprise had a structural answer, and it's the most useful thing here.** Within 6W, **PC1 is 43% of the variance and everything loads on it**: IEG −0.71, proliferation +0.62, contamination −0.62, MYC +0.59, mt% −0.51. They aren't different signals — they're one signal seen from five angles. That's *why* the null comes out flat, and it isn't a property of the death sets at all. It also means the axis is **mixed**: contamination can't be biological, proliferation can, and both load on it. So I can't call it technical, and I've stopped implying I can.

**What's actually left standing after all of this:** your content result (Myc +21%, p=0.0006, genotype-clean), the contamination refutation, and the PART C null. The mitonuclear imbalance is **not refuted** — it's untested, because at n=12 with one 43% axis, the couplings that were offered as evidence for it can't discriminate anything.

That's five errors today, and the pattern is now unmistakable: every one was a test whose premise I hadn't checked, and every one was caught by you asking a plain question rather than by my own validation. This last one is the sharpest version — I built a test that the hypothesis under study already predicted would fail. I've written that down as its own check.

Script 33 needs a re-source; the verdict is rewritten and it now saves `dominant_axis`, `ieg_teb_test`, and `mt_vs_nuclear_anticorrelation` (explicitly labelled *not* a direction test).

ASSISTANT  2026-07-16 23:47:26

Both questions have clean answers, and they go in opposite directions.

**First, two corrections to your framing.**

"12W more stressed" is right (IEG 0.72/0.60 → 1.03/1.02, p=0.0003). But **"which determines PC1" isn't** — and your instinct to check script 02 was the right one. The original QC PCA (all 24 samples, `plotPCA` top-500) gives **PC1 = 35%, and it is not timepoint (p=0.81), not genotype (p=0.96), and not IEG (rho=−0.18, p=0.40).** My PC1 was computed *within* 6W only — a different analysis at a different level. So globally the dominant axis is *none* of the things we've been discussing, which is its own uncomfortable fact about this dataset.

**Q1 — does the batch difference cause the attenuation? No. Tested three ways, and the attenuation comes out protected.**

| | 6W | 12W |
|---|---|---|
| median within-group SD | 0.3515 | **0.2935** (ratio 0.83) |
| median lfcSE (Myc contrast) | 0.251 | **0.259** |
| median \|LFC\| | 0.268 | **0.204** |
| genes padj<0.05 | 1967 | 135 |

1. **IEG is genotype-independent (p=0.49)**, so a batch offset cancels inside each timepoint's Myc-vs-WT contrast — it can't bias either endpoint of the attenuation.
2. **12W is not noisier — it's slightly *less* variable**, and the standard errors are essentially identical (0.251 vs 0.259, 3% apart). So the DE collapse 1967 → 135 is **not** a power artifact.
3. The collapse tracks the **|LFC| falling** (0.268 → 0.204, a real 24% shrink) at constant SE. That's genuine magnitude attenuation.

This is the one piece of good news in two days: **Issue #4's attenuation is not touched by any of this.**

**Q2 — and here the answer is the opposite of your premise. The imbalance does not "still stand" — it was never tested.**

`imbalance ~ timepoint * genotype`, per sample:

| term | beta | p |
|---|---|---|
| timepoint | −0.586 | **0.313** |
| genotype | +0.368 | **0.523** |
| interaction | −0.085 | **0.916** |
| Myc effect at 6W alone | +0.368 | **0.249** |

**Nothing is significant on any term.** The pattern everyone quotes — 0.130 / 0.499 / −0.456 / −0.173, "peaks at 6W_pos, inverts by 12W" — is **four group means that were reported descriptively and never subjected to a contrast**. When you fit one, there's nothing there. And adding IEG removes the time term entirely (−0.586 → −0.011).

So your sentence has to split in two: the death coupling failing the null is one problem, and the imbalance lacking any statistical support of its own is a *separate, prior* one. It isn't that the imbalance stands but fails to couple to death — **it's that neither half was ever tested, and both fail when they are.**

**The honest qualifier:** n=6/group and mitoPPS values are noisy, so this is *unsupported*, not *refuted*. The pattern could be real and underpowered. But it cannot be reported as a finding on this evidence, and "peaks at 6W_pos, inverts by 12W" reads as a demonstrated effect when it's a description of four averages with p=0.31 between them.

Want me to add both of these to script 33 — the imbalance's own statistics (which is where the claim should have been tested all along) and the attenuation-is-not-batch check (which protects Issue #4)? They belong in the record rather than in this conversation, and the second one is worth having written down given how much else has moved.

       null_for_axis <- function(x, label, idx = i6) {
         r_sets <- apply(scores[, idx, drop = FALSE], 1,
                         function(s) suppressWarnings(stats::cor(s, x[idx], method = "spearman")))
         r_sets <- r_sets[is.finite(r_sets)]
         r_obs  <- suppressWarnings(stats::cor(ds$pro_comp[idx], x[idx], method = "spearman"))
         tibble::tibble(axis = label, rho_vs_pro_comp = r_obs,
           null_median = stats::median(r_sets), ...
           perm_p = mean(abs(r_sets) >= abs(r_obs)),
           verdict = dplyr::case_when(
             mean(abs(r_sets) >= abs(r_obs)) > 0.10 ~ "NOT SPECIFIC (any gene set does this)",
             mean(abs(r_sets) >= abs(r_obs)) > 0.05 ~ "marginal",
             TRUE ~ "beats the null"))
       }

While those trace the code, here's the direct answer to your first question, read off `scripts/33_mtdna_axis_and_coupling_null.R:278-294`.

## 1. How the null is calculated

**It is entirely within 6W. It never touches the 6W→12W axis.**

```r
null_for_axis <- function(x, label, idx = i6) {
  r_sets <- apply(scores[, idx], 1, function(s) cor(s, x[idx], method="spearman"))
  r_obs  <- cor(ds$pro_comp[idx], x[idx], method="spearman")
  perm_p = mean(abs(r_sets) >= abs(r_obs))
```

`i6` is the 12 six-week samples (`33:132`). For a candidate axis X (the imbalance, `bio_comp`, `mt_pct`…), it correlates X across those 12 animals against each of the 884 GSVA-scored library sets, then asks where the *published* coupling — X vs the pro-death composite — falls in that distribution.

Three things are worth being precise about, because they bound what the failure means:

**It is a competitive/specificity null, not a permutation.** Nothing is shuffled. The question is not "is r=0.75 bigger than chance" but "is `pro_comp` special *among gene sets* in how it tracks X". The answer is no: the null median is +0.62 for the imbalance and **+0.79 for `bio_comp`** — i.e. the observed 0.83 is at the median. This is the same logic `scripts/21_ap6_permutation_null.R` applied to fGSEA, transplanted to per-sample composites.

**The null distribution is not centred on zero, and that's the finding.** Within 6W, PC1 = 43% of variance and every measure loads on it (`33:365-384`). With one dominant axis at n=12, 73–81% of *all* sets couple at |rho|>0.5. So the flat null is structural, not a quirk of the death sets.

**The consequence for your second question: the null falsifies a cross-sectional statement, not a longitudinal one.** What died is "*across 6W animals, the more mitonuclear-imbalanced ones are the more death-primed ones*" — a between-animal, single-timepoint claim. The null says nothing whatsoever about whether death priming *changes* from 6W to 12W, because it was never computed on that contrast.

**A gap I should flag now:** the walkthrough's claim has two halves — coupling 0.75 at 6W and *collapse* to 0.07 at 12W. Only the 6W half was null-tested (`idx = i6` for every call at `33:296-301`). The collapse is arguably the more distinctive half, and by Fisher's z the 0.75→0.07 difference at n=12/12 is itself only p≈0.06. That test doesn't exist on disk either way.

# 2. The death-priming change

**Headline: the death-priming *change* is the mitonuclear imbalance's error repeated — four group means quoted as a change whose contrast was never significant. What survives is a genotype main effect: Myc raises apoptotic priming at 6W. That it *falls* by 12W is not supported by this RNA-seq.**

## First, a correction that matters for your question

**`r=0.75, p=0.005` is not in script 25.** It's `23_death_timing_substrate.R:326-327` (Pearson). Script 25 Part B recomputes it as Spearman and gets **0.671, with no p-value at all** (`25:140-148` calls `stats::cor`, not `cor.test`). Script 33's header (`33:270`) attributes it to 25. The null tested the Spearman 0.67, so the null itself is sound — but the famous number and the null-tested number are from different scripts and different methods.

## What every test of the *change* actually says

| test | statistical unit | result |
|---|---|---|
| Per-sample composite interaction (`23:162-167`) | n=24 `lm` | PRO **int p=0.177**; priming **p=0.263**; ANTI 0.953; p53 0.799 |
| fGSEA on the real DESeq2 interaction (`12:158`) | gene ranks | CD_Apoptosis NES −0.944, **padj=0.914**; all 15 modalities padj>0.12 |
| Branch-1 binomial (`16:133`) | gene signs | 52.7%, **p=0.273** |
| CAMERA/ROAST on apoptosis sets (`17:367-383`) | correlation-aware | **nothing at FDR** |
| **Gate 2** (`14:91`) | one-sample t, 23 genes | **p=0.023** ← the sole positive |

**Four of five methods return null, and the one positive is the least rigorous instrument in the set.** Gate 2 is a one-sample t-test treating 23 genes as independent draws. Script 17 *measured* the inter-gene correlation in these library sets at 0.25–0.36. At rho≈0.3, the effective n for 23 genes is roughly 23/(1+22×0.3) ≈ **3**, not 23. This is precisely the error that CAMERA was brought into script 17 to fix — and when the correlation-aware version of this same question was run, it found nothing. Gate 2 also reports only **1 of 23 genes** individually significant, with mean interaction LFC −0.130.

The "**~3x more at 6W**" (walkthrough:726) is group means **+0.48 vs +0.15** — the difference is `int_p=0.177/0.263`. **Never tested as a difference.** That is retraction #3 and the imbalance's E1 failure, a third time.

## Three structural problems, beyond the null

**1. The coupling is circular.** `pro_comp` is `MITOCARTA_APOPTOSIS_PRO` — 25 hand-curated **mitochondrial** apoptosis genes (`08_mitoPPS_analysis.R:285-290`: Bax, Bbc3, Bid, Cycs, Diablo, Bnip3…). The imbalance is a mitoPPS ratio. "The mitochondrial state couples to death priming" is **mitochondrial genes correlating with mitochondrial genes**. Your own Issue #3 log flagged this (`2026-07-08_BlockA_revision_plan.md:236`: *"priming mito-defined (mito↔priming partly circular)"*) — it was never applied to the death spine itself. This is independent of the null and arguably deeper.

**2. The Tang NES −1.38 is a shared developmental decline, not a Myc effect.** The walkthrough cites `temporal_pos NES −1.38 (padj 0.016)` as death-spine evidence. But **`temporal_neg` is −1.31** — WT declines essentially as much. By Issue #6's own exact identity, a decline shared by both genotypes **cancels in the genotype gap** and cannot produce an attenuation.

**3. The "selective decoupling" is selective to the uninformative axis.** prolif~death is invariant (0.68→0.65), bio~death barely moves (0.77→0.56), and only imbalance~death collapses (0.75→0.07). H3 was read as *"the timing is mito-specific, not generic proliferation."* The one axis that collapses is the one that fails the null.

## What this leaves — and the mechanism

**Survives, powered, genotype-based** (hence protected by the IEG axis's genotype-independence, p=0.49): **Myc raises pro-apoptotic priming** — PRO +0.278 (p=0.037), PRO−ANTI +0.317 (p=0.038), myc_6W PRO +0.20 (p=0.041) — and the rheostat is **BCL2-family, not p53** (p53/ARF null). That is canonical Myc-induced apoptosis, and it is real here.

**The mechanistic reframe: the paper is running two different mitochondria together.**

- **(i) mitochondrion-as-biosynthetic-organelle** — content +21–27%, OXPHOS, biogenesis. Solid, new, genotype-powered.
- **(ii) mitochondrion-as-apoptotic-gateway** — BH3/BCL2 rheostat, MOMP, PUMA/Bbc3, Bax.

The bridge assumed **(i) causes (ii)**. Nothing supports that. But **(ii) doesn't need (i)**: Evan/Lowe Myc biology is that Myc sensitises to apoptosis through BH3-only proteins directly. Your data already point there — `Bbc3`/PUMA is the one gene moving in the right direction on the interaction (myc6 +0.26 → myc12 −0.28, **z=−2.6**, padj 0.84).

**So the parsimonious mechanism, consistent with everything that survives:** priming is *part of* the Myc program; the Myc program attenuates ~66% fade + ~34% WT-convergence (Issue #6); priming attenuates with it. No death-specific gate, no mitochondrial-state mechanism. **This predicts the death attenuation is not in excess of the global attenuation — and that has never been tested.** It's the single most decisive test available, and the data are on disk.

You're right, and the challenge lands. The within-6W null is the correct null for the claim *"at 6W the imbalance couples to priming"* — but that is **not your question**. Your question has two parts, and the 6W null addresses neither:

- **"Does increased priming at 6W collapse at 12W?"** — that's a *level* question (a genotype×time interaction on priming). No null needed; the contrast exists and is null (`int_p=0.263`). The 6W null is simply irrelevant to it.
- **"Does the collapse correlate with mitochondrial reprioritisation?"** — that's a question about two *changes*, which the 6W null cannot see.

So the null needs rethinking, and here is the specific hole your question exposes:

**The collapse `0.75 → 0.07` was never null-tested, and there is an obvious confound nobody checked.** If the ambient correlation structure differs between the timepoints — PC1 is 43% *within 6W*, and **PC1 within 12W was never computed** — then *every* gene set's coupling would collapse from 6W to 12W, and the imbalance's collapse would mean nothing. Script 33's own numbers make this testable in one line: the null median at 6W is +0.62. If the null median at 12W is ~0.15, the "collapse" is just the ambient correlation collapsing.

The right null for a claimed collapse is a **Δrho null**: for each of the 884 sets compute `Δ = rho_6W(X, set) − rho_12W(X, set)`, and locate the observed `Δ` in that distribution. That extends `null_for_axis()` to the longitudinal claim, which is what your question actually asks.

One structural limit I have to state plainly: **the design is cross-sectional — different animals at 6W and 12W.** There is no within-animal Δ. So "the priming collapse correlates with mito reprioritisation" is not estimable per-sample at all; it can only ever be two 4-point group trajectories moving together, which carries no inference. What *is* estimable is whether the two share a genotype×time interaction — and both are null (priming 0.263, imbalance 0.916).

Let me write the plan with the corrected null design.

Committed as `34361ea`, working tree clean. I haven't pushed — say the word if you want it on `origin/paper-figures`.

## The verdict you asked to wait for

**Your challenge was right, and following it through has taken the death arm apart.** The corrected null gives a sharper answer than the 6W one, but not in the direction the manuscript needs.

**On your first question — is priming increased at 6W?** The composite rises (geno p=0.017/0.037). But `pro_comp` **is `MITOCARTA_APOPTOSIS_PRO`** — 25 mitochondrial genes. Script 32 established Myc raises nuclear MitoCarta ~19% wholesale, so *any* MitoCarta subset rises whatever its label. Tested against an expression-matched **MitoCarta** background, APOPTOSIS_PRO rises **+0.196 vs +0.364 (z = −2.42, p = 0.012)** — *below average for a mitochondrial gene*. On the 404 **non-mito** pro-death genes the effect doesn't reproduce at all (−0.106, p=0.078, wrong sign). The composite goes up because its genes are mitochondrial, not because they're pro-apoptotic. This independently reproduces script 23's own mitoPPS finding (Apoptosis-PRO de-prioritised −0.21, padj 0.022) — the walkthrough filed that as a "two-lens nuance" beside the priming claim; it's better read as the *explanation* of it.

**On your second question — does it collapse at 12W?** The interaction is null: **PRO p=0.177, priming p=0.263**. Those numbers have been sitting in `death_timing_substrate.rds$h1$state_tests` since script 23 was written. The narrative quoted the group means instead (+0.48 vs +0.15, "~3x more at 6W"). That's the retracted-error pattern a third time — and the worst instance, because here the test already existed on disk.

**On whether the collapse tracks mitochondrial reprioritisation** — the honest answer is that it *isn't estimable*. The design is cross-sectional: 6W and 12W are different animals, so no within-animal Δ exists. Any such correlation could only be two 4-point group trajectories co-moving. Both interactions are null anyway (priming 0.263, imbalance 0.916).

**Where I'd resist over-correcting.** The Δrho null gives the death arm its best showing of anything so far: the collapse sits at the **96th percentile** (perm p=0.066), Fisher z p=0.055 — two independent tests converging at p≈0.06. That is *marginal, not null*, and far better than the 6W coupling (p=0.49) ever was. But it's **Pearson-only** (Spearman p=0.31, so it rides outliers at n=12), it fails multiplicity, and it **evaporates on every non-mito death axis** (p=0.19–0.92). The only axis that gets that far is the circular one. Context: the median gene set's coupling already falls **0.71 → 0.35** across this window while **PC1 is unchanged (43% → 46%)** — so "12W has less structure" is *not* the explanation, yet everything decouples anyway.

**The mechanism.** Nothing attenuates more than expression-matched genes — not death, not OXPHOS (z=0.90), not the MYC core (z=0.29), all BH p>0.14. The comparators failing is the control that *validates* the test: Issue #4's attenuation is global. So **priming fades because the Myc programme fades** — canonical Evan/Lowe Myc-induced apoptosis through BH3-only proteins. No death-specific gate, no mitochondrial-state gate, and none needed.

The paper is running **two different mitochondria** together: the biosynthetic organelle (content +21–27%, solid) and the apoptotic gateway (BH3/MOMP/PUMA). The bridge assumed the first causes the second. The second never needed the first — and `Bbc3`/PUMA is still the one gene moving correctly on the interaction (z=−2.6, padj 0.84).

**On the framing you deferred:** the RNA-seq should claim *no* death result. The phenotype is external and untouched; the 6W-vs-12W timing rests entirely on it; **BH3 profiling** is the experiment, and it measures the gateway directly and independently of the content claim. That makes your experiments the payoff rather than a confirmation.

Two things for you: **re-source script 23 first** — the saved `death_timing_substrate.rds` is stale (9-row convergence table vs the committed script's 11, so Parts 2b/5b have never run) — then source 34.

One correction to my own process: my read-only harness leaked on the first pass. `ggplot2::ggsave` is namespaced and my override didn't catch it, so three PDFs really were written to `outputs/` before I noticed. I patched the binding inside the namespace, confirmed the blocks, and removed the strays; `results/` was never touched and the tree is clean. The ceiling stands throughout — at n=6/group, **unsupported is not refuted**.

AMBIENT-CORRELATION DIAGNOSTIC -- AND IT IS NOT WHAT PC1 WOULD HAVE TOLD YOU. PC1 is
43% of variance within 6W vs 46% within 12W -- essentially UNCHANGED, so 'the 12W
cohort has less structure' is NOT the explanation. But the ambient COUPLING level
collapses anyway: the imbalance's couplings to ALL 884 library sets have median |r|
0.71 at 6W vs 0.35 at 12W, and 74% vs 11% of sets exceed |r|=0.5. So at 6W almost
everything correlates with almost everything and by 12W most of that is gone. ANY
axis's coupling to ANY set collapses over this window. That is the baseline the
published r 0.75 -> 0.07 must be judged against, and it is why PART B compares the SIZE
of the collapse to the size of an arbitrary set's collapse rather than asking whether a
collapse happened.

THE COLLAPSE NULL (the test the claim never had) -- AND THIS IS THE DEATH ARM'S BEST
SHOWING, SO READ IT CAREFULLY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The published collapse (imbalance~PRO
r=0.75 at 6W -> 0.07 at 12W) gives delta=0.68 against a null median delta of 0.32 --
i.e. the ambient coupling ALREADY falls a long way, but the imbalance falls about twice
as far, landing at the 96th percentile of its collapses against all 884 sets. perm
p=0.066 (marginal); Spearman p=0.308. As a direct difference, Fisher z=1.91, p=0.055 at
n=12/12. TWO INDEPENDENT TESTS CONVERGE AT p~0.06. SO: this is NOT the flat null that
the WITHIN-6W coupling gave (perm p=0.49, script 33 PART C) -- the COLLAPSE is a better
claim than the 6W coupling ever was, and it should not be dismissed as noise. But it
does NOT reach significance on either test, and it does not survive multiplicity (3
axes x 2 methods). The comparators do not come close: bio_comp p=0.20, MASC_comp
p=0.21. VERDICT: MARGINAL -- suggestive, unproven, and NOT reportable as a finding at
n=12/12. CRITICAL CAVEAT: the only axis that gets even this far is the CIRCULAR one
(pro_comp IS a MitoCarta set, like the imbalance). PART F re-runs this on non-mito
death axes -- read that before believing this number.

DOES PRIMING COLLAPSE? THE CONTRAST WAS FITTED, SAVED, AND NEVER READ.
`death_timing_substrate.rds$h1$state_tests` has carried the answer since script 23 was
written: PRO int_p=0.177, priming(PRO-ANTI) int_p=0.263, ANTI 0.953, p53 0.799 --
NOTHING significant on the interaction. The narrative instead quoted the GROUP MEANS
('~3x more at 6W' = +0.48 vs +0.15). That is the retracted-error pattern a THIRD time
(cf. the mtDNA 'difference' and the mitonuclear imbalance) -- and it is the worst
instance, because here the test existed on disk. WHAT IS POWERED AND SURVIVES: the
GENOTYPE main effect -- PRO geno_beta=+0.278 (p=0.037), priming +0.317 (p=0.038). Myc
RAISES apoptotic priming. That is a genotype contrast, so the genotype-independent IEG
axis (p=0.49) cannot bias it. CEILING: at n=6/group, the interaction being null is
UNSUPPORTED, not REFUTED.

THE MECHANISM DISCRIMINATOR: IS THE DEATH ATTENUATION IN EXCESS OF THE MYC PROGRAMME
FADING? Aligned per-gene attenuation vs an expression x dispersion-matched null (script
21's idiom; the null genes get the SAME sign-alignment, so the regression-to-the-mean
bias cancels). pro_comp's 23 mito genes: observed +0.199 vs matched null +0.152,
z=0.97, p_emp=0.337 => not distinguishable from the global attenuation. The
non-circular 404 non-mito pro-death genes: observed +0.223 vs null +0.208, z=0.71,
p_emp=0.479 => not distinguishable from the global attenuation. THE CONTROL THAT
VALIDATES THE TEST: OXPHOS subunits -- whose attenuation Issue #4 ESTABLISHED -- are
ALSO not in excess (z=0.90, p_emp=0.367), and neither is the MYC-target core (z=0.29,
p=0.776). That is not the test failing; it is the point. The attenuation is GLOBAL
(Issue #4: median |LFC| 0.268 -> 0.204 across the transcriptome), so NO programme
attenuates more than expression-matched genes -- death included. CONCLUSION: priming
fades because the MYC PROGRAMME fades. That is canonical Evan/Lowe Myc-induced
apoptosis via BH3-only proteins, and it needs no death-specific gate and no
mitochondrial-state gate. Neither is supported here.

THE TANG NES -1.38 IS A SHARED DEVELOPMENTAL DECLINE, NOT A MYC EFFECT. The walkthrough
cites apoptosis temporal_pos NES=-1.38 as death-spine evidence ('the apoptotic
programme DECLINES in Myc+ with age'). But temporal_neg (WT) = -1.31 -- the WT gland
declines 95% as much. By Issue #6's OWN exact identity, a decline SHARED by both
genotypes CANCELS in the genotype gap and therefore cannot create an attenuation. The
Myc-specific excess is 0.07 NES units. Do not cite temporal_pos alone.

GATE 2's p=0.023 IS THE WRONG TEST. Reproduced: PRO mean interaction LFC = -0.1302,
t-vs-mu=0 p=0.023, with only 0 of 23 genes individually padj<0.05. Two failures. (i)
mu=0 is not the null: under the GLOBAL attenuation every Myc-induced module has a
negative mean interaction LFC. Against an expression x dispersion-MATCHED null:
observed -0.1302 vs null -0.0600, z=-1.27, p_emp=0.208 => not distinguishable from the
global attenuation. (ii) It treats 23 genes as independent. The MEASURED inter-gene
correlation is 0.08, giving an effective n of 8.4 -- not 23. Gate 2's own question,
asked correlation-aware, is CAMERA: p=0.298, FDR=0.926. Script 17 already ran it and
found nothing at FDR across the whole apoptosis category. The one positive in the death
arm does not survive being asked properly.

BREAKING THE CIRCULARITY -- AND THIS IS WHERE THE DEATH ARM ACTUALLY DIES. pro_comp IS
a mitochondrial gene set (MITOCARTA_APOPTOSIS_PRO, 25 genes), and so is the imbalance
-- so 'the mitochondrial state couples to death priming' has been correlating mito
genes with mito genes. Rebuilt on the 404 NON-mitochondrial pro-death genes of
cell_death_genes_consolidated, the Myc genotype effect is -0.106 (p=0.078) -- against
the MITO axis's +0.449 (p=0.017). The effect does NOT merely weaken; on non-mito death
genes it does not reproduce. Interaction: p=0.738 (non-mito) vs 0.177 (mito). And the
marginal collapse of PART B evaporates the moment the shared mito membership is
removed: the circular mito axis gives perm p=0.066, the non-mito pro-death axis
p=0.897, the non-mito priming axis p=0.433, CDC_PRODEATH_APOPTOSIS p=0.915. The ONLY
death axis whose coupling to the imbalance collapses more than an arbitrary gene set's
is the one that SHARES GENES with the imbalance. That is what a circularity looks like
when you test it. See PART F3 (`mito_background_verdict`) for whether the genotype
effect itself is just script 32's mito-content effect wearing a death label.

IS 'MYC RAISES APOPTOTIC PRIMING' A DEATH EFFECT OR THE MITO-CONTENT EFFECT? IT IS THE
CONTENT EFFECT -- AND LESS OF IT THAN AVERAGE. pro_comp is a MitoCarta set, and script
32 established that Myc raises nuclear MitoCarta ~19% WHOLESALE, so ANY MitoCarta
subset rises whatever its label. UNCONDITIONAL (vs all genes): APOPTOSIS_PRO Myc LFC6
+0.196 vs null +0.052, z=1.80, p=0.072 => not distinguishable from the transcriptome.
CONDITIONAL (vs expression-matched OTHER MitoCarta genes -- the test that separates a
death effect from the content effect): observed +0.196 vs a MitoCarta background of
+0.364, z=-2.42, p=0.012 => BELOW the matched background. Read the SIGN: the
pro-apoptotic mito genes rise by HALF what a typical mito gene rises by. So 'Myc raises
apoptotic priming' (geno p=0.037/0.038) is not a death-specific induction at all -- it
is BELOW-AVERAGE participation in the wholesale mito-content rise. The composite goes
up because its genes are MITOCHONDRIAL, not because they are PRO-APOPTOTIC. IMPORTANT
-- THIS IS NOT NEW, IT IS A CONVERGENCE: script 23 already found exactly this by
mitoPPS ('Myc raises PRO absolutely (+0.20) but RELATIVELY de-prioritises Apoptosis-PRO
within the mito compartment, mitoPPS diff -0.21, padj 0.022 -- biogenesis crowds it
out', walkthrough:762-764). Two independent methods agree. The walkthrough reported it
as a 'two-lens nuance' alongside the priming claim; it is better read as the
EXPLANATION of the priming claim. Same membership-looseness that produced the retracted
'commissioned but unbuilt' claim -- see [[mitocarta-sets-are-membership-loose]].

AMBIENT-CORRELATION DIAGNOSTIC -- AND IT IS NOT WHAT PC1 WOULD HAVE TOLD YOU. PC1 is
43% of variance within 6W vs 46% within 12W -- essentially UNCHANGED, so 'the 12W
cohort has less structure' is NOT the explanation. But the ambient COUPLING level
collapses anyway: the imbalance's couplings to ALL 884 library sets have median |r|
0.71 at 6W vs 0.35 at 12W, and 74% vs 11% of sets exceed |r|=0.5. So at 6W almost
everything correlates with almost everything and by 12W most of that is gone. ANY
axis's coupling to ANY set collapses over this window. That is the baseline the
published r 0.75 -> 0.07 must be judged against, and it is why PART B compares the SIZE
of the collapse to the size of an arbitrary set's collapse rather than asking whether a
collapse happened.
THE COLLAPSE NULL (the test the claim never had) -- AND THIS IS THE DEATH ARM'S BEST
SHOWING, SO READ IT CAREFULLY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The published collapse (imbalance~PRO
r=0.75 at 6W -> 0.07 at 12W) gives delta=0.68 against a null median delta of 0.32 --
i.e. the ambient coupling ALREADY falls a long way, but the imbalance falls about twice
as far, landing at the 96th percentile of its collapses against all 884 sets. perm
p=0.066 (marginal); Spearman p=0.308. As a direct difference, Fisher z=1.91, p=0.055 at
n=12/12. TWO INDEPENDENT TESTS CONVERGE AT p~0.06. SO: this is NOT the flat null that
the WITHIN-6W coupling gave (perm p=0.49, script 33 PART C) -- the COLLAPSE is a better
claim than the 6W coupling ever was, and it should not be dismissed as noise. But it
does NOT reach significance on either test, and it does not survive multiplicity (3
axes x 2 methods). The comparators do not come close: bio_comp p=0.20, MASC_comp
p=0.21. VERDICT: MARGINAL -- suggestive, unproven, and NOT reportable as a finding at
n=12/12. CRITICAL CAVEAT: the only axis that gets even this far is the CIRCULAR one
(pro_comp IS a MitoCarta set, like the imbalance). PART F re-runs this on non-mito
death axes -- read that before believing this number.
DOES PRIMING COLLAPSE? THE CONTRAST WAS FITTED, SAVED, AND NEVER READ.
`death_timing_substrate.rds$h1$state_tests` has carried the answer since script 23 was
written: PRO int_p=0.177, priming(PRO-ANTI) int_p=0.263, ANTI 0.953, p53 0.799 --
NOTHING significant on the interaction. The narrative instead quoted the GROUP MEANS
('~3x more at 6W' = +0.48 vs +0.15). That is the retracted-error pattern a THIRD time
(cf. the mtDNA 'difference' and the mitonuclear imbalance) -- and it is the worst
instance, because here the test existed on disk. WHAT IS POWERED AND SURVIVES: the
GENOTYPE main effect -- PRO geno_beta=+0.278 (p=0.037), priming +0.317 (p=0.038). Myc
RAISES apoptotic priming. That is a genotype contrast, so the genotype-independent IEG
axis (p=0.49) cannot bias it. CEILING: at n=6/group, the interaction being null is
UNSUPPORTED, not REFUTED.
THE MECHANISM DISCRIMINATOR: IS THE DEATH ATTENUATION IN EXCESS OF THE MYC PROGRAMME
FADING? Aligned per-gene attenuation vs an expression x dispersion-matched null (script
21's idiom; the null genes get the SAME sign-alignment, so the regression-to-the-mean
bias cancels). pro_comp's 23 mito genes: observed +0.199 vs matched null +0.152,
z=0.97, p_emp=0.337 => not distinguishable from the global attenuation. The
non-circular 404 non-mito pro-death genes: observed +0.223 vs null +0.208, z=0.71,
p_emp=0.479 => not distinguishable from the global attenuation. THE CONTROL THAT
VALIDATES THE TEST: OXPHOS subunits -- whose attenuation Issue #4 ESTABLISHED -- are
ALSO not in excess (z=0.90, p_emp=0.367), and neither is the MYC-target core (z=0.29,
p=0.776). That is not the test failing; it is the point. The attenuation is GLOBAL
(Issue #4: median |LFC| 0.268 -> 0.204 across the transcriptome), so NO programme
attenuates more than expression-matched genes -- death included. CONCLUSION: priming
fades because the MYC PROGRAMME fades. That is canonical Evan/Lowe Myc-induced
apoptosis via BH3-only proteins, and it needs no death-specific gate and no
mitochondrial-state gate. Neither is supported here.

Both scripts reproduce exactly. But reading your full tables — not the verdicts — surfaced three things, and the first is one I should have caught myself.

## 1. I made the error I was diagnosing

My `matched_null()` draws genes **independently** from their bins. That makes the null of the mean too narrow for co-regulated sets, so its p is **anti-conservative** — and script 21's own header documented exactly this ("raw z inflated by inter-gene correlation → use **effect-size** ranking, not absolute z"). I criticised Gate 2 for assuming gene independence while quoting `p=0.012` from a null that assumes gene independence. Same mistake, one level up.

What survives that:
- **Non-significant matched-null results are safe** — a proper correction only widens the null. So "nothing attenuates more than background" (PART D) and the Gate 2 failure (PART E, p=0.21) are **firm**.
- **The F3 result no longer rests on its p.** It rests on the **effect size** — APOPTOSIS_PRO rises +0.196 against a MitoCarta background of +0.364, *half* — and on the fact that script 23's mitoPPS found the same thing independently (−0.21, padj 0.022). That convergence is what carries it. Don't quote the 0.012.

## 2. The direction is the *opposite* of the narrative

This is in your `noncircular_stats` and I'd underplayed it. **All four** non-mito/general death axes have a **negative** Myc genotype effect, two significant after BH: `APOP_BH3_REACTOME` **−0.367 (p=0.031)**, `CDC_PRODEATH_APOPTOSIS` **−0.149 (p=0.015)**.

So on every death axis that isn't mito-defined, **Myc lowers the death programme at 6W** — it doesn't raise it. The only one that goes up is the MitoCarta one, and that one goes up *less* than a typical mito gene.

The reading has to go **through** survivor bias, not around it: you sequence the cells that didn't die, so a suppressed-looking survivor pool is exactly what oncogene-induced apoptosis leaves behind. The walkthrough calls survivor bias "a conservative floor" on Myc's death engagement. These numbers suggest it can **invert the sign**, not merely shrink it. Either way the transcriptome cannot be cited as showing Myc primes for death — and that's a statement about the assay, not about your biology.

## 3. The binomial's null was never 50%, and fixing it flips branch 1

`genomewide_baseline` is the sharpest single number in the run: **59.6%** of expressed genes have ΔLFC>0 — and **93.9% among Myc-induced genes**. Because the Myc programme attenuates globally, ΔLFC>0 is what an induced gene does *by construction*.

So the 239 pro-death genes at **58.6% "supporting"** look significant against 50% (binom p=0.010) but sit **1.1 points below** the genome-wide baseline. Script 16's published 52.7%/p=0.27 reached the right conclusion through the wrong null — and had the set scored a few points higher, it would have reported a significant death result that was nothing but the global attenuation.

## Also fixed

A direction bug your output caught: the two-sided verdict printed "IN EXCESS" for a **negative** z — the opposite claim. Labels now say ABOVE/BELOW. Set labels carry mapped counts (**404** non-mito, not the roster's 471). `atten_excess` and `noncircular_stats` carry BH.

Committed `af72643`. **Your run predates all of it — please re-source 34.** Note your `pc1_by_timepoint` confirmed the thing I'd guessed wrong: PC1 is *unchanged* (43% → 46%), yet the ambient coupling still collapses 0.71 → 0.35. "12W has less structure" was never the explanation.

The bottom line is unchanged but firmer: **the RNA-seq supports no death claim in either direction.** The phenotype is external and untouched; BH3 profiling measures the gateway directly and is independent of both the content claim and the survivor bias. Still nothing pushed — say the word.
