axes x 2 methods). The comparators do not come close: bio_comp p=0.20, MASC_comp
p=0.21. VERDICT: MARGINAL -- suggestive, unproven, and NOT reportable as a finding at
n=12/12. CRITICAL CAVEAT: the only axis that gets even this far is the CIRCULAR one
(pro_comp IS a MitoCarta set, like the imbalance). PART F re-runs this on non-mito
death axes -- read that before believing this number.

DOES PRIMING COLLAPSE? THE CONTRAST WAS FITTED, SAVED, AND NEVER READ.
`death_timing_substrate.rds$h1$state_tests` has carried the answer since script 23 was
written: PRO int_p=0.177, priming(PRO-ANTI) int_p=0.263, ANTI 0.953, p53 0.799 --
NOTHING significant on the interaction. The narrative instead quoted the GROUP MEANS
('~3x more at 6W' = +0.48 vs +0.15). That is the retracted-error pattern a THIRD time
(cf. the mtDNA 'difference' and the mitonuclear imbalance) -- and it is the worst
instance, because here the test existed on disk. WHAT IS POWERED AND SURVIVES: the
GENOTYPE main effect -- PRO geno_beta=+0.278 (p=0.037), priming +0.317 (p=0.038). Myc
RAISES apoptotic priming. That is a genotype contrast, so the genotype-independent IEG
axis (p=0.49) cannot bias it. CEILING: at n=6/group, the interaction being null is
UNSUPPORTED, not REFUTED.

THE MECHANISM DISCRIMINATOR: IS THE DEATH ATTENUATION IN EXCESS OF THE MYC PROGRAMME
FADING? Aligned per-gene attenuation vs an expression x dispersion-matched null (script
21's idiom; the null genes get the SAME sign-alignment, so the regression-to-the-mean
bias cancels). pro_comp's 23 mito genes: observed +0.199 vs matched null +0.152,
z=0.97, p_emp=0.337 => not distinguishable from the global attenuation. The
non-circular 404 non-mito pro-death genes: observed +0.223 vs null +0.208, z=0.71,
p_emp=0.479 => not distinguishable from the global attenuation. THE CONTROL THAT
VALIDATES THE TEST: OXPHOS subunits -- whose attenuation Issue #4 ESTABLISHED -- are
ALSO not in excess (z=0.90, p_emp=0.367), and neither is the MYC-target core (z=0.29,
p=0.776). That is not the test failing; it is the point. The attenuation is GLOBAL
(Issue #4: median |LFC| 0.268 -> 0.204 across the transcriptome), so NO programme
attenuates more than expression-matched genes -- death included. CONCLUSION: priming
fades because the MYC PROGRAMME fades. That is canonical Evan/Lowe Myc-induced
apoptosis via BH3-only proteins, and it needs no death-specific gate and no
mitochondrial-state gate. Neither is supported here.

THE TANG NES -1.38 IS A SHARED DEVELOPMENTAL DECLINE, NOT A MYC EFFECT. The walkthrough
cites apoptosis temporal_pos NES=-1.38 as death-spine evidence ('the apoptotic
programme DECLINES in Myc+ with age'). But temporal_neg (WT) = -1.31 -- the WT gland
declines 95% as much. By Issue #6's OWN exact identity, a decline SHARED by both
genotypes CANCELS in the genotype gap and therefore cannot create an attenuation. The
Myc-specific excess is 0.07 NES units. Do not cite temporal_pos alone.

GATE 2's p=0.023 IS THE WRONG TEST. Reproduced: PRO mean interaction LFC = -0.1302,
t-vs-mu=0 p=0.023, with only 0 of 23 genes individually padj<0.05. Two failures. (i)
mu=0 is not the null: under the GLOBAL attenuation every Myc-induced module has a
negative mean interaction LFC. Against an expression x dispersion-MATCHED null:
observed -0.1302 vs null -0.0600, z=-1.27, p_emp=0.208 => not distinguishable from the
global attenuation. (ii) It treats 23 genes as independent. The MEASURED inter-gene
correlation is 0.08, giving an effective n of 8.4 -- not 23. Gate 2's own question,
asked correlation-aware, is CAMERA: p=0.298, FDR=0.926. Script 17 already ran it and
found nothing at FDR across the whole apoptosis category. The one positive in the death
arm does not survive being asked properly.

BREAKING THE CIRCULARITY -- AND THIS IS WHERE THE DEATH ARM ACTUALLY DIES. pro_comp IS
a mitochondrial gene set (MITOCARTA_APOPTOSIS_PRO, 25 genes), and so is the imbalance
-- so 'the mitochondrial state couples to death priming' has been correlating mito
genes with mito genes. Rebuilt on the 404 NON-mitochondrial pro-death genes of
cell_death_genes_consolidated, the Myc genotype effect is -0.106 (p=0.078) -- against
the MITO axis's +0.449 (p=0.017). The effect does NOT merely weaken; on non-mito death
genes it does not reproduce. Interaction: p=0.738 (non-mito) vs 0.177 (mito). And the
marginal collapse of PART B evaporates the moment the shared mito membership is
removed: the circular mito axis gives perm p=0.066, the non-mito pro-death axis
p=0.897, the non-mito priming axis p=0.433, CDC_PRODEATH_APOPTOSIS p=0.915. The ONLY
death axis whose coupling to the imbalance collapses more than an arbitrary gene set's
is the one that SHARES GENES with the imbalance. That is what a circularity looks like
when you test it. AND THE DIRECTION IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE NARRATIVE: ALL 4
non-mito/general death axes tested have a NEGATIVE Myc genotype effect (2 of them
significant after BH) -- APOP_BH3_REACTOME -0.367 (p=0.031) and CDC_PRODEATH_APOPTOSIS
-0.149 (p=0.015). On every death axis that is not mito-defined, Myc LOWERS the death
programme at 6W rather than raising it. READ THAT WITH THE SURVIVOR BIAS, NOT AROUND
IT: we sequence the cells that did NOT die, so the most death-primed cells are missing
by construction, and a suppressed-looking survivor pool is exactly what
oncogene-induced apoptosis would leave behind. The walkthrough calls survivor bias 'a
conservative floor' on Myc's death engagement; these numbers suggest it can INVERT the
sign, not merely shrink it. Either way the transcriptome cannot be cited as showing Myc
primes for death. See PART F3 (`mito_background_verdict`).

IS 'MYC RAISES APOPTOTIC PRIMING' A DEATH EFFECT OR THE MITO-CONTENT EFFECT? IT IS THE
CONTENT EFFECT -- AND LESS OF IT THAN AVERAGE. pro_comp is a MitoCarta set, and script
32 established that Myc raises nuclear MitoCarta ~19% WHOLESALE, so ANY MitoCarta
subset rises whatever its label. UNCONDITIONAL (vs all genes): APOPTOSIS_PRO Myc LFC6
+0.196 vs null +0.052, z=1.80, p=0.072 => not distinguishable from the transcriptome.
CONDITIONAL (vs expression-matched OTHER MitoCarta genes -- the test that separates a
death effect from the content effect): observed +0.196 vs a MitoCarta background of
+0.364, z=-2.42, p=0.012 => BELOW the matched background. Read the SIGN: the
pro-apoptotic mito genes rise by HALF what a typical mito gene rises by. So 'Myc raises
apoptotic priming' (geno p=0.037/0.038) is not a death-specific induction at all -- it
is BELOW-AVERAGE participation in the wholesale mito-content rise. The composite goes
up because its genes are MITOCHONDRIAL, not because they are PRO-APOPTOTIC. IMPORTANT
-- THIS IS NOT NEW, IT IS A CONVERGENCE: script 23 already found exactly this by
mitoPPS ('Myc raises PRO absolutely (+0.20) but RELATIVELY de-prioritises Apoptosis-PRO
within the mito compartment, mitoPPS diff -0.21, padj 0.022 -- biogenesis crowds it
out', walkthrough:762-764). Two independent methods agree. The walkthrough reported it
as a 'two-lens nuance' alongside the priming claim; it is better read as the
EXPLANATION of the priming claim. Same membership-looseness that produced the retracted
'commissioned but unbuilt' claim -- see [[mitocarta-sets-are-membership-loose]].
STATISTICAL CEILING ON THIS ONE, STATED BECAUSE IT IS THE TRAP THIS SCRIPT IS ABOUT:
the matched null samples genes INDEPENDENTLY, so p=0.012 is ANTI-CONSERVATIVE (script
21's own AP6.2 caveat -- 'raw z inflated by inter-gene correlation'). DO NOT QUOTE THE
p. What carries this claim is (a) the EFFECT SIZE -- half the background rise -- and
(b) the INDEPENDENT mitoPPS convergence above. Non-significant matched-null results
(PARTs D/E) are safe; significant ones need corroboration. This one has it.

THE BRANCH-1 BINOMIAL'S NULL WAS NEVER 50%, AND CORRECTING IT FLIPS THE READ. `16:133`
runs binom.test(supporting, total, p = 0.5) on the sign of dLFC = myc_6W - myc_12W. But
the Myc programme attenuates GLOBALLY, so dLFC > 0 is what a Myc-INDUCED gene does BY
CONSTRUCTION. Measured genome-wide: 59.6% of expressed genes have dLFC>0 -- and among
Myc-INDUCED genes, 93.9%. THAT is the null, not 50%. Consequence: the 239 pro-death
genes are 58.6% 'supporting', which vs 50% looks significant (binom p=0.010) but sits
-1.1 points against the genome-wide baseline of 59.6% => AT OR BELOW the genome-wide
baseline. So the pro-death set does not front-load at 6W any more than an average gene
does; it front-loads slightly LESS. Script 16's published 52.7%/p=0.27 'clean negative'
reached the right conclusion through the wrong null -- and had the set scored a few
points higher it would have reported a significant death result that was nothing but
the global attenuation.

AMBIENT-CORRELATION DIAGNOSTIC -- AND IT IS NOT WHAT PC1 WOULD HAVE TOLD YOU. PC1 is
43% of variance within 6W vs 46% within 12W -- essentially UNCHANGED, so 'the 12W
cohort has less structure' is NOT the explanation. But the ambient COUPLING level
collapses anyway: the imbalance's couplings to ALL 884 library sets have median |r|
0.71 at 6W vs 0.35 at 12W, and 74% vs 11% of sets exceed |r|=0.5. So at 6W almost
everything correlates with almost everything and by 12W most of that is gone. ANY
axis's coupling to ANY set collapses over this window. That is the baseline the
published r 0.75 -> 0.07 must be judged against, and it is why PART B compares the SIZE
of the collapse to the size of an arbitrary set's collapse rather than asking whether a
collapse happened.
THE COLLAPSE NULL (the test the claim never had) -- AND THIS IS THE DEATH ARM'S BEST
SHOWING, SO READ IT CAREFULLY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The published collapse (imbalance~PRO
r=0.75 at 6W -> 0.07 at 12W) gives delta=0.68 against a null median delta of 0.32 --
i.e. the ambient coupling ALREADY falls a long way, but the imbalance falls about twice
as far, landing at the 96th percentile of its collapses against all 884 sets. perm
p=0.066 (marginal); Spearman p=0.308. As a direct difference, Fisher z=1.91, p=0.055 at
n=12/12. TWO INDEPENDENT TESTS CONVERGE AT p~0.06. SO: this is NOT the flat null that
the WITHIN-6W coupling gave (perm p=0.49, script 33 PART C) -- the COLLAPSE is a better
claim than the 6W coupling ever was, and it should not be dismissed as noise. But it
does NOT reach significance on either test, and it does not survive multiplicity (3
axes x 2 methods). The comparators do not come close: bio_comp p=0.20, MASC_comp
p=0.21. VERDICT: MARGINAL -- suggestive, unproven, and NOT reportable as a finding at
n=12/12. CRITICAL CAVEAT: the only axis that gets even this far is the CIRCULAR one
(pro_comp IS a MitoCarta set, like the imbalance). PART F re-runs this on non-mito
death axes -- read that before believing this number.

IS 'MYC RAISES APOPTOTIC PRIMING' A DEATH EFFECT OR THE MITO-CONTENT EFFECT? IT IS THE
CONTENT EFFECT -- AND LESS OF IT THAN AVERAGE. pro_comp is a MitoCarta set, and script
32 established that Myc raises nuclear MitoCarta ~19% WHOLESALE, so ANY MitoCarta
subset rises whatever its label. UNCONDITIONAL (vs all genes): APOPTOSIS_PRO Myc LFC6
+0.196 vs null +0.052, z=1.80, p=0.072 => not distinguishable from the transcriptome.
CONDITIONAL (vs expression-matched OTHER MitoCarta genes -- the test that separates a
death effect from the content effect): observed +0.196 vs a MitoCarta background of
+0.364, z=-2.42, p=0.012 => BELOW the matched background. Read the SIGN: the
pro-apoptotic mito genes rise by HALF what a typical mito gene rises by. So 'Myc raises
apoptotic priming' (geno p=0.037/0.038) is not a death-specific induction at all -- it
is BELOW-AVERAGE participation in the wholesale mito-content rise. The composite goes
up because its genes are MITOCHONDRIAL, not because they are PRO-APOPTOTIC. IMPORTANT
-- THIS IS NOT NEW, IT IS A CONVERGENCE: script 23 already found exactly this by
mitoPPS ('Myc raises PRO absolutely (+0.20) but RELATIVELY de-prioritises Apoptosis-PRO
within the mito compartment, mitoPPS diff -0.21, padj 0.022 -- biogenesis crowds it
out', walkthrough:762-764). Two independent methods agree. The walkthrough reported it
as a 'two-lens nuance' alongside the priming claim; it is better read as the
EXPLANATION of the priming claim. Same membership-looseness that produced the retracted
'commissioned but unbuilt' claim -- see [[mitocarta-sets-are-membership-loose]].
STATISTICAL CEILING ON THIS ONE, STATED BECAUSE IT IS THE TRAP THIS SCRIPT IS ABOUT:
the matched null samples genes INDEPENDENTLY, so p=0.012 is ANTI-CONSERVATIVE (script
21's own AP6.2 caveat -- 'raw z inflated by inter-gene correlation'). DO NOT QUOTE THE
p. What carries this claim is (a) the EFFECT SIZE -- half the background rise -- and
(b) the INDEPENDENT mitoPPS convergence above. Non-significant matched-null results
(PARTs D/E) are safe; significant ones need corroboration. This one has it.

THE BRANCH-1 BINOMIAL'S NULL WAS NEVER 50%, AND CORRECTING IT FLIPS THE READ. `16:133`
runs binom.test(supporting, total, p = 0.5) on the sign of dLFC = myc_6W - myc_12W. But
the Myc programme attenuates GLOBALLY, so dLFC > 0 is what a Myc-INDUCED gene does BY
CONSTRUCTION. Measured genome-wide: 59.6% of expressed genes have dLFC>0 -- and among
Myc-INDUCED genes, 93.9%. THAT is the null, not 50%. Consequence: the 239 pro-death
genes are 58.6% 'supporting', which vs 50% looks significant (binom p=0.010) but sits
-1.1 points against the genome-wide baseline of 59.6% => AT OR BELOW the genome-wide
baseline. So the pro-death set does not front-load at 6W any more than an average gene
does; it front-loads slightly LESS. Script 16's published 52.7%/p=0.27 'clean negative'
reached the right conclusion through the wrong null -- and had the set scored a few
points higher it would have reported a significant death result that was nothing but
the global attenuation.

Re-run reproduces cleanly. But `death_decomp` contains a bug I introduced — and it's the **same bug I fixed in script 32 two days ago**.

Look at the `expressed` rows:

```
APOP_BH3_REACTOME (n=7)        atten 0.065   conv_pct -310.4%   fade_pct 410.4%
APOP_INTRINSIC_REACTOME (n=40) atten 0.057   conv_pct -263.2%   fade_pct 363.2%
```

`conv_pct = 100 * wt_conv / atten` — when `atten` is near zero the ratio explodes. That is exactly the `pct_retained = 388%` artifact you had me fix in script 32 on 2026-07-17: **a percentage of a near-zero denominator**. I carried the ratio over from script 31 without checking that its premise (a substantial `atten`) holds for small death sets. Third instance of me repeating a documented error class in this project.

Also visible: `MITOCARTA_APOPTOSIS_PRO` in the `divergent` universe is **n=5** — five genes at the function's floor, decomposed into a "programme". Not meaningful.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

**You're right that hypothesis generation doesn't need a null.** Over-nulling exploratory work is a real failure mode, and if the RNA-seq's job is to nominate something you then test at the bench, a suggestive correlation is a perfectly good reason to spend an experiment. ## Where the ceiling comes from — it's none of your three candidates

| candidate | test | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Low n?** | chance floor at n=12 (permuted labels) = **0.22** vs observed 0.82 | **No** |

**What it actually is: one global per-sample axis.** `mito_oxphos` correlates with **the mean of all 884 set scores at 0.979** — it is very nearly just a readout of "how high this mouse's scores are overall". Remove that global mean and the ceiling falls to **0.287**, essentially chance.

**So: methodological in form, biological *and* technical in origin.** GSVA scores each sample against the cohort but doesn't centre *within* a sample — so any global shift in a mouse (Myc's known global RNA amplification, prep/IEG stress, cell composition, library complexity) lifts *every* set score together. It isn't noise, and it isn't an artefact you could prep your way out of. It's real global variation being read through a method that lets it propagate to all 884 scores.

**This is fixable, which changes the answer to your original question.** You don't have to live with the ceiling *or* null everything — you can remove its cause and then your per-sample correlations mean what you always thought they meant.

**But I have to flag a caution rather than sell it.** Two ways of removing the global axis disagree: regressing it out gives a ceiling of 0.287, subtracting it gives 0.671 — and under the second, `mito_oxphos → prolif` drops to 0.40 while `mito_biogenesis → prolif` *rises* to 0.57. **The OXPHOS-over-biogenesis ordering may invert depending on the correction.** That needs doing properly in a script, not in a shell one-liner, before either of us believes it.

## Where the docs and the current analysis agree
- **The ceiling is real and my provisional probe numbers are the right diagnostics.** 0.678 random pairs, `cor(mito_oxphos, global mean)=0.979`, 0.82→0.287 on removal — doc 1 §1 formalises exactly this as a **rank-one common-mode latent factor**. - **Don't overcorrect — the global factor may *be* the biology** (doc 1 §14). This is the answer to the author's "biological or methodological" question: report the factor as a phenotype in its own right, not just as nuisance.

## Where the docs upgrade my plan (they are right, I should change)
1. **Mean-subtraction is the wrong correction — and this dissolves my "unresolved centring sensitivity."** My old plan flagged that subtract-and-recompute (0.671, OXPHOS/biogenesis ordering can invert) disagrees with regress-out (0.287), and said "report, don't resolve." Doc 1 §4 *explains* it: mean-subtraction assumes equal loadings and imposes a compositional sum-to-zero constraint that manufactures spurious negatives. The **design→PC1→residual** regression is the principled one. So the sensitivity isn't an open mystery to park — it's a known artifact of the inferior method. That's a real resolution, not a caveat.
2. **Estimate the global factor *after* removing the design, not from raw scores** (doc 1 §7). My probes estimated the axis on the raw matrix, which conflates it with the four-group contrast. This **reframes "the ceiling is mostly Myc dose"**: once design is residualised, the *residual* global factor is a within-group broad axis — and my own 0.71-within-`6W_pos` probe (one genotype, one age, contrast gone) says that within-group axis is *large*. So the raw ceiling decomposes into (between-group contrast, much of it Myc) + (within-group global axis, prep/IEG/composition). The memory headline "mostly Myc dose" conflates the two; the author's hierarchy disentangles them and the headline may move.
3. **Doc 2's quantifier critique is legitimate.** GSVA's nonlinear competitive score has no clean covariance interpretation, so even a *corrected* GSVA correlation is harder to read than a linear mean-z-score, whose correlation is literally average cross-gene covariance. And the **signed-score** point (doc 2 §6) is currently unhandled — TF/MYC signatures with up+down members may be self-cancelling.

## Where I'd push back on the docs
- **The bootstrap + leave-pair-out + CI apparatus is confirmatory-grade, and we already decided these couplings are exploratory.** Doc 1 §10 itself concedes a residual r≈0.287 "can easily arise under the null" at n=24 — so per-pair CIs will mostly straddle zero and confirm nothing. The payload of the author's pipeline is the **cleaner ranking** and the **global-factor-as-phenotype**, not p-values. I'd build the correction and the cross-method robustness, but treat bootstrap CIs as optional/descriptive, not the deliverable.
- **Scope must stay bounded:** none of this touches the load-bearing claims — content is raw count shares, attenuation is DESeq2 LFCs. The whole global-axis problem lives only in the exploratory coupling layer. The revision re-ranks leads; it does not reopen the contrasts.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Done. Everything is built, validated read-only, and committed on `paper-figures` (not pushed).

## What I did

**Confronted the two method notes against the current state** — they're a genuine upgrade, and I adopted them:
- **Mean-subtraction was the wrong correction** (equal-loading + sum-to-zero artifact) — that dissolves the "unresolved centring sensitivity" the old plan parked. The principled fix is **design → PC1 → residual**, factor estimated *after* the design, leave-pair-out per pair.
- **Switched the coupling instrument to the linear mean gene-wise z-score** (its correlation *is* average cross-gene covariance), with **singscore** as the cohort-independent robustness arm and GSVA for continuity. Gene- vs score-level design adjustment agree to ~0.02.
- Kept the **ranking + global-factor-as-phenotype** framing you chose — no confirmatory CIs.

**Script 36** (`36_linear_pathway_coupling.R`, + `singscore` in `00_setup_packages.R`) — dry-ran read-only (nothing written to `results/`/`outputs/`).

## The result is genuinely different — and cleaner

The dry-run surfaced a trap I had to fix before it shipped a false claim: `mito_oxphos→prolif` global-adjusted flips to **−0.62 "across all methods"** — but OXPHOS carries **r²=0.94** with the global mean, so that's noise-on-noise, **not antagonism**. I added a `resid_frac` gate. The honest, sharper conclusions:

- **The ceiling is one global per-sample axis** — not low n (chance 0.13), not curation (0.54), not the Myc split alone (0.83 within `6W_pos`); `cor(oxphos, global mean)=0.968`, removable to 0.13. Part four-group contrast, part within-group **composition/prep** axis (residual PC1 tracks epithelial +0.79, contamination −0.70, prolif +0.65, MYC +0.44).
- **"OXPHOS is central" is UNTESTABLE** (the axis *is* the global factor) — the cleanest form of its failure.
- **`redox → MB2 fork` is the one robust, testable lead**: −0.63, same sign across all three quantifiers, axis r²=0.03, **Myc-independent**. Lower redox/glutathione ↔ tumorigenic fork.
- **`cholesterol/mevalonate → fork` is DEMOTED** to +0.14 — its script-35 96th-pct headline was a raw-ambient artifact.

Propagated to the synthesis doc (§0.5/§0.6 + ledger + leads table), CLAUDE.md, memory, and the artifact (same URL, [📏](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/a2827606-7f33-467a-91cd-542a20fa740c)).

## For you to run (Option A)
- **Source script 36** — `singscore` is installed. All my numbers are **provisional** until your run (read-only scratchpad, same discipline as before).
- Still carried, not blocking: **run script 35**, **re-source script 23** (stale rds). Script 36 doesn't depend on either.
- Commit `94dc55d` is **not pushed**.

One thing worth your eye when you run it: `redox→fork` being the survivor is a real, bench-testable, Myc-independent hypothesis — but it's negative and n=24, so it's a lead for a redox assay, not a result.

WHERE THE CEILING COMES FROM -- ONE COMMON-MODE AXIS, NOT n, NOT CURATION. On the LINEAR
z-score: mito_oxphos correlates with the per-sample mean of all 884 set scores at r=0.968
(GSVA 0.955), and random set-set pairs sit at median |rho|=0.54 (GSVA 0.53). It is NOT low
n -- the chance floor from permuting the axis's own sample labels is 0.13, far below the
observed ambient of 0.80. It is NOT the genotype contrast alone -- WITHIN 6W_pos (one
genotype, one age, contrast gone) the ambient is still 0.83. And it is REMOVABLE: regress
the per-sample global mean out of every set and the axis's ambient drops to 0.13 (~chance).
So the raw ceiling is a single global per-sample offset that every score rides -- part the
four-group contrast (much of it Myc), part a within-group common-mode axis. PART C says
which is which.

IS THE COMMON FACTOR BIOLOGICAL OR METHODOLOGICAL? BOTH -- and the residual within-group
axis is measurable. The RAW PC1 explains 76% of variance and 79% of set loadings share one
sign (a common mode, not a contrast); it correlates with the group label at r=0.48, so a
large part of the raw ceiling IS the four-group design. The RESIDUAL PC1 (design removed)
explains 70% and its strongest correlates among measured covariates are: epithelial
(rho=+0.79); contamination (rho=-0.70); proliferation (rho=+0.65). Biological state
(MYC/proliferation/composition) and technical/prep tells (IEG, library size, mt%) both load
-- so the axis is neither cleanly biological nor cleanly technical, exactly as the docs
warn. IT IS NOT NOISE: it is a real broad sample-level programme, and it is the thing a raw
coupling mostly measures. Report it as a phenotype (PART C table) AND remove it for
specific coupling.

Confirmed and complete. Every number matched the read-only run, so the doc, CLAUDE.md, memory, and artifact are all validated as-is — nothing to correct.

## What the run settles for the narrative

**The method holds.** design→PC1→residual on a linear score, cross-checked against singscore and GSVA; gene-level vs score-level design adjustment agree (0.74 vs 0.76). The ceiling is now a *named object*, not an adjective: one global per-sample axis, `cor(oxphos, global mean)=0.968`, removable to the chance floor.

**Three things you can now write with confidence:**

1. **The global factor is itself a phenotype** — 70% of residual variance, tracking epithelial purity (+0.79), contamination (−0.70), proliferation (+0.65), MYC (+0.44). For enzymatically-dissociated non-FACS MECs this is exactly the expected composition/prep axis riding a real biological state. Worth a supplementary panel: *the dominant axis in these samples is a broad epithelial-state programme, and a raw pathway coupling mostly measures participation in it.*

2. **"OXPHOS is central" is not just weak — it is untestable.** OXPHOS has ~4% of its variance independent of the broad state; there is no separable coupling to test in either direction. That is the cleanest possible retirement of that claim, and it makes the biogenesis-bystander half the whole of Q4.

3. **redox → MB2 fork is your one readable coupling.** −0.62 to −0.73 across all three quantifiers, on an axis Myc barely touches (r²=0.03 with the global factor, 92% of variance surviving). **Lower redox/glutathione capacity tracks the tumorigenic fork, independent of Myc dose.** It's negative and n=24 — a lead for a redox/GSH:GSSG assay on the fork, not a result — but it's the only mito/metabolic coupling in the corpus that isn't an artifact of the ceiling. If the paper wants a metabolism-couples-to-tumorigenesis thread, it runs through redox, not OXPHOS or biogenesis.

Nothing to commit from the run itself (`results/`/`outputs/` are gitignored); commit `94dc55d` already carries the script and docs, still unpushed. The two carried items remain open and independent: **run script 35**, **re-source script 23**.

ASSISTANT  2026-07-18 00:07:55

This is decisive, and it changes my answer on one of your three points. Here's what the data say, then the inventory.

## First — you're right about the framing

The global shift is a caution on **one class of analysis** — per-sample correlations *between* pathway scores — not on the backbone of the paper. Most of your results are **contrasts** (fold-changes between groups) or **ratios/normalised values**, and those do not ride the shift. I over-weighted it in the summary by letting it colour everything. It should be scoped, not headline. Agreed.

## The three points

**Point 2 (OXPHOS decline over the timeline) — you're completely right.** That is a DESeq2 contrast (a fold-change with a standard error), not a per-sample correlation. The ceiling is a property of *cross-sectional correlations*; a fold-change is immune to it. And the decline is **72–90% Myc-specific** (a genotype×time effect), and the genotype dimension is exactly the one the shift can't touch (the axis is genotype-independent, p=0.49). Keep it as a quantified fact.

**Point 3 (mitoPPS) — right, with one border.** mitoPPS is pairwise-ratio-based on linear counts, so a whole-transcriptome shift cancels by construction. mitoPPS **reallocation among nuclear pathways** (the Issue #4 reprioritisation) is background-robust — safe. The **one exception** is any mitoPPS measure that includes the **mtDNA-encoded arm**: mitoPPS cancels a *global* shift but not variation in the *mitochondrial fraction itself* (which swings 3.4→40% across samples), and subtracting the mtDNA arm imports that variance. That exception is exactly the imbalance — which is point 1.

**Point 1 (mtDNA:nuDNA ratio) — here I have to push back with the numbers, and withdraw my earlier wording.** My "artefact of the arithmetic" phrasing was wrong — a ratio *can* be the right correction, as you say. But this particular ratio, tested, does **not** cancel the background; it's dominated by it. The imbalance is built (`33:261`) as `mean(nuclear-OXPHOS mitoPPS) − mtDNA mitoPPS`, and:

| imbalance vs… | rho | r² | 
|---|---|---|
| **mt% (mito fraction)** | **−0.95** | **0.73** |
| contamination | −0.83 | 0.28 |
| IEG / prep-stress | −0.68 | 0.27 |

And its own contrast test:

| term | β | p |
|---|---|---|
| timepoint (12W vs 6W) | −0.59 | 0.31 |
| genotype (Myc vs WT) | +0.37 | 0.52 |
| **timepoint, adjusted for the IEG axis** | **−0.01** | **0.985** |

So the apparent 6W→12W *decline* in the imbalance (group means 0.50→−0.17 in Myc, 0.13→−0.46 in WT) is **entirely the prep axis** — adjust for it and the time slope goes from −0.59 to −0.01. The reason the ratio didn't cancel the background is that the nuclear and mtDNA arms load in **opposite** directions on the contamination/prep axis, so the *difference* amplifies it instead of cancelling. The subtraction cancels the *global* shift but keeps (in fact doubles down on) the mt-fraction axis, which is the one unresolved technical-vs-biological variable.

So: the imbalance isn't "dismissed for being a ratio" — it's tested, doesn't reach significance even raw (n=6/group), and what trend it has is prep, not time. The **one axis-independent piece** is the genotype offset (Myc higher at both timepoints, +0.37) — but that's ns here. **mtDNA qPCR** measures the physical ratio directly, cancels all of this, and would test that genotype offset cleanly. That's the honest positive: the imbalance is a live hypothesis for qPCR, not a refuted one — but it is not readable *from this RNA-seq*, in either the raw or the ratio form.

## Inventory: what does NOT depend on the global shift

**Independent (the backbone — contrasts, ranks, and true ratios):**

| result | why it's clean |
|---|---|
| Myc raises mitochondrial **content +21–27%** | genotype contrast on read-*shares*; adjustment-robust |
| Myc raises **absolute nuclear OXPHOS** (d=1.27/1.15) | genotype contrast |
| **OXPHOS declines 6W→12W** (72–90% Myc-specific) | DESeq2 LFC contrast — *point 2* |
| The **attenuation** (66% fade + 34% convergence) | genotype×time contrast (Issue #4/#6 identity) |
| **mitoPPS reallocation** among nuclear pathways | pairwise-ratio, cancels the global shift — *point 3* |
| Myc **amplifies** the pubertal programme (d=2.3–3.0); **BMYO suppression** | genotype main effects |
| Myc **bends off the WT developmental trajectory** | correlation of *gene* LFCs, not a per-sample pathway coupling |
| **fGSEA** enrichments per contrast (incl. Tang RCD modalities) | ranks on the Wald statistic of a contrast |
| Developmental-trajectory validation (4-method floor) | contrasts |

**Dependent on the global shift (the exploratory coupling layer only):**

| result | the exposure |
|---|---|
| "OXPHOS is central" / biogenesis / metabolic-axis **couplings** | per-sample GSVA correlations — scripts 28/35/36 |
| The **mitonuclear imbalance as a *time* claim** | dominated by mt%/IEG axis (−0.59 → −0.01) — *point 1* |
| **mt%** as a standalone readout | entangled with prep; technical-vs-biological unresolved |
| The **mito→death coupling** | circular + rides the axis (the script-36 negative control) |
| Any single-timepoint cross-sectional per-sample correlation | the ceiling |

The pattern is clean: **fold-changes, rank-enrichments, and content shares are safe; correlations between two pathway scores are not.** Points 2 and 3 sit squarely in the safe column. Point 1 is the one measure that *looks* like it should be safe (it's a ratio) but empirically isn't — because the thing it fails to cancel is the very axis we can't yet resolve.

I'll hold here for your detailed proposal. When it comes, the useful question will be how much narrative weight the mitonuclear story should carry given it rests on qPCR rather than the RNA — and whether the redox→fork lead earns a place alongside it.

## What the doc is, and what's actually new for us

The doc is a strong, correct framework — but mapped against script 36 and this dataset's constraints, it splits three ways:

**Not executable on this dataset (the load-bearing gap):**
- §3.1 + Steps 2–3, the doc's *preferred first move* — "remove anchored technical variation, then estimate the biological axis." I confirmed it: **there is no batch, RIN, lane, mapping-rate, duplication, viability, or negative-control metadata anywhere on disk** — only comments documenting its absence. The doc's own §3.1 identifiability note is exactly our situation, and worse (we have no batch variable at all, confounded or otherwise). So `G_bio` and `G_tech` are **formally unseparable here** — which is precisely why 36 could only say the residual axis is *mixed* (epithelial +0.79, contamination −0.70, prolif +0.65, MYC +0.44). The doc doesn't rescue that; it explains why it can't be rescued.
- §3.6 bifactor/sparse — the author's own text says unreliable at n=24. Agree; skip.

**Genuinely new, executable, and valuable — two escapes from the ceiling we haven't used:**
1. **§3.3 loading + condition-dependent loading** (`OXPHOS ~ G * genotype * timepoint`). This is the real prize. It reframes the *untestable* "is OXPHOS central" coupling into a *testable* question: is OXPHOS a top-loading pathway on the axis, and **does MYC change its loading?** The loading *level* is near-tautological (OXPHOS ≈ the axis, r²=0.94) — but the *change in loading by genotype* is a contrast, and genotype is the one dimension the axis can't touch (p=0.49). That's a positive, defensible statement.
2. **§3.4 δ-interaction coupling** (`B ~ A * genotype * timepoint`) — tests whether a coupling *changes* by condition. Same logic: the conditional shift is readable even when the level isn't.

Plus cheap add-ons: §1.6 D_eff/scree (a one-number "how low-dimensional"), §3.5 gene-submodule probe (where a specific OXPHOS↔death signal could hide below an aggregate that shows nothing), §3.8 mediation, Step-10 bootstrap.

## The reality check on your three scientific questions

- **OXPHOS in proliferation** — answerable *only* as loading/participation (§3.3), never as residual coupling (it's the axis). Honest deliverable: "OXPHOS is a top loader; MYC raises its loading" — not "OXPHOS drives proliferation."
- **OXPHOS in cell death** — doubly compromised: the death composites are MitoCarta-defined (mito↔death is circular, script 34) *and* the death phenotype is external (IHC). The **only** non-circular transcriptomic death readout is the existing Tang RCD fGSEA (Wald-rank, a *contrast* — already safe). A new death coupling would re-import both problems.
- **MYC vs PGC1a biogenesis** — **there is no PGC1a/PPARGC1A target set.** PGC1a is a coactivator with no DNA motif; its programme is only representable through its coactivated TFs — and those *do* exist in the library (`TFT_ESRRA_*`, `TFT_NRF1_*`, `TFT_GABPA_*`, `TFT_YY1_*`). The real, tractable question underneath yours is: **is a PGC1a/ESRRA-effector axis even separable from MYC dose in these 24 samples, or do they co-load?** That connects directly to the Menegollo/Bentham ESRRA companion paper.

Done. Script 37 is written, verified, and committed on `paper-figures` (`392e6f9`, not pushed).

## What script 37 does — and what it found

It implements Parts 1+2 of your low-dimensional-structure doc, treating the global axis as a **phenotype to dissect** rather than noise to delete. All numbers below are from my read-only run (`results/pathway_loading.rds` + 3 PDFs when you run it in Positron); the gate reproduced script 36's `cor(mito_oxphos, global mean) = 0.968` exactly.

**Dimensionality, quantified (doc §1.6).** Linear-z-score PC1 = **76%** of variance, effective dimensionality **1.7** of a possible 23 — the 884 pathways genuinely move along one axis.

**The positive reframe — this is the answer to "OXPHOS in proliferation."** As a composite, **OXPHOS is the single strongest-loading programme; it *is* the dominant axis** (loading 0.968). That LEVEL statement is robust and defensible — but I kept it honest: it's near-tautological, a *description* of the axis, not a coupling. `redox` sits at the 42nd percentile — the one axis Myc doesn't drive, as expected.

**The loading-CHANGE is where I pulled back hard.** The `S ~ G*genotype*timepoint` model makes loading-change a genotype *contrast* (readable where the residual coupling was untestable). OXPHOS hints at a genotype increase (+71% relative), but I flagged it as **exploratory, not a result**: near-collinear slopes at n=6/group, and `mito_biogenesis` shows no such change — so it is not a blanket mito effect. My first draft had reported it as "MYC raises loading, p<0.001," which leaned on a tiny SE from collinearity; I corrected that.

**Both-lenses correction, with the over-correction rail firing.** The design-only axis and the contamination/IEG-removed axis correlate r=0.57. The named risk landed: the RNA anchors absorb **r²=0.67 of proliferation variance** (IEG↔prolif −0.75), so the second lens removes biology, not just prep — design-only stays primary, prep-driven loadings flagged.

**New fact recorded: batch = timepoint.** Genotype balanced within each batch → the design absorbs it → genotype/interaction clean, developmental reading confounded. In CLAUDE.md, the what-survives doc, and a new `batch-equals-timepoint` memory.

ASSISTANT  2026-07-19 21:03:24

Both good questions, and they have distinct answers because script 37 computes loading two different ways.

## How pathway loading is calculated

The pipeline (`scripts/37_...R:96-131`, `220-274`):

1. **Score each pathway per sample** — `M_z` (`37:114`): take VST expression → gene-wise z-score across the 24 mice (`row_z`) → for each set, the **mean z-score of its member genes** (`score_linear`, ≥5 genes required). This is the linear z-score quantifier; its correlation *is* average cross-gene covariance. Result: an 884 × 24 score matrix.
2. **Remove the design** — `Sd <- resid_on(M_z, X)` (`37:220`): residualise every set's row on `~ timepoint * myc_status`. This strips the four-group means (and, since batch = timepoint, the batch effect) so what's left is the *within-group* covariation.
3. **Define the axis** — `G_bio_design <- pc1_oriented(Sd, gm_z)` (`37:225`): PC1 of that design-residual matrix, sign-flipped to track the per-sample global mean. `$g` = the 24 sample scores of the dominant axis; `$load` = the per-set PC1 rotation coefficients.

Then **"loading" is measured at two granularities:**

- **Per-set loading** = `G_bio_design$load`, the raw prcomp rotation coefficient for each of the 884 sets. Used in `loading_ranks` (`37:282`) — this is where "OXPHOS sits at the **73rd percentile** of all 884 |loadings|" comes from.
- **Named-axis loading** = `cor(composite_design_resid, G_bio_design$g)` (`axis_loadings`, `37:263-274`). A "composite" is the mean z-score of a *curated group* of sets (e.g. `mito_oxphos` = 19 OXPHOS-pattern sets), residualised on the design, then correlated with the axis. **This is what figure B plots.**

## Figure B — no, it is not all 884 pathways

`B_axis_loadings.pdf` plots the `axis_loadings` table: **11 named composite axes**, not 884 individual pathways. Its x-axis is the composite↔axis correlation:

| axis | member sets | loading (design lens) |
|---|---|---|
| tca | 3 | 0.968 |
| **mito_oxphos** | **19** | **0.963** |
| nucleotide | 9 | 0.947 |
| myc_sig | 17 | 0.934 |
| mito_biogenesis | 21 | 0.910 |
| prolif | 14 | 0.864 |
| … | | |
| redox (control) | 3 | 0.259 |

So each dot is a *hand-defined programme built from a handful of member sets*, ranked by how tightly it tracks the dominant axis.

**Where all 884 do enter:** they build the axis those 11 dots are measured against (step 3 runs PC1 over the full 884 × 24 matrix, `n_sets = 884` confirmed), and the separate percentile statement — OXPHOS member sets at the **72.7th percentile of all 884 per-set |loadings|** (`loading_ranks`) — is computed over the whole library. That percentile is the "is OXPHOS a top loader among *everything*" check; figure B is the "how do the *named programmes* rank against each other" view.

One nuance worth carrying into the narrative: the 0.963 in figure B (OXPHOS composite) and the 72.7th-percentile statement are **different quantities** — a named-composite correlation vs. a median over individual per-set rotations. Both say "OXPHOS is a top loader," but they are not the same number, so cite them to the right claim.

## Q1 — Does the ranking stratify biogenesis vs OXPHOS vs priming? **No — it reads "generic mito" only.**

Joining the 218 `_MITO` TF lanes to the shortlist's `n_oxphos` / `n_mitoribo` / `apop_balance`:

- `cor(|loading|, mitoribo_frac) = +0.148`
- `cor(|loading|, apop_balance) = +0.219`
- loading spread across all 218 lanes: **min 0.883, median 0.981, max 0.997** — they are **all pinned to the mito ceiling.**

So an OXPHOS-heavy lane and a mitoribosome-heavy lane load essentially identically. The ranking cannot separate the sub-programmes — they saturate. The only place that faint separation survives is the *composite* level (`axis_loadings`: OXPHOS 0.963 vs biogenesis 0.910), and even that gap is small. **The per-set ranking confers "mito as a block," not oxphos-vs-biogenesis-vs-priming resolution.**

## Q2 — Are there non-mito sets in the high rankings? **Yes — and this is the crux.**

The headline enrichment is real and striking: mito-defined sets are **44% of the library but 100% of the top 100 and 195/200 of the top 200.** But "no non-mito sets at the top" is **false**. The highest-loading genuinely-non-mito sets:

**Three reasons this does not support "primary mitochondria-mediated regulation":**

1. **Non-mito growth programmes load essentially as high.** The 0.99-vs-0.98 gap between the top mito set and the top nucleotide/proliferation set is within noise (median set already loads 0.85). The axis is a *coordinated Myc anabolic-proliferative-mitochondrial growth state*, not a mito-specific one.

2. **The mito monopoly of the very top is inflated by construction.** 44% base rate + the 218 `_LE_MITO` and biogenesis-discrimination `_MITO` sets are **subsets of MitoCarta by definition** (doc §2c: TF-program ∩ MitoCarta, promoted at FDR<0.01 & ≥15 mito genes). They are the purest reads of the mito common mode, so they load ~0.99 tautologically. The clean proof is the same-TF check: `TFT_MYC_GRAY_BA_LE_MITO` = **0.993 (rank 6)** but the same TF's non-mito lane `TFT_MYC_GRAY_AP_HE` = **0.013 (rank 881)**. The loading tracks *mito gene content*, not the regulator.

3. **Loading is covariation, not primacy.** The common mode it measures is Myc-dose + proliferation + prep-stress. A correlation ranking cannot order the arms of a co-regulated programme or say which is upstream. "Primary/causal" is exactly the claim n=24 observational bulk cannot make — the same wall as "OXPHOS is central is untestable" (script 36) and the PGC1a untestability (script 38).

## What *is* defensible (the honest strong version)

> Mitochondrial programmes are the single **largest and highest-loading block** of the dominant Myc-driven transcriptional axis — 44% of the curated library, the entire top 100 of per-set loadings, at 0.96–0.99 — co-equal with nucleotide synthesis, the pentose-phosphate pathway, and proliferation, and above the redox control (0.26).

That is a real, citable *descriptive* statement about the architecture of the response. It is consistent with a Myc-coordinated mito-anabolic programme. It is **not** evidence that mitochondria are *primary/upstream* — that needs the perturbation experiments already on the list (ESRRA/PGC1a, mito-targeted).

Reproduced cleanly (Spearman, n=24) — these match the committed doc:

```
mt% (13 mtDNA genes / total counts):  3.4% … 10.5% … 40.1%     <- a 12-fold range
cor(mtDNA-arm , mt%) = +0.952     cor(imbalance , mt%) = -0.922
cor(priming   , mt%) = -0.597     cor(nuclear-OXPHOS, mt%) = -0.685

mtDNA-arm  <-> priming :  raw -0.714  |  mt%-adjusted -0.202   (collapses)
imbalance  <-> priming :  raw +0.697  |  mt%-adjusted +0.343   (halves)
nuclear-OX <-> priming :  raw +0.458  |  mt%-adjusted +0.477   (survives)
```

## What mt% is

**mt% = the fraction of the transcriptome coming from the 13 mtDNA-encoded genes** (`mt-Nd*`, `mt-Co*`, `mt-Atp6/8`, `mt-Cytb`) — `colSums(counts[13 mt genes]) / colSums(all counts)`. It's the "percent mitochondrial" number, the same `percent.mt` used as a QC flag in single-cell.

## Why it's a confound *here specifically*

mt% is the **one axis in this dataset that cannot be resolved as biological vs technical**, for a chain of reasons that all sit in CLAUDE.md:

- These MECs were purified by **warm enzymatic dissociation, not FACS**. When a cell is stressed or dying, its membranes leak — **cytoplasmic (nuclear-encoded) mRNA escapes faster than mitochondria-enclosed mtRNA**, so the *relative* mt fraction rises. High mt% is the canonical marker of a damaged/dying cell.
- There is **no dissociation-batch, viability, or RIN metadata** on disk, and **batch = timepoint**, so there is nothing to adjust against.
- mt% spans **3.4%–40%** — a 12-fold range that is far too wide for pure biological mito-content variation; it is the fingerprint of prep-quality variation mixed in.

So mt% is a genuinely **mixed axis** — some real mito content/copy-number, some dissociation damage, not separable with these data.

## Why that "invalidates" the imbalance coupling

The mitonuclear imbalance was operationalised as **nuclear-OXPHOS − mtDNA-OXPHOS** (mitoPPS space). But the mtDNA term *is* the 13 mt genes, i.e. **the imbalance is mt% wearing a different label**: `cor(imbalance, mt%) = −0.92`, `cor(mtDNA-arm, mt%) = +0.95`. It is not an independent measurement of a nuclear-vs-mitochondrial mismatch — numerically it's the QC axis.

Because of that, **any correlation the imbalance shows is mostly a correlation of mt% with that thing.** priming also rides mt% (−0.60), so the imbalance↔priming coupling of −0.71 is largely mt% × mt%. Partial out mt% and it **collapses −0.71 → −0.20** — ~72% of it was the confound.

Two precise points on the word "invalidate":

1. It invalidates the **transcriptomic evidence offered for the imbalance**, not the *physical existence* of a mitonuclear mismatch. A real imbalance could exist; this RNA-seq just can't testify to it, because its measurement lives on an unresolvable technical axis.
2. The imbalance was **already unsupported on its own terms** independently of mt% — no fitted contrast survives (time p=0.31, genotype p=0.52, interaction p=0.92; it was only ever four group means reported as if a trend). The mt% finding explains *why the one correlation that looked strong is spurious.*

## The clean contrast — and the fix

The **nuclear OXPHOS ↔ priming** lead does *not* depend on mt% (+0.458 → **+0.477** when mt% is removed), even though nuclear OXPHOS itself anticorrelates with mt% (−0.69). That's the one weak-but-real transcriptomic lead → BH3 profiling. The mtDNA/imbalance question needs **mtDNA qPCR**, which measures copy number physically and is immune to the read-share confound.

## Why mitoPPS didn't already fix it (the "mtDNA-arm border")

mitoPPS is a pairwise **ratio**, so it cancels a global multiplicative shift (library size, global amplification) — that's why it dropped the ambient ceiling 0.80 → 0.42. But a ratio **cannot cancel variation in the mtDNA fraction itself**, because the mtDNA genes form their own arm whose share *is* mt%. So mitoPPS cleans the common mode but leaves the mt% axis fully intact — and anything riding mt% (imbalance, mtDNA-arm) is not protected. That boundary is exactly why this coupling slips through when the others are clean.

The addendum figure I just specified is unrelated to this (it's mito-vs-non-mito *loading* on the global axis) — so this doesn't change the plan. I'll re-present it for approval.

But the group separation (6.7 vs 15.6) is smaller than the within-group spread, so any per-sample coupling is dominated by the noisy, prep-linked part.

So when the imbalance (= −mt%, essentially) couples to priming at −0.71, a large share of that is being driven by a handful of high-mt samples like the 40% outlier — exactly the kind of coupling that should be tested with mtDNA qPCR, not read off this axis.

ASSISTANT  2026-07-20 00:29:06
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

`cor(mt%, prolif) = −0.614` — essentially identical to `cor(mt%, priming) = −0.597`. That closes the loop. Here's the untangling:

## The negative sign doesn't contradict the paper's death ideas — it contradicts a mis-reading of what mt% *is*

The key correction: **mt% is not a mitochondrial-*content* measure.** It's the *mtDNA-encoded fraction* — the share of the 13 mt-genes. And in this dataset it runs **opposite** to nuclear mitochondrial content: `cor(nuclear-OXPHOS, mt%) = −0.685`. Myc raises nuclear mito content (+21–27%) while mt% *falls*. So "high mt%" ≠ "more mitochondria" here; if anything it's "mtDNA arm relatively dominant / nuclear arm relatively low."

Once you see that, both of the paper's candidate mito→death models actually **predict** the negative sign:

| model | mechanism | prediction |
|---|---|---|
| **content / biogenesis → death** | Myc ↑ **nuclear** mito content → lower apoptotic threshold. Nuclear content is *high when mt% is low*. | mt% ↔ priming **negative** ✓ |
| **mitonuclear imbalance → death** | nuclear OXPHOS outruns mtDNA (low mtDNA = low mt%) → proteostatic stress primes death | mt% ↔ priming **negative** ✓ |
| naive "high mt% = death" | reads mt% as *content* — but mt% isn't content here | mt% ↔ priming positive ✗ |

The only model that predicts a *positive* sign is the one that equates mt% with mito content, which is exactly the equation that fails in this data. Internally the whole sign structure is coherent with the imbalance/nuclear-content story: `imbalance↔mt% −0.92`, `imbalance↔priming +0.70`, `nuclear-OX↔priming +0.46`, `mtDNA-arm↔priming −0.71` all point the same way. So your instinct that "something is off" was right — but the fix is that mt% was being read as content when it's the inverse.

## Why this still doesn't rescue the imbalance (the deeper reason, now sharper)

The sign being *consistent* with the biology is not evidence *for* it, because the negative correlation is over-determined — three different things all produce it and they can't be separated:

1. **The imbalance *is* mt%** (r=−0.92). "imbalance ↔ priming" is literally "mt% ↔ priming" relabeled. Adjusting for mt% collapses it (0.70→0.34) not because a rival confound explains it away, but because the imbalance carries **no information beyond mt%** — it inherits mt%'s unresolvability wholesale.

2. **mt% is a proliferation artifact of the denominator.** `cor(mt%, prolif) = −0.61 ≈ cor(mt%, priming) = −0.60`. mt% is a *fraction*: a proliferating cell pours out nuclear/cytoplasmic mRNA, inflating the denominator and mechanically deflating mt% — with **zero change in mtDNA copy number**. 6W_pos having the lowest mt% (6.7%) is exactly what "6W_pos is the most proliferative group" predicts. So the negative mt%↔priming can be entirely mediated by proliferation (the dominant global axis), no mitonuclear biology required.

3. **mt% is also prep quality** (the 40% outlier, the 10-fold within-group spread). Unresolvable without QC metadata.

So mt% is a **three-way-confounded fraction** — real mtDNA content × proliferation denominator × prep damage — and every death-priming correlation that rides it is consistent with all three at once. The coherent sign structure tells you the *bookkeeping* is self-consistent; it cannot tell you *which mechanism* wrote the books.

**Bottom line:** the negative sign is a point *for* the imbalance/nuclear-content reading over the naive one, but it doesn't lift the coupling above "hypothesis" — because the measurement conflates the biology you want with two things you can't remove. The clean test is still **mtDNA qPCR** (absolute copy number, denominator-free, prep-robust) paired with a real death readout — that's the only way to ask whether mtDNA genuinely lags, rather than reading it off a fraction that proliferation and prep quality both move.

## You're right: "prep-stress → death → high mt%" is contradicted

Your syllogism is: *if* the mt% variation comes from a prep-stress→death process, the stressed (high-mt%) samples should be the death-primed ones → positive mt%↔priming. The data say the opposite at every link: mt% tracks prep-stress strongly (IEG +0.74), but **priming falls with prep-stress (−0.45)** and falls with mt% (−0.60). The most prep-stressed samples are the *least* death-primed transcriptionally. So the specific hypothesis "mt% is elevated because those cells/samples underwent a death process" is not supported — good catch, that reading is out.

## The refinement: prep-stress raises mt% *without* going through death

The reason this prunes the argument but doesn't clear mt% is that **"prep-stress → high mt%" never needed a death middle-term.** The mechanism is *compositional*, not apoptotic:

- Enzymatic dissociation damages membranes → nuclear-encoded cytoplasmic mRNA leaks out/degrades → the recovered pool is relatively enriched in mitochondrially-sequestered transcripts → mt% rises. That's a **mechanical/quality** effect, not the cell transcribing apoptosis genes.
- The apoptotic *program* (what "priming" measures) takes hours a rapid digest+lysis doesn't allow, and priming is a **nuclear/nuclear ratio** that largely cancels uniform leak. So a sample can be prep-damaged (high mt%, high IEG) while its transcriptome is *not* death-primed.
- The IEG signature itself (Fos/Jun/Egr1) is an immediate-early *stress/survival* response — distinct from, and here anticorrelated with, apoptotic priming.

So the chain the data support is **prep-stress → mt% (yes) but prep-stress → priming (no, negative)** — no contradiction, because the "death" link you inserted is exactly the one that's absent. mt% is a prep-stress/quality axis *and* a proliferation-denominator axis, and **both are death-agnostic.**

## What it all collapses to: one proliferation↔stress axis

Every correlation above is one axis seen from different sides:

| pole | proliferation | IEG stress | mt% | priming |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **growth** | high | low | low | **high** |
| **stressed/low-growth** | low | high | high | **low** |

priming sits on the growth pole; mt% sits on the stress/low-growth pole; hence the negative mt%↔priming, mediated by proliferation — not by death in either direction.

## Net effect on the imbalance

Your pruning actually cuts *against* the death claim, not for it:

- It removes the "mt% is a QC-death artifact" worry (mt% isn't tracking apoptosis) — fair.
- But it does **not** make the imbalance a citable death coupling. The imbalance *is* mt% (r=−0.92), so imbalance↔priming inherits **mt%↔priming = the proliferation/stress axis**, not a mitonuclear→death mechanism. If anything, showing mt% is death-agnostic means the imbalance axis is death-agnostic too — so "mitonuclear imbalance primes death" loses its mechanism, not gains one.

So: mt% is confounded, just not by *death* — it's prep-quality + proliferation-denominator, and priming rides proliferation the other way. The imbalance→death reading still needs **mtDNA qPCR** (absolute copy number, denominator- and leak-free) plus a real death readout; the transcriptome here is measuring growth state, not an apoptotic gate.

ASSISTANT  2026-07-20 00:53:37
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Read the relevant parts — this is the Lesner et al. (M. Celeste Simon lab) bioRxiv preprint, and it tests almost exactly our question in TCGA + mouse HCC. It's highly relevant, and it cuts in a precise direction: it **validates the phenomenon but reframes the mechanism, and it does not rescue the priming coupling.**

## What the paper actually shows (Fig 1)

- MitoCarta-based scoring of paired tumor/normal across TCGA; then — the key move — **they separate mito genes by genomic origin.** Result (Fig 1D/E, LIHC and pan-cancer): **MYC-high tumors enrich nuclear-encoded mito transcripts but deplete mtDNA-encoded transcripts** — "induction of a nuclear mitochondrial gene-expression program without a corresponding increase in mitochondrial genome-derived transcripts."
- Control: a **non-mitochondrial MYC score** (Hallmark MYC minus MitoCarta overlap).
- Mechanism they land on: *not* biogenesis. mtDNA transcripts fall because of **elevated mitochondrial turnover** — fission (DRP1/DNM1L) + **receptor-mediated mitophagy (FUNDC1, PGAM5, BNIP3/NIX; not PINK1/Parkin)**, driven by **MYC → NRF1 → DRP1/FUNDC1**, plus (liver-specific) ammonia/HIF-driven OXPHOS uncoupling.
- Death/survival link runs the *protective* way: DRP1 knockout **reduces** mitophagy/ROS and **improves survival** (mitophagy keeps tumor cells alive); conversely forced **fusion** (MFN2/OPA1) → apoptosis, synergistic with **BCL-2 inhibitors**.
- Mouse validation of the mtDNA arm: **qPCR of mtDNA copy number, mt-ND2 normalized to nuclear Pecam1** (Methods p20).

## Relevance to our question

**1. It independently validates our "imbalance" *phenomenon* — and kills the "it's our dissociation" worry.** Our observation (Myc raises nuclear mito content +21–27% while the mtDNA arm lags) *is* the Lesner discordance, in a mammary model. Crucially, **TCGA is flash-frozen bulk tissue — no enzymatic dissociation** — and they see the same nuclear-up/mtDNA-down signature across cancers including LIHC, corroborated by proteomics (ETC protein down) and mouse qPCR. So the *direction* is a real, cross-cancer, MYC-associated transcriptional state, not an artifact of our warm digest. That's strong external support for the half of our story that survives.

**2. It does NOT make our mt%↔priming coupling citable — and it reframes the death arm the way our data already hinted.** Their mechanism for mtDNA depletion is **turnover/mitophagy**, not a nuclear/mtDNA regulatory imbalance, and its functional meaning is **survival** (mitophagy protective; apoptosis engaged by the *opposite* manipulation + BH3 mimetics). So a low-mtDNA state is, if anything, pro-survival in their model — entirely consistent with our finding that the transcriptomic "imbalance → death priming" coupling is null/uninterpretable. The paper effectively replaces the unsupported "imbalance primes death" bridge with a **turnover/mitophagy + BH3** framework — which is exactly the BH3-profiling direction we'd already landed on.

**3. It endorses our proposed experiments and hands us the methods.** Everything we said the question needs, they did:
- **mtDNA qPCR (mt-ND2 / nuclear Pecam1)** — precisely the assay I recommended to escape the mt% confound; now we can cite their protocol.
- **non-mito MYC score** (Hallmark MYC minus MitoCarta) — directly usable against our correlation-ceiling / "is it just MYC dose" problem (scripts 35/36).
- **NRF1 is the mediator** (MYC→NRF1→DRP1/FUNDC1), and they ran **sgNRF1 / sgDRP1 / sgFUNDC1** perturbations. That is the same axis our script 38 flagged as inseparable-from-MYC-in-bulk (PGC1a/**NRF1**/ESRRA), and `NRF1_MITO` was a top loader in this session's ranking. Our "needs an ESRRA/PGC1a/NRF1 perturbation" conclusion is exactly what they performed.

## The honest nuance to carry into the narrative

Their discordance is a **MYC (genotype-like) contrast.** In *our* data, the nuclear-up half reproduces cleanly as a **genotype** effect (+21–27%, d≈1.2), but the mtDNA-down half **does not reach a genotype contrast** — mt%/the mtDNA arm is genotype-*independent* (p≈0.49) and its "rise" in our data is a **time (6W→12W, batch-confounded)** effect, not a Myc effect. So Lesner:
- validates that the discordance is a real MYC phenomenon *worth* testing, and
- pinpoints exactly where our data is underpowered/confounded (the mtDNA arm) — which is *why* qPCR is the answer, not a reason to claim we've demonstrated the genotype contrast ourselves.

And a scope caveat: their **mechanism** is liver-specific in parts (hyperammonemia, urea cycle, HIF/hypoxia) — those won't transfer to mammary MEC. The transferable core is **MYC → NRF1 → mito-turnover (fission/mitophagy) with OXPHOS suppressed despite nuclear induction**; whether MMTV-Myc mammary engages that same NRF1/DRP1/FUNDC1 turnover axis is an open, testable question our loading/PGC1a results point straight at.

## Bottom line

This paper is a strong citation and a partial rescue — of the *phenomenon*, not the *death coupling*. It lets the manuscript say: the MYC nuclear-induction / mtDNA-lag discordance is an independently established, cross-cancer state (Lesner et al., TCGA + mouse HCC); our mammary data show the nuclear-induction half as a clean genotype effect; the mtDNA half and its link to apoptotic priming are underpowered/confounded here and should be resolved by **mtDNA qPCR + BH3 profiling + NRF1/mitophagy perturbation** — the very assays that paper used. It replaces the retracted "imbalance→death" bridge with a literature-anchored, testable turnover/mitophagy model.
