Committed locally (`e27d1ad`), not pushed — script 40 needs your run first.

## What to run

```r
source(here::here("scripts", "40_background_vs_myc_decomposition.R"))   # ~1 min, writes results/background_vs_myc.rds
source(here::here("figures", "fig03_background_vs_myc.R"))
```
Then the `if (FALSE)` sandbox in 40 prints the tables in the order the argument needs them. fig03 reads its annotations from the object, so the percentiles self-update from your canonical run (mine was a reduced-permutation dry run).

## The answer to your question

**No — and the negative is sharper than the positive would have been.**

**Myc's effect is rescaled, not reshaped.** The 12W Myc profile *is* the 6W profile at 55% amplitude (slope 0.55, boot 0.51–0.60, R² 0.80, rho 0.84; per-tier 0.53–0.83). R² sits at the 100th percentile of gene-label shuffles that preserve set size, expression *and* pathway overlap. Nothing about which pathways Myc favours changes.

**What Myc adds over the timeline is a uniform offset.** `Myc+time ~ WTtime`: the slope (0.75) is not distinguishable from an arbitrary matched panel (null 0.63, 82nd pct); the intercept (−0.17) is at the 0th percentile — and it is the only batch-clean term, since a common offset cancels in the difference.

**The background moves away, not toward.** WT-time projects onto the Myc vector at 0.064 vs a null of 0.24 — *below* an arbitrary panel — and cos −0.34/−0.39 in the biogenesis+OXPHOS arms. Meanwhile cos(Myc+time, Myc@6W) = **−0.84** (0th pct): over the timeline Myc+ retraces its own programme backwards. That is the attenuation.

**And the WT-convergence term does not survive its control.** This is the new result and it touches Issue #6 directly: `myc_6W = pos6 − neg6` and `timepoint_neg = neg12 − neg6` share the 6W WT baseline *with opposite signs*, so noise in that baseline manufactures convergence. Splitting the six 6W_neg mice across all 20 three-vs-three partitions:

| | published | split |
|---|---|---|
| ALL genes (global) | 0.630 | **0.478** (chance) |
| Amino acid / lipid | 0.77 / 0.73 | **0.65 / 0.63** (survives) |
| OXPHOS subunits | 0.269 | **0.382** (diverges, survives) |
| MYC-target core | 0.273 | **0.360** (diverges, survives) |

conv_pct globally: **+42% → −12%**. The programme-specificity was the whole result; the global "~34% WT-convergence" was the artifact. Script 31 is untouched on disk — 40 tests it and reports the correction; whether to rewrite 31 is your call.

## Two things you should know before writing

**An artifact ledger, saved with the object.** `cor(WT-time, change in Myc effect)` = −0.185 (content) / −0.327 (priority) — and the value the marginals *force* is exactly −0.185 / −0.327. Same for `cor(retention, WT-time)` = −0.52 and the mitoPPS baseline-vs-effect correlations (−0.79/−0.88). None of them can be cited; they're in `$artifact_ledger` with verdicts so the next reader meets them labelled.

**The attenuation has no single size.** Same gene sets: the share ruler retains 77–83% of the genotype gap at 12W, the LFC rulers 54–63%. Sign and direction agree; magnitude is normalisation-dependent. The section quotes the range rather than picking.

Two judgement calls I made and flagged in-script: the synthetic mtDNA-encoded pathway is excluded from every fit (a 4–6.5 SD outlier that alone moved the shared slope 0.75→0.84), and the 13 mt genes are dropped from the OXPHOS tier's content share (they made it an mt% readout). Both are visible in the code, neither is hidden in an aggregate.

Script 40. Is Myc's mitochondrial effect shaped by a changing background?

PART A. Three rulers, 144 MitoPathways. The identity (Myc@12W - Myc@6W) ==
  (Myc+ temporal - WT temporal) holds exactly on BOTH the content and the priority
  ruler, so the two decompositions below are of the same quantity. The synthetic
  mtDNA-encoded pathway is flagged `is_mtdna` and EXCLUDED from every fit, null and
  geometry: it is a 4-6.5 SD outlier on every temporal contrast and alone moves the
  shared-vector slope 0.75 -> 0.84. Its row stays in `ruler`, reported separately.
PART B. Regression 1 (rescale): the 12W Myc profile IS the 6W profile times a
  constant -- read `regressions` for the slope and `regression_null` for where it
  sits against expression-matched random sets. Regression 2 (shared): the slope is
  the shared temporal component, the INTERCEPT is the batch-clean interaction.
  TWO nulls, both CONTENT-ruler only (mitoPPS has no random-set analogue -- it is
  a ratio built on the MitoCarta partition; its ambient is script 38's ~0.42):
  PRIMARY = within-decile LABEL SHUFFLE, which preserves set size, expression and
  the pathway OVERLAP structure (MitoPathways nest, and that nesting alone creates
  cross-pathway correlation); SECONDARY (`_rs` columns) = decile-matched
  resampling, which does not preserve overlap.
PART C. THE CONTROL THAT MATTERS. Issue #6's WT-convergence shares the 6W WT
  baseline with the genotype contrast, which manufactures apparent convergence.
  `split_summary` recomputes it over all 20 three-versus-three splits of the
  6W_neg mice. `conv_pct_shared` is the same-quantifier control (log-mean, no
  split) and tracks `conv_pct_published` (script 31, effect universe), so the
  split is the only thing that changes. PRIMARY READ = `frac_wt_toward`, the
  fraction of genes whose WT temporal change points toward Myc (0.5 = chance);
  conv_pct is a ratio of noisy quantities and is reported as a ratio of means,
  never a mean of ratios. No p is offered against 0.5 -- genes within an arm are
  correlated -- so the 20-split range is what is read.
PART D. Geometry: cos and projection of the WT 6->12 vector on the Myc(6W) vector,
  whole compartment and per tier, against the same null.
PART E. The attenuation's SIZE is normalisation-dependent (share vs DESeq LFC vs
  expression-weighted LFC vs gene-wise z). Quote the range, not one number.
PART F. `state_table` = the 7 Level-1 tiers x 4 groups in (priority, content)
  space; fig03 panel A draws the WT 6->12, Myc+ 6->12 and genotype arrows on it.
PART G. `artifact_ledger`: statistics whose observed value equals the value the
  algebra forces. They are not evidence. Do not cite them. It is computed on the
  FULL 144-pathway table on purpose -- these are the numbers a reader would get.

SCOPE. Descriptive/exploratory, n=6/group. BATCH = TIMEPOINT: the batch offset
cancels in the interaction (regression 2's intercept) but NOT in the
convergence/fade split, and 'developmental' stays an interpretation of the shared
vector. The split removes the shared-baseline ARTIFACT, not the batch confound. , now running the figure

The canonical run reproduces the dry run exactly. But the per-tier geometry (new to me) and one pattern in PART C need a check before you build narrative on it.

**The problem:** splitting the baseline uses 3 mice instead of 6, which adds noise to `d = sign(myc_6W)`. Sign noise pulls `frac_wt_toward` toward 0.5 **from both sides** — and that is exactly what the table shows (convergent arms fall 0.63→0.48, 0.77→0.65; divergent arms *rise* 0.27→0.36, 0.40→0.38). So part of the collapse could be attenuation-toward-chance rather than removal of the artifact. The published-vs-split comparison confounds the two.

The fix is a matched control: same 3-mouse baseline, **shared** between the two contrasts vs **split**. Same `d`, same universe, same noise — the only difference is the sharing.

Mouse orthologs are one-to-one and all 10 are in the matrix (MXI1 *is* MXD2, so the family is complete without a separate entry).

## Myc itself — the assumption holds, and then some

| | 6W WT | 6W Myc+ | 12W WT | 12W Myc+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Myc, normalised counts | 2543 | 8142 | 2143 | 7578 |

Genotype gap **+1.64 log2 at 6W → +1.80 at 12W** (both p<1e-5). Within genotypes: WT −0.25 (p=0.053), Myc+ **−0.08 (p=0.72)**, interaction p=0.51. The DESeq2 contrasts agree (+1.68 / +1.82, both padj<0.001; interaction padj 1.0).

So Myc message does not decline in Myc+ across the window — if anything the genotype gap is marginally *wider* at 12W.

## The network is flat, with two hints

Nothing in MAX/MXD1/MXD3/MXD4/MXI1/MNT/MGA/MLX moves on the clean genotype axis. Two exceptions, both on the **MLX arm** and both on the batch-confounded time axis:

- **Mlxip (MondoA)** — 3279 → 2883 in Myc+ while WT rises 3117 → 3467; Myc+ time p=0.0013, genotype@12W p=0.0052 (DESeq padj 0.061). Well-expressed, so not a low-count artifact.
- **Mlxipl (ChREBP)** — falls in Myc+ (p=0.0076), but at 30–63 counts it is fragile.

Neither clears BH over the 11 × 4 family, and the genome-wide DESeq2 **interaction** padj — the batch-clean quantity — is >0.05 for every network gene (Mlxip 0.83). A lead about the glucose-sensing paralogue arm, not a result.

Also: the repressor sum rises slightly with age in both genotypes (+0.25 WT, +0.16 Myc+, both ns), so Myc *relative* to its competitors does not fall either — Myc:repressors +1.65 → +1.90.

## The panel-C payoff

Measured identically, at 6W → 12W:

| | genotype gap 6W | 12W | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Myc | +1.64 | +1.80 | **+0.17** |
| Myc : MAX | +1.42 | +1.74 | **+0.32** |
| Myc : repressor sum | +1.65 | +1.90 | **+0.25** |
| MYC targets (Hallmark V2) | +1.32 | +0.95 | **−0.36** |
| MYC signature (Felsher) | +1.42 | +1.10 | −0.32 |

**Every measure of the driver widens; the output narrows.** That is an internal control for `sec-attenuation` stronger than the literature citation the assumption was resting on — the attenuation cannot be a dose decline, because the dose measured four ways goes the other way.

One caveat I've recorded in the script rather than buried: these are reads on the mouse *Myc* locus, so total Myc message in Myc+ is transgene + endogenous and the two aren't separable here. "Constant dose" is a statement about total Myc message — which is what the substrate actually sees, so it's the right quantity for this argument, but it can't tell you whether transgene expression specifically drifted.

All 31 resolved in the matrix. Answer first, then the problem with it.

## Yes — five are down, and two up

`timepoint_pos` (12W Myc+ vs 6W Myc+), genome-wide DESeq2 FDR; the same five survive BH within this 31-gene panel:

| gene | LFC | padj | baseMean | same contrast in **WT** | interaction padj |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Trim6** | −1.01 | 0.015 | 39 | −0.40 (p 0.19) | 1.000 |
| **Pias4** | −0.40 | 0.031 | 278 | −0.27 (p **0.047**) | 1.000 |
| **Fbxw7** | −0.35 | 0.050 | 780 | −0.00 (p 0.98) | 1.000 |
| **Usp36** | −0.33 | 0.022 | 1131 | −0.16 (p 0.13) | 1.000 |
| **Huwe1** | −0.24 | 0.006 | 11662 | −0.13 (p **0.049**) | 1.000 |
| *Ep300* | +0.25 | 0.041 | 3533 | +0.27 (p 0.002) | 1.000 |
| *Sirt1* | +0.76 | <0.001 | 967 | +0.56 (p <0.001) | 1.000 |

## Three reasons I don't think this supports the hypothesis

**1. Nothing is Myc-specific.** The interaction padj is **1.000 for all 31 genes**, and BH within the panel gives nothing either. Pias4, Huwe1, Ep300 and Sirt1 move in WT too — this is the batch-confounded time axis, which is exactly the axis we agreed is descriptive.

**2. The panel is not moving more than the genome.** Against expression-matched genes the panel median is **−0.087 vs a null of −0.071 (p = 0.83)**; on the interaction, −0.111 vs −0.077 (p = 0.49). This is the global attenuation passing through the panel, not a targeted change in the MYC-stability machinery. (Same lesson as script 34's `atten_excess`.)

**3. The directions point the wrong way.** FBXW7 and HUWE1 are the two best-established degradative E3s for MYC — both **down**, which predicts *more* stable MYC protein at 12W, not less. The one hit in the right direction is **Usp36** (a MYC-stabilising DUB, −0.33), but it falls in WT too. And the arms move together: E3 ligases median −0.25, DUBs median −0.24 — the ubiquitin balance doesn't shift.

The **T58 phosphodegron axis is completely flat**: Mapk1 +0.17, Mapk3 +0.18, Gsk3b +0.02, Pin1 +0.04, Ppp2ca −0.00, Ppp2cb +0.04, no p below 0.18. So the canonical ERK-S62 / GSK3β-T58 / PIN1 / PP2A route shows no transcriptional change at all. Meanwhile the proliferation-linked kinases stay Myc-induced at both ages (Cdk1 +0.82/+0.73, Skp2 +0.91/+0.94, Aurka +1.13/+0.67).

## The limitation that matters most

Post-translational regulation is, by definition, not visible in transcript levels. This panel can rule out a *large transcriptional reprogramming* of the stability machinery — and it does — but it cannot rule out a change in its **activity**. A constant Fbxw7 mRNA with altered T58 phosphorylation would look exactly like this. So the honest conclusion is "no transcriptional evidence for it", not "it isn't happening".

If MYC protein stability is now a live hypothesis, the reagents that would settle it: MYC protein blot at both ages (does protein track the flat mRNA?), phospho-T58/S62 blot, and a cycloheximide chase in 6W vs 12W tumour cells. That's a bench question, not one this dataset can answer.

Want me to keep this? Two options: a `figS9` panel (the 31 genes as small multiples plus the arm-level summary and the matched-background null), or just a table written to `outputs/` with the numbers above. Say which and I'll build it — otherwise it stays in the scratchpad.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **BATCH = TIMEPOINT**: 6W/12W were extracted as two batches, so genotype/interaction contrasts are clean and the pure temporal axis is batch-confounded and not separable.
   - **The exact identity**: `(Myc@12W − Myc@6W) == (Myc+ temporal − WT temporal)`, verified to machine precision on both the content and priority rulers.
   - **Three rulers**: content = DESeq2 set-average **raw** log2FC; priority = mitoPPS pairwise diff (Monzel 2025, content-blind ratio); share = % of nuclear transcriptome (script 32, 13 mt-* genes out of numerator and denominator).
   - **Shared-baseline artifact**: `myc_6W = pos6 − neg6` and `timepoint_neg = neg12 − neg6` share `neg6` with opposite signs, so `cov = +var(neg6) > 0` — noise manufactures apparent WT-convergence.
   - **Matched control**: each of the 20 C(6,3) partitions run twice off the *same* half baseline (shared vs split) — identical `d`, universe and noise, so the paired difference isolates the sharing artifact from attenuation-to-chance.
   - **Two nulls**: primary = within-decile gene-**label shuffle** (preserves set size, expression, and pathway **overlap**, since MitoPathways nest); secondary = decile-matched resampling.
   - **Artifact ledger**: statistics whose observed value equals the value the algebra forces (cor(WTtime, Δ-Myc-effect) = −0.185/−0.327 exactly).
   - **`recon_to_ensembl` / `functions/reconcile_gene_symbols.R`**: mandatory vintage-aware symbol→Ensembl mapping for any set aggregation.
   - Figure layer: `figures/theme_myc.R` (`theme_myc()`, `save_panel()` cairo_pdf, `fig_w` = 89/120/183mm, `group_cols`/`group_labels`), guarded save via `options(myc.fig.nosave=TRUE)`, patchwork, ggrepel.

       b  <- setdiff(idx[["6W_neg"]], a)      # anchors the WT TEMPORAL contrast (split only)

       dplyr::bind_rows(
         one_run(m6a, gm_of(idx[["12W_neg"]]) - gm_of(a), sh_tp, "half_shared", k),
         one_run(m6a, gm_of(idx[["12W_neg"]]) - gm_of(b), sh_tp, "half_split",  k))
     }))
     ```

     ```r
     paired <- split_runs |>

       tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = mode, values_from = c(frac_wt_toward, wt_conv)) |>
       dplyr::group_by(program, arm) |>
       dplyr::summarise(
         frac_artifact = mean(frac_wt_toward_half_shared - frac_wt_toward_half_split),
         frac_artifact_sd = stats::sd(frac_wt_toward_half_shared - frac_wt_toward_half_split),

Checked the numbers your model rests on before answering.

## Your premise is correct

On the content ruler, per Level-1 tier (median set log2FC):

| tier | Myc@6W | WT 6→12W | Myc+ 6→12W | attenuation | % of pathways WT-down |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| OXPHOS | +0.46 | **−0.14** | −0.27 | −0.18 | 63% |
| Protein import | +0.52 | **−0.06** | −0.28 | −0.22 | 75% |
| Central dogma | +0.47 | +0.05 | −0.19 | −0.24 | 10% |
| Metabolism | +0.40 | +0.08 | −0.11 | −0.18 | 12% |

The genes Myc pushes hardest are genuinely the ones sliding down in the untransformed gland. That is real and it is the strongest thing your model has.

## Three things argue against the *selective* version

1. **The attenuation is uniform.** Rescaling slope 0.55, R²=0.80, per-tier slopes 0.53–0.83, and script 34 found no programme attenuating more than expression-matched genes. A specific NR repressing specific mito genes should leave a selective dent. There is none. Note also the tier pattern runs the *wrong* way — central dogma's background moves *with* Myc yet attenuates most — though that comparison is partly forced by the algebra, so I'm not counting it as evidence either way.
2. **No repressor is induced.** I scanned 111 candidates — NRs, corepressors, PRC, DREAM/repressive E2Fs, circadian, mammary differentiation TFs. Six move in the background at FDR<0.05; **zero** have a significant interaction. And the movers point the wrong way: *Esrrb* (an ESRR **activator**) up +1.58, *E2f7* (a repressive E2F) **down** −0.83.
3. **The canonical antagonists are flat** — figS8 already showed MXD1/3/4, MXI1, MNT, MGA unchanged, with the Myc:repressor ratio *widening*.

## Two structural problems you should know about

4. **The obvious test is rigged.** "Genes where the background falls are the genes where Myc is blunted" is `cor(WT-time, ΔMyc-effect)` — in script 40's artifact ledger, observed = algebraically forced, to the decimal. Any predictor built from the same group means is contaminated. Also, your predictor lives entirely on the batch-confounded axis while the outcome (interaction) is the clean one.
5. **A repressor acting equally in both genotypes cancels in the genotype gap.** To shrink the gap its *effect* must scale with MYC. And a lower baseline normally leaves *more* headroom for induction, not less — so the model needs active blockade, not a lowered set point.

## Where your model actually gets strong

Point 5 is not a refutation — it's a specification, and one mechanism class satisfies it natively: **HLH sequestration / E-box competition**, whose effect scales with the activator present and therefore needs no interaction in its own expression. Two such factors *do* rise in the background: **Id4 +1.53 (padj 0.0013)** and **Hes1 +0.59 (0.012)**, both equally in Myc+.

And if the antagonist is **global rather than selective**, it predicts exactly the uniform ×0.55 rescaling we observe. That fits better than my "the programme autonomously decays" — which is really just a description. It also converges with yesterday's protein-stability idea: both are *effective MYC activity falls at constant message*. So I'd rank it: global damper on MYC's effective activity ≫ selective repression by induced NRs.

One gap worth knowing: Issue #5 (script 30) tested whether a Myc-independent axis absorbs the attenuation and found none — but every axis it tested was **activating** (luminal differentiation, ESRRA/NRF1/GABPA, proliferation). A **repressive** axis has never been tested. Your model is not a re-run of Issue #5.

## What we could find in favour

- **T1 — the de-confounded split test.** Estimate the WT background move from one half of the WT mice and the attenuation from the other half (both timepoints split), so no mouse is shared: does background direction predict attenuation once the algebra is broken? Script 40 PART C's machinery already does this. Necessary condition — if it fails, the model is done.
- **T2 — systematic TF-regulon excess-attenuation scan.** Across the library's TF lanes + the ChEA shortlist, whose regulon attenuates *more* than expression-matched background? A named repressor coming out is positive evidence, and it is the one thing that would make this publishable rather than speculative.
- **T3 — the repressive-axis moderation test.** Id4/Hes1/Id1-3 as a per-sample axis in script 30's moderation model — the untested arm of Issue #5.
- **T4 — bench (the only thing that truly settles it).** MYC CUT&RUN/ChIP at 6W vs 12W on the same promoters. Occupancy unchanged with output down ⇒ the block is at co-activator/elongation. Occupancy down at constant protein ⇒ competition, your model. Pairs with the MYC blot already planned.

**The numbers (DESeq2, genome-wide FDR — figS8's brackets are unadjusted simple-effect *p*):**

| gene | baseMean | Myc@6W | Myc@12W | WT 6→12W | Myc+ 6→12W | interaction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mlxip | 3187 | +0.07 (0.58) | −0.27 (**0.061**) | +0.15 | −0.19 (0.12) | −0.34 (**0.83**) |
| Mlxipl | 45 | +0.38 (0.80) | −0.26 (1.00) | −0.39 | −1.03 (**0.037**) | −0.64 (**1.00**) |
| Txnip | 3982 | −0.20 (0.62) | −0.18 (0.91) | −0.20 | −0.19 (0.75) | +0.02 (1.00) |

**The sign problem.** MondoA and ChREBP are E-box competitors. If they *fall* in Myc+, competition *decreases* — MYC gets more access, not less. As stated, that predicts the Myc effect should hold up better at 12W, the opposite of what we see.

**But there is a rescue, and it's a good one.** MLX is a shared partner: it dimerises with MondoA/ChREBP *and* with MXD1, MXD4 and MNT. Lose MondoA/ChREBP and you free MLX to form MXD:MLX repressive complexes at E-boxes. That is H2b — and it requires **no repressor transcript to change**, which is exactly why the flat MXD/MNT/MGA scan doesn't refute it. It's a stoichiometry hypothesis, not an expression one, so RNA-seq is structurally the wrong instrument for it. Co-IP or occupancy is the only read.

**Three things that currently hold it back:**

1. **The interaction is null** — padj 0.83 (Mlxip) and 1.00 (Mlxipl). "Down in Myc+" is a within-genotype change on the batch-confounded axis; the batch-clean quantity says nothing. That said, Mlxip is the *only* network gene whose shape would give an interaction if powered (WT +0.15 vs Myc+ −0.19) — it is the most interesting single gene in figS8 panel B.
2. **Txnip is flat** (−0.20 at 6W, −0.18 at 12W, both ns). TXNIP is MondoA's most sensitive output. If MondoA activity were genuinely falling, TXNIP should follow. It doesn't — so the functional readout of the mechanism is absent.
3. **Mlxipl is not usable**: baseMean 45, and the WT falls too (−0.39). Mammary is not a ChREBP tissue.

The alternative reading — MondoA/ChREBP as *co-activators* whose loss removes a second driver from shared metabolic targets — doesn't survive either: those targets straddle the global 55% retention rather than attenuating in excess (Ldha 85%, Elovl6 78%, Slc2a1 65%, Acly 51%, Acaca 50%).

So: worth naming in the write-up as **the one concrete H2b candidate**, explicitly as a protein-stoichiometry hypothesis that this data type cannot test, rather than as evidence.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/gs/.claude/skills/bio-reporting-quarto-reports

## Version Compatibility

Reference examples tested with: Quarto 1.4+, knitr 1.45+, pandoc 3.1+ (bundled), scanpy 1.10+, matplotlib 3.8+

Before using code patterns, verify installed versions match. If versions differ:
- CLI: `quarto --version`, `quarto check`, `quarto render --help`

Some flags and project keys move between Quarto releases (e.g. the file-based `--execute-params`); confirm against `quarto render --help`. If a render fails, run `quarto check` and adapt to the installed version rather than retrying.

# Quarto Reports

**"Create a Quarto analysis report"** -> Write a document mixing code (R/Python/Julia), narrative, and figures that executes through a computational engine and renders to HTML/PDF/Word.
- CLI: `quarto render report.qmd --to html`

## The Pipeline: Engine, Then Pandoc

Both Quarto and R Markdown end at pandoc; what differs is what runs before it. Quarto first picks a computational ENGINE, then pandoc converts to the target format. The engine is a property of the document's languages, and it determines what runtime the rendering machine needs:

- Any `{r}` chunk present -> **knitr** engine (same knit -> md -> pandoc path as R Markdown).
- Only `{python}`/`{julia}` chunks -> **jupyter** engine (executes via a Jupyter kernel, then pandoc).
- **Both R and Python -> knitr + reticulate in ONE process**, so R and Python share a session and can pass objects back and forth. (This is why mixed-language docs "just work" through knitr, not jupyter.)
- Override in YAML: `engine: knitr` / `engine: jupyter`, or pin a kernel with `jupyter: python3`.

The consequence: a Python-only `.qmd` on the jupyter engine needs a registered Jupyter kernel; switched to knitr+reticulate it needs R+reticulate instead. Freeze (below) lets CI skip needing either.

## Cache vs Freeze (the load-bearing distinction)

These solve DIFFERENT problems and are constantly conflated:

> knitr **cache** makes a SINGLE render faster by skipping unchanged chunks. Quarto **freeze** lets a DIFFERENT machine (CI / a website build) render with NO language runtime installed, by reusing stored results.

| | cache (`execute: cache`) | freeze (`execute: freeze`) |
|---|---|---|
| Granularity | per-chunk (knitr) / per-notebook (jupyter-cache) | per-document |
| Problem solved | skip unchanged chunks during a render | skip ALL execution on publish/CI |
| Key | MD5(code + evaluating options); data only via `cache.extra` | source-file hash (`auto`) or never re-run (`true`) |
| Lives in | `*_cache/` (per-doc) | `_freeze/` (project - **commit it**) |
| Runtime needed to render? | yes (still renders, skips some chunks) | **no** - CI renders with no R/Python |
| Invalidates on upstream DATA change? | NO unless `cache.extra` | only via source change (`auto`); data not auto-tracked |
| Scope | within one render | only FULL project renders |

Two edges that trip everyone:
- **The stale-cache footgun:** `cache=TRUE` keys on chunk CODE, not the data it reads. If `data.csv` changes but the chunk code is byte-identical, the cached (stale) result is served. Bind the data into the key: `cache.extra = tools::md5sum('data.csv')`. Cross-chunk dependencies need `dependson='chunkA'` (or `autodep=TRUE`, best-effort).
- **Freeze only acts on FULL project renders.** `quarto render onefile.qmd` and `quarto render subdir/` always execute, ignoring `freeze:`. Arrange CI to do a whole-project `quarto render` so frozen results are honored. Commit `_freeze/` so others render without reproducing the environment.
- **They compose, not conflict.** Freeze decides whether the project re-executes at all; when it does (source changed), knitr cache still skips unchanged chunks within that run.

## The Working-Directory Trap

Chunks execute with the working directory set to the document's folder, NOT the project root (default `execute-dir: file`). So `pd.read_csv('data/x.csv')` works interactively from the project root but breaks on render when the `.qmd` lives in `reports/`. Set `project: execute-dir: project` in `_quarto.yml` to run all chunks from the project root, or use root-anchored paths (`here::here(...)` in R). Never `setwd()` in a chunk - it desyncs figure/cache file placement.

## Cross-References Need the Type Prefix

A Quarto label is a cross-reference ONLY if it starts with a reserved lower-case type prefix: `fig-`, `tbl-`, `sec-`, `eq-`, `lst-`, theorem/callout families. `#| label: scatter` is a dead anchor; `#| label: fig-scatter` is referenceable as `@fig-scatter`. This is the #1 cause of a reference rendering as `?@fig-x`.

````markdown
```{python}
#| label: fig-umap
#| fig-cap: "UMAP embedding colored by cluster"
sc.pl.umap(adata, color='leiden')
```
See @fig-umap. Methods are in @sec-methods.
````

A figure/table from a code cell needs both the prefixed `label` and a `fig-cap`/`tbl-cap`. Section refs need `{#sec-methods}` on the heading AND `number-sections: true`. (Base R Markdown cannot cross-reference at all - that requires bookdown; see reporting/rmarkdown-reports.)

## Parameters: knitr vs jupyter Differ

- **knitr engine:** YAML `params:` block, accessed read-only as `params$x`. Override: `quarto render doc.qmd -P alpha:0.2`.
- **jupyter engine:** there is NO `params:` block. Designate a cell tagged `parameters` (papermill convention) with default assignments; variables are then top-level names. A `params:` YAML block on a jupyter-engine document is silently ignored - a common bug.

````markdown
```{python}
#| tags: [parameters]
input_file = "adata.h5ad"
n_top_genes = 2000
```
````

`-P key:val` overrides on the CLI for both engines.

## Document Basics and Layout

```yaml
---
title: "Analysis Report"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
    embed-resources: true   # one portable self-contained HTML
execute:
  warning: false
  freeze: auto
---
```

Per-cell options use the `#|` hash-pipe (`#| echo: false`, `#| fig-width: 8`, `#| cache: true`). Tabsets group alternative views under `::: {.panel-tabset}`; callouts (`::: {.callout-note}`) flag notes/warnings/tips. Render multiple formats by listing them under `format:` and `quarto render` (or `--to pdf`); PDF needs a TeX engine (`quarto install tinytex`).

## Self-Contained Output

`embed-resources: true` base64-inlines images, CSS, and JS into one portable HTML (maps to pandoc `--embed-resources --standalone`; the older `--self-contained` is deprecated since pandoc 2.19). htmlwidgets (plotly, DT) get inlined too, so an interactive report is one openable file - but each widget library inflates the size.

## The Document Captures Code, Not the Environment

Quarto does not pin package versions or the interpreter. A `.qmd` that renders perfectly today can silently change output next year when a dependency updates. The document gives byte-reproducible output only if code, data, AND versions are unchanged - and versions are not in the repo unless pinned. For real reproducibility add a lockfile/container: `renv::snapshot()` (`renv.lock`) for R, `environment.yml`/`requirements.txt` for Python, Docker/Apptainer when the OS, TeX, and pandoc must also be pinned. **Freeze is not reproducibility** - `_freeze/` lets CI skip execution, but the frozen results came from an uncaptured environment. Record provenance with `sessionInfo()` / `sessioninfo::session_info()` (provenance, not a restore mechanism). For journal submission, Quarto manuscript/journal templates (`quarto-journals/...`) produce article-formatted output from the same source.

## Common Errors

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `@fig-x` renders as `?@fig-x` | label missing the type prefix | name it `fig-x`/`tbl-x` and give it a caption |
| `params:` ignored on a Python doc | jupyter engine uses a `parameters`-tagged cell, not `params:` | tag a cell `parameters`, or use the knitr engine |
| Stale results after editing data | `cache` keys on code, not data | `cache.extra = tools::md5sum('data.csv')` |
| CI re-runs everything despite freeze | single-file/subdir render ignores freeze | do a full-project `quarto render`; commit `_freeze/` |
| `read_csv('data/..')` fails on render | working dir = doc folder, not project root | `execute-dir: project` or `here::here()` |
| Report reproduces differently months later | environment not pinned | renv.lock / conda env / container |
| PDF render fails | no TeX engine | `quarto install tinytex` |

- reporting/rmarkdown-reports - R-focused alternative; needs bookdown for cross-references
- reporting/jupyter-reports - Parameterized notebook execution Quarto can consume
- reporting/publication-tables - Formatted tables to embed in the report
- data-visualization/ggplot2-fundamentals - Figures for R-engine reports

## The line through it

Your two propositions aren't competing — they answer different questions, and the designs say which is which:

**MMTV-Myc is a dose experiment.** MYC protein −50% at constant transcript, and script 40's rescaling is ×0.55. Those are the same number. Output per unit MYC is unchanged, which retrospectively explains every negative we've accumulated: no reshaping, no programme in excess, no repressor, no moderating axis. There was nothing to find. Your mito and BAX/BIM/PUMA protein falls are that ×0.55 propagating to protein — they need no separate explanation.

**MYC-ER is a competence experiment**, and one design feature does the decisive work: **those 12W animals had never seen MYC before induction.** So the substrate change cannot be MYC-driven selection. It has to be developmental. That kills both of your dose-flavoured sub-hypotheses — "MYC engages PGC1a more at 6W" and "MYC pushes PGC1a over a threshold" are both dose mechanisms, and MYC-ER holds dose constant. Only (iii) survives. It also means the SS/passaged-PGC1a selection experiments belong to the *tumour-progression* half of the story, not the 6→12W half — that's the easiest mistake available here.

## What answers "why is PUMA lost"

MYC builds a death-ready mitochondrion at **both** ages — `Htra2` **+1.49 (padj 2.6e-08)**, the strongest apoptotic gene in the dataset and, per your own PUMA notes, the executioner released through the BAX/BAK pore; `Bax` +0.48; `Bcl-xL` **−0.42**, the brake removed; biogenesis up. What it loses by 12W is the **trigger**, and the evidence is a contrast that carries its own control:

| | 6W | 12W | retention |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bax : Bcl-xL | +0.90 | +0.50 | **0.55** — the global rate (46th pct) |
| PUMA : Bcl-xL | +0.67 | −0.06 | **−0.09** (92nd pct, int p 0.037; **0.006** purity-adjusted) |

The matched-pair null's own median retention is **0.53** — script 40's ×0.55 rebuilt from random genes, so the instrument is calibrated. And PUMA is the BH3-only your PGC1a work singles out, so the pair was pre-specified, not fished.

For the mechanism you were reaching for: **the Gray/ChEA shortlist lists `Bbc3` as a MYC/MYCN/E2F1 target only in the `AP_TEB` context**, and `Gray_et_al_developmental_TFS_selection.md` already records "**NRF1 → Bbc3** … the biogenesis TFs that build mito mass also touch pro-apoptotic effectors — a candidate co-regulation of apoptotic sensitivity", plus "the HS_TEB context is apoptosis-loaded". So: the promoter context in which MYC and the biogenesis TFs reach PUMA is a property of the pubertal gland, and it leaves with the end buds.

Committed as `5503aeb` (not pushed). Both changes are in.

**The correction stands as you made it.** Your (ii) is a two-input model — the substrate falls, not MYC — so MYC-ER holds MYC fixed and varies exactly the input the hypothesis names. It's the test, not the refutation. And it's the better frame for three reasons now written into both the script and the doc: proliferation needs one input and death two, so the 80%-vs-30% asymmetry follows with no extra assumption; a threshold on the product explains why PUMA priming collapses *through* zero rather than merely attenuating; and it's the title thesis stated literally.

**The mitoPPS strand was the real gap, and it's the strongest one.** The reason is structural: mitoPPS is a pairwise ratio, so a uniform ×0.55 dose scaling **cancels in it**. The content ruler is dose-dominated — that's the whole of section 1 — and the priority ruler is not. OXPHOS is still the most de-prioritised tier on both temporal axes, and within it the **structural subunits** carry it (−0.109 WT / −0.153 Myc+) while assembly factors don't move (−0.002 / −0.029). The subunits are the PGC1a/NRF1/ERRα output. So the arm PGC1a builds loses priority, and that is not the dose effect.

That gave three convergent strands, and script 38 PART B already supplied the third: OXPHOS-ratio ↔ priming-ratio, design-adjusted **+0.70 against a null of 0.48**, with `redox` failing as the control axis, **neither circular nor ceiling-bound**. Script 38's own conclusion was that this question "needs an ESRRA/PGC1a perturbation vs the Myc substrate, not n=24 bulk" — and that perturbation now exists in your cell arm.

One bound I'd keep visible: the apoptosis **composites** are flat over the timeline (PRO +0.054, ANTI +0.046 — they move together). That's why script 34 found nothing and why this had to be gene-level, and it's exactly what your cell data predicts, since PGC1a induces PUMA and not the other BH3-onlys. A 25-gene PRO composite is the wrong instrument.

The spine in §9 now runs observation → hypothesis → causal test in cells → back to the mouse, with a closing note on why leading with the phenotype instead invites the reader to weigh the correlation as evidence. The compositional/TEB reading stays as an explicitly parallel second input rather than a competitor.

Two things for you:

- Script 42 now reads `docs/library_reference/gray_chea_mito_tf_shortlist.csv`, which is still **untracked**. It's guarded with `file.exists()` so the script won't break, but an analysis dependency sitting outside git is worth fixing — say the word and I'll add it.
- Script 42 is unrun in all its parts. PART H is the one to read sceptically: check the `redox_ppd` rows first, because if the control axis behaves like the OXPHOS axis, the OXPHOS rows say nothing.

DOSE vs COMPETENCE. The MMTV-Myc 6W->12W timeline is a DOSE experiment: MYC protein
falls ~50% at constant transcript, and the transcriptome rescales x0.55 with no
reshaping (script 40), no programme in excess (script 34) and no repressor (the
2026-07-25 scans). Output per unit MYC is unchanged. The MYC-ER mouse is a COMPETENCE
experiment: equal or higher MYC protein, ~80% less death, ~30% less proliferation --
and since those animals never saw MYC before induction, the substrate change cannot be
MYC-driven selection. It is developmental. The two are not rival explanations; they
answer different questions.

PART B is the headline and it is a CONTRAST, not a p-value: within one panel sharing
the Bcl-xL denominator, Bax:Bcl-xL priming retains the global rate while PUMA:Bcl-xL
priming collapses. PUMA is the BH3-only the PGC1a cell experiments single out, so the
pair was pre-specified externally -- but the 9-pair panel is exploratory context and
int_p_bh is reported for it.

THREE NEGATIVES, to be quoted as prominently as the positives:
 1. PART C3 -- the per-sample OXPHOS<->PUMA coupling sits at or below the ambient. The
    OXPHOS-PUMA bundle is carried by the CELL PERTURBATIONS, never by in-vivo
    correlation. Do not claim it from these data.
 2. PART D -- Bbc3 is NOT in the TEB-vs-ductal signature. The TEB claim is about
    TF-binding CONTEXT (Gray/ChEA AP_TEB regulons contain Bbc3), not about PUMA being
    a TEB transcript.
 3. PART D -- the MEC state composites are not significant. Only markers move, so the
    substrate change is documented at marker level, not as a compartment shift.

CEILING. n=6/group, exploratory, ranking not confirmatory. WT temporal statements are
on the BATCH-CONFOUNDED axis (batch = timepoint) and are DESCRIBED, not claimed; their
mitigation is that the protein blots move the same way off the RNA batch entirely.
Script 34's circularity caveat still binds COMPOSITE death scores (Bbc3, Bax and
Bcl2l11 are all MitoCarta APOPTOSIS members) -- this script makes no composite
correlation claim. Ppargc1a is baseMean ~30 here and is NOT readable; ESRRA/NRF1/GABPA
lanes are the activity proxy, as in script 38 PART C.

PART E bounds the whole enterprise: there is no efferocytosis signature at 6W, so bulk
RNA cannot see the death. It also UNDER-reports the 6W pro-apoptotic induction, because
the cells that died are not in the library -- making the PUMA collapse a lower bound.

THE EPISTEMIC CONTRACT for PARTS G and H. The in-vivo transcriptome GENERATES the
hypothesis; the cell perturbations (PGC1a gain sensitises; SS and passaged cells lose
biogenesis and resist) PROVE it. No correlation here is asked to carry a causal claim.

PART G -- why the priority ruler earns its place. mitoPPS is a PAIRWISE RATIO within the
mitochondrial compartment, so a uniform x0.55 dose scaling CANCELS in it. The content
ruler is dose-dominated; the priority ruler is not. OXPHOS is nevertheless the most
de-prioritised Level-1 tier on BOTH temporal axes, carried by the structural SUBUNITS
while the assembly factors do not move -- and the subunits are the PGC1a/NRF1/ERRalpha
output. So the arm PGC1a builds loses priority, and that is NOT the dose effect.
Note in the same table that the apoptosis COMPOSITE balance is flat over the timeline
(PRO and ANTI move together): the death finding is gene-specific to PUMA, which is why
script 34's composite analysis found nothing and is exactly what the cell work predicts
(PGC1a induces PUMA 'but not other BH3-only proteins').

PART H -- the coincidence model. Death needs MYC AND a competent substrate; the substrate
input falls developmentally. This is NOT a dose model, and MYC-ER (fixed MYC, varied
substrate) TESTS it rather than excluding it. Three things it buys: the death >>
proliferation asymmetry follows with no extra assumption (one input vs two); a THRESHOLD
on the product explains why PUMA priming collapses THROUGH ZERO rather than attenuating;
and it is the manuscript's title thesis stated literally.
WHAT PART H CANNOT DO: it tests the biogenesis LEVEL and PRIORITY, never PGC1a ACTIVITY.
Ppargc1a is baseMean ~30 here; a coactivator's activity is post-translational. A null
bounds the level version and leaves the activity version untouched.
Two findings to carry forward with their weight attached: (a) the biogenesis LEVEL does
NOT mediate the PUMA collapse, and adjusting for it can make the interaction stronger --
whereas Bax priming IS largely absorbed by it, so in vivo BAX tracks mitochondrial mass
and PUMA does not, which is the opposite of the cell result and must be said; (b) nothing
in PART H separates from timepoint at n=24 -- the axis x Myc terms shrink once tp*myc is
in the model. Read PART H as RANKING candidate second inputs, nothing more. and the `docs/library_reference/gray_chea_mito_tf_shortlist.csv` wasn't committed because there is another copy of it in data/genesets_from_library/

Your reading was right and it's the priority ruler that carries it: three times the TEB axis, eight times the level axis, the only one that partially survives the timepoint confound, and the control sits at chance. **And the size objection dies in the right space** — the WT developmental fall is 26% of the Myc effect on the level ruler but **97% of it on the priority ruler**, where dose cancels. That was the strongest argument against your model and it doesn't hold once measured properly.

**Four things I had wrong, corrected in place:**

1. **The absorption test is unusable — I should have caught this before running it.** `redox` "absorbs" 41% of the PUMA interaction, more than any real axis. So absorption measures nothing here, and I've dropped it in both directions — including as evidence *against* the biogenesis route. My earlier "the level doesn't mediate" claim goes with it.
2. **PUMA's specificity is graded, not binary.** Bmf (−0.83) and Bcl2l11 (−0.45) have more extreme retentions — but non-significant 6W effects (p 0.41, 0.46), and a retention is a ratio of two noisy quantities. Among the pairs with a real 6W effect (Bax 0.55, Bid 0.42, Bak1 0.27, PUMA −0.09, Bax:Mcl1 0.84), PUMA is the only one that *reverses*. That's the defensible claim.
3. **The AP_TEB finding is about chromatin, not transcription factors.** `Bbc3` sits in **72** AP_TEB regulons — TP53, ESR1, JUN, SOX2, POU5F1 — and in **no other context**. That's a broadly accessible promoter in one cell state, not TF specificity; I over-read it. What survives is sharper and better: **MYC and E2F1 reach `Bbc3` only in AP_TEB, and reach Bid/Bok/Bak1/Pmaip1 everywhere else** — which BH3-only MYC can touch is context-dependent.
4. Purity-adjusted interaction p is **0.017**, not 0.006 (that was epi-only from the scratchpad).

One extra that came free: `Htra2` is a good internal control — the most strongly Myc-induced apoptotic gene here attenuates **less** than matched genes (37th percentile), so the PUMA collapse isn't a property of Myc-induced apoptotic genes in general.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **DOSE vs COMPETENCE** — the central conceptual split: MMTV-Myc 6→12W is a dose experiment (MYC protein −50% ⇒ ×0.55 rescaling; output per unit MYC unchanged); MYC-ER is a competence experiment (equal/higher MYC, 80% less death), and its animals had **no prior MYC exposure**, so the substrate change is developmental, not selection.
   - **The coincidence (two-input) model** — death requires MYC **and** a competent mitochondrial substrate. Explains the death≫proliferation asymmetry (one input vs two), the threshold explains PUMA collapsing *through* zero, and it is the manuscript's title thesis literally.
   - **BATCH = TIMEPOINT** — genotype/interaction contrasts clean; the pure temporal axis is batch-confounded and not separable.
   - **Two rulers**: content = DESeq2 set-average **raw** log2FC (dose-dominated); priority = mitoPPS pairwise ratio (Monzel 2025) — **a uniform dose scaling cancels in a ratio**, so an OXPHOS decline surviving on mitoPPS is not the dose effect.
   - **Priming ratios**: per-mouse `log2(pro) − log2(anti)`; `lm(r ~ tp*myc + epi + imm)`.
   - **Matched-pair null** conditional on an equally large 6W effect — the conditioning makes it a test of *selective loss* rather than of effect size; its median retention (0.55) independently reproduces script 40's global rate as a built-in positive control.
   - **Aligned attenuation** (script 34): `sign(lfc6) * (lfc6 − lfc12)` against a baseMean × |lfc6| doubly-matched null.
   - **Absorption/moderation** in script 30's idiom (`30_attenuation_moderation.R:174 absorb_one`) — **failed its control here** (redox absorbs 41%).
   - **Within-timepoint permutation null** — shuffle the axis score inside each timepoint so timepoint structure is preserved and only the mouse-to-mouse link breaks.
   - **Artifact ledger** (script 40) — `cor(WT-time, Δ-Myc-effect)` is algebraically forced; never citable.

THe narrative is sound. One big question remains though. Why are we doing this? How to start? WHay are we looking at the death by Myc? This is the current introduction. Introduction

Breast cancer remains the primary cause of cancer-related mortality in women, with metastasis associated with the worst prognosis.1–3 It is now established that bioenergetic and metabolic adaptations are fundamental for tumourigenesis and progression, making tumour-specific metabolic features an attractive therapeutic target.4–7 A plethora of studies have sought to identify what drives this highly heterogeneous metabolic adaptation, implicating the intrinsic genetic makeup of the cancer cell, the tumour microenvironment, and the systemic metabolic state of the host,⁸⁻¹⁵ yet the metabolic phenotype of a given tumour remains difficult to predict. Indeed, a further, underexplored layer of metabolic heterogeneity operates along the temporal axis of oncogenesis, the stage-dependent remodelling and reprioritisation of metabolic programmes, as cancer advances from initial cellular transformation through primary tumour growth to metastatic dissemination. Most studies have captured metabolism at fixed stages, comparing established tumours to normal tissue, tumour-derived cells with high versus low metastatic potential, or tumours under pharmacological challenge¹⁶⁻¹⁸, providing cross-sectional snapshots of what is fundamentally a dynamic process. How and why metabolic priorities are remodelled across the continuum of cancer progression therefore remains poorly understood, limiting the development of stage-appropriate metabolic therapies.

Among these metabolic pathways, mitochondrial content and function stand out as a particularly heterogeneous axis, with direct consequences for tumour bioenergetics and survival. Our previous unbiased biclustering of the breast cancer transcriptome, seeded on the mitochondrial proteome, across more than 2,000 human breast tumours (METABRIC, with independent confirmation in TCGA and Oslo2) identified the largest coordinately regulated transcriptional switches in the disease, stratifying tumours by cell-of-origin, proliferative state, histology, and clinical outcome (Menegollo et al. 2024). Among these switches, MYC signalling emerged as one of the principal oncogenic drivers associated with distinct mitochondrial bicluster types. This establishes, in a large and unbiased human cohort, that mitochondrial gene programmes constitute a principal, oncogene-linked axis of breast cancer transcriptional state, and identify MYC as a key driver whose engagement of these programmes in vivo we set out to resolve.

The oncogene c-MYC is deregulated, through gene amplification or constitutive upstream signalling, in about half of all cancers, and its deregulation carries a worse prognosis in breast cancer.¹⁹ MYC drives a transcriptional programme that promotes cell growth, proliferation, and pro-tumorigenic metabolic change, including mitochondrial biogenesis.¹⁴,²⁰⁻²⁵ Yet the same deregulation also sensitises cells to apoptosis, a barrier that must be overcome for transformation to proceed.²⁶⁻³⁰ Mitochondria sit at the centre of both processes: they generate ATP through oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and act as the gatekeepers of intrinsic apoptosis through BAX/BAK-mediated cytochrome c release.³¹ MYC therefore places competing demands on the same organelle, and how mammary epithelial cells reconcile them, shaping mitochondrial abundance and function to support survival and transformation while evading MYC-induced apoptosis, remains poorly understood. Much of what is known about MYC-driven metabolic change comes from established tumours and tumour-derived cell lines that have already adapted to this apoptotic stress, or from models in which it is pre-empted by loss of tumour suppressors such as p53 or amplification of Bcl-2, leaving the adaptation itself, at the point where transformation begins, largely uncharacterised.³²,³³. Here, we use deregulated MYC-driven mouse models to temporarily resolve the mitochondrial remodelling that supports tumour initiation, tumour development and subsequent metastasis.

Although MYC is reported to stimulate overall mitochondrial biogenesis, we find that its effect on the mitochondrial transcriptome is not uniform, and the dynamics of mitochondrial pathway reprioritisation is central to how transformation proceeds. MYC plays a part and interacts with the transcriptional trajectory of normal mammary development, leading to a robust increase in mitochondrial biogenesis. However, key mitochondrial pathways are selective reprioritised, holding OXPHOS restrained. Reduced abundance of OXPHOS complexes is associated with a desensitisation to MYC-induced apoptosis, opening a permissive window for tumourigenesis at the adult developmental stage. This dynamic landscape is extended to tumour progression, thus while restrained OXPHOS favours initial transformation, higher OXPHOS activity is subsequently required to support metastasis. Together, our in vitro and in vivo findings define the mitochondrial transcriptome as an active and stage-dependent axis of MYC-driven breast cancer, reprioritised to permit transformation early and re-engaged to enable progression.
 Evaluate critically whether this justifies the narrative or it should be modified, where the emphasis should be put? What is the question?

I've read the intro against §9, and against the 2026-07-13 alignment doc (which did this exercise once already — `docs/2026-07-13_BlockA_revision_walkthrough_and_intro_alignment.md:884-1066`). Critical evaluation below.

## What is the question?

The intro contains three candidate questions and commits to the weakest one.

- **¶1** asks: *how are metabolic priorities remodelled across the stages of progression?* Descriptive, survey-shaped — and this dataset is a poor instrument for it (two timepoints, batch = timepoint, and the 6→12W contrast turns out to be dominated by a dose change).
- **¶2** asks: *how does MYC engage mitochondrial programmes in vivo?* Also descriptive, and largely already answered in humans by Menegollo 2024.
- **¶3** asks the real one, and then abandons it: *MYC drives biogenesis and apoptotic sensitivity through the same organelle — how is that conflict resolved so that transformation can proceed?*

**¶3 is the paper's question.** It is the only one with a mechanism, the only one the cell perturbations can prove, and it is the title thesis stated as a question. And the answer §9 delivers is better than the one ¶3 anticipates: **the conflict is not resolved by the cell — it is dissolved by the tissue.** Mitochondria are a coincidence detector; MYC supplies one input; the gland's own mitochondrial priority supplies the other; as the gland matures it de-prioritises the OXPHOS arm, the second input falls, MYC-driven death is lost *at unchanged MYC*, and the window opens.

In one line: **what licenses a MYC-driven cell to survive its own oncogene — and does that licence come from the cell, or from the tissue it sits in?** Our answer is the tissue, and mitochondria are where the two signals meet.

## Does the intro justify §9? Partly — it front-loads the wrong gap

**¶3's last sentence is the best gap statement in the intro and is currently a throwaway.** "Much of what is known comes from established tumours and cell lines that have already adapted, or from models where it is pre-empted by loss of p53 or amplification of Bcl-2." That is a strong, specific, defensible gap: **the field has studied MYC's mitochondrial metabolism almost exclusively in systems where the apoptotic barrier is already gone — so it could not have seen that the same organelle is the gate.** That justifies the in-vivo work far better than "most studies are cross-sectional snapshots," which invites the reviewer to notice we have two timepoints.

**The single best thing we have is missing entirely: development, not adaptation.** MYC-ER animals never saw MYC and still resist — so the substrate change cannot be selection. Set against ¶3's own list of the field's answers (p53 loss, Bcl-2 amplification, adapted lines), that is the distinguishing claim, and we have *both* halves: SS/passaged cells = selection, MYC-ER = development. §9 point 8 already has the sentence.

## Four factual fixes in ¶4 — one of them changed last week

1. **"holding OXPHOS restrained"** — agent ambiguity that will read as *MYC represses OXPHOS*, which contradicts our own genotype result (MYC raises nuclear OXPHOS, content +21–27%). The restraint is relative-within-compartment, and substantially **developmental** — WT falls on the priority ruler too.
2. **"Reduced abundance of OXPHOS complexes"** — this is where the blot changed the answer. The 2026-07-13 alignment made the centrepiece a *"largely Myc-specific (72–90%) de-amplification"* of nuclear OXPHOS. Post-blot that decline is largely **the ×0.55 dose effect** — explained, not a finding. What survives is the other half: **the de-prioritisation on the mitoPPS ratio ruler, where a uniform dose scaling cancels**, OXPHOS is the most de-prioritised tier on *both* temporal axes, and structural subunits carry it while assembly factors don't. The clause needs re-pointing from the Myc-specific decline to the dose-independent one. That is also the half the coincidence model needs and the half MYC-ER samples.
3. **"is associated with a desensitisation to MYC-induced apoptosis"** — in vivo this association **fails** (§5 negative 1: OXPHOS↔PUMA +0.00 / −0.40, at or below ambient). It is proven in cells. Attribute it, or restate it as the two-input claim: co-decline in vivo, causation from perturbation. §0 requires this.
4. **"interacts with the transcriptional trajectory"** — our result is closer to additive superposition (rescaling without reshaping). "Interacts" invites a search for an interaction we explicitly did not find.

Also missing and flagged by §8 as needing to be said "early": **PGC1a is canonically protective** (muscle atrophy, neurodegeneration, FOXO3 sequestration). One sentence in the intro sets up our inversion instead of letting a reviewer supply it.

## Emphasis, as weights

| | now | proposed |
|---|---|---|
| temporal / stage-heterogeneity framing | ~40% | ~15% — becomes the *method*, not the gap |
| METABRIC human anchor | ~20% | ~20% — keep; re-point its hand-off from "engagement" to the puzzle |
| MYC's two-faced demand + the apoptotic barrier | ~25% | **~40% — the spine** |
| results preview | ~15% | ~25% — rebuilt around two inputs → window → metastatic re-engagement |

One thing I can't judge and you can: **do the METABRIC biclusters contain both mitochondria-high and mitochondria-low MYC-associated classes?** If so, that is the puzzle *in human data* and the strongest possible hand-off from ¶2 into ¶3 — the human cohort already shows MYC does not determine one mitochondrial state.

And one number to reconcile before the OXPHOS sentence is written: Issue #6 says the decline is 72–90% Myc-specific (WT barely moves), while script 40's ruler gives WT −0.255 vs Myc+ −0.405 for OXPHOS subunits on content (63% shared) and −0.109 vs −0.153 on priority (71% shared). Different sets and metrics, but the intro sentence turns on which framing is right, so it needs a read-only check against `results/background_vs_myc.rds`.

Done and committed (`3d2a07a`), not pushed. `docs/2026-07-26_introduction_alignment_and_the_question.md`.

**The question, as the doc states it:** *what licenses a MYC-driven cell to survive its own oncogene — and does that licence come from the cell, or from the tissue it sits in?* It was already in your ¶3 and then abandoned in ¶4. The answer — the tissue, not the cell — is the paper's distinguishing claim and was absent from the intro entirely. With all three stages in, it takes the two-clause form that makes the stage axis load-bearing: the mitochondrial state is a second, tissue-supplied input, and the required match changes with stage (de-prioritised respiration licenses survival early; respiratory capacity is re-engaged for dissemination).

**One correction found while reconciling the OXPHOS clause, and it runs in your favour.** The 2026-07-13 alignment built that clause on *"WT OXPHOS barely declines; the decline is 72–90% Myc-specific."* Issue #6's arithmetic is right — but that gloss is a **frame error**. Script 31 decomposes convergence of the genotype *gap*; because Myc+ sits above WT on OXPHOS, a falling wild-type registers as *anti*-convergence. Scripts 29 and 40, two independent code paths agreeing to six decimals, say the wild-type gland declines **−0.255** against Myc+ **−0.405** (fGSEA NES **−2.670 vs −2.715**, i.e. 98%). And **OXPHOS is the only mitochondrial arm the normal gland withdraws from at all** — every other arm's WT NES is near zero or positive (TCA +0.58, lipid +1.49, amino-acid +1.84, mitoribosome −0.61).

So the intro's OXPHOS sentence moves from *"the Myc+ gland de-amplifies its own OXPHOS"* — which the blot has since reduced to the ×0.55 dose artifact — to *"the maturing gland itself withdraws from the respiratory arm, and it is the only one it withdraws from; the Myc gland merely does the same thing slightly harder."* That is the substrate fall the coincidence model needs, in normal glands, which is exactly what MYC-ER samples. Memory corrected.

The doc also carries the clause-by-clause verdict on all four paragraphs (the four fixes: agent ambiguity in "holding OXPHOS restrained"; "reduced abundance of complexes"; "associated with a desensitisation", where the in-vivo association fails and causality is the cells'; "interacts with" → "superimposed on"), the emphasis map, a **full drafted Introduction** at axis level with all three stages, and what stays out — the dose result belongs early in Results, not the intro.

Before I write this up, three answers came out of the data — and one of them contradicts your Q3 hypothesis. Let me put the numbers up, then ask what I can't determine.

**Q3 — is the adult OXPHOS decline just the loss of the TEB-proliferation axis? No.** Wild-type 6→12W, set-mean raw LFC, same code path as script 40:

| arm (WT 6→12W) | WT | Myc+ | WT as % of Myc+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OXPHOS subunits** | **−0.255** | −0.405 | 63% |
| PROLIF_* pooled (731 genes) | **−0.047** | −0.149 | 32% |
| nucleotide metabolism | **+0.0002** | −0.183 | 0% |
| mitoribosome | −0.024 | −0.252 | 10% |
| TEB-vs-ductal signature | **−0.422** | −0.220 | 191% |

The normal gland's respiratory withdrawal is **5.4× its proliferative withdrawal**, and the two arms most tied to growth — nucleotide metabolism and mitoribosome — don't withdraw at all. Individual markers agree (Mki67 −0.04, Ccnb1 +0.15, Plk1 +0.11, Aurka +0.31; only Top2a −0.41 and E2f1 −0.35 fall). So the adult gland **de-respires without de-proliferating**. What it loses is the **TEB identity programme** (−0.42) — and your library reference already flags `HS_TEB` as *"apoptosis-loaded (TEB lumen clearance by apoptosis during pubertal elongation)"*. The physiological answer is morphogenetic, not proliferative: the pubertal gland keeps a death-ready mitochondrion because it needs apoptosis to cavitate ducts, and stands it down when morphogenesis ends. That is far better for you than the proliferation answer — it dissociates the second input from proliferation, which is exactly what the two-input asymmetry needs.

**Q1 — the MYAZ+Bcl-xL result reframes the whole thing, and I think it's the most important datum you've given me.** It says respiration is not merely a liability: it is **an asset whose benefit is masked by the death it causes**. That converts the model from a permissive gate into a **coupled trade-off**, and it unifies your two arms — respiration comes back for metastasis not because a new requirement appears, but because once the tumour is buffered the constraint that suppressed it is gone. Consistent with the in-vivo dissociation above (proliferation doesn't need OXPHOS) and with MYC-ER (30% proliferation vs 80% death).

**Q2 — the second hit is a state, not a lesion.** The field's answer to "MYC alone is not enough" is a lesion that disables apoptosis (p53/ARF loss, BCL-2/BCL-xL — Eµ-Myc; and Pelengaris/Evan's β-cell MycER + Bcl-xL, which is the exact precedent for your Bcl-xL rescue). Your claim is that normal development supplies a transient, mutation-free phenocopy of that hit. That is what makes it a *window*.

Also checked: the anti-apoptotic buffer does **not** move in the wild-type gland (Bcl2, Bcl2l1, Mcl1, Bcl2l2 all padj ≥ 0.37 on the WT timeline), so §6 of the death narrative stands — the gland solves it by de-prioritising, not by buffering. Three distinct solutions to one trade-off: development, selection, buffering.

Committed `5c21d40`, not pushed. Here's where the three questions landed.

**Q1 — the MYAZ result changes the frame, and it's the most valuable thing you've given me.** With both comparator arms present, PGC1a *kills* MYAZ and PGC1a+Bcl-xL grows *better than Bcl-xL alone*. That's a sign reversal of one intervention's fitness effect conditional on apoptotic competence — so respiration isn't a liability to be shed, it's simultaneously the strongest pro-growth and pro-death input. The paper's question becomes:

> **Mitochondrial respiratory capacity is both an asset and a liability to a MYC-driven cell: it supports growth, and it primes death. When, and how, does an incipient tumour capture the asset without paying the liability?**

Three solutions, and you have all three: development gives it away free (the window); selection finds it expensively (SS/passaged cells lose the *asset* along with the liability); buffering solves it properly. And the closing claim: **what changes across progression is not what the tumour needs from its mitochondria, but what it can afford** — which makes metastasis follow from initiation rather than sit beside it.

On "is proliferation supported by OXPHOS": in vivo they're dissociable, the cross-sectional coupling is *untestable* not weak (script 36 — OXPHOS *is* the global axis), and in mitoPPS ratio space there's a **sign** asymmetry with a working control: `myc × OXPHOS-priority` is +6.09 (p 0.005) on the PUMA trigger with `redox` null, and *negative* on both proliferation composites. And that in-vivo negative is what the trade-off predicts — the asset limb only shows when death is blocked, and in the gland the high-respiration cells are the ones dying and missing from the library.

**Q3 — your hypothesis is contradicted, and the model is better for it.** The adult gland **de-respires without de-proliferating**: OXPHOS subunits −0.255 vs PROLIF pooled −0.047, while nucleotide metabolism (+0.0002), the mitoribosome (−0.024) and — the internal control — the assembly factors of the *same complexes* (+0.001) don't move at all. Against matched random sets OXPHOS sits at the 0th percentile; the paired null, which is what the comparative claim actually needs, puts OXPHOS-minus-proliferation at the 0th too. The physiological answer is **morphogenetic**: it loses the TEB, and your own library reference already flags `HS_TEB` as *"apoptosis-loaded (lumen clearance by apoptosis during pubertal elongation)"*. The pubertal gland keeps a death-ready mitochondrion because duct cavitation needs apoptosis. Had respiration fallen only because proliferation fell, the two-input model would collapse into "less proliferation, less death" and MYC-ER's 80%-vs-30% would have no explanation.

**Q2 — the second hit is a state, not a lesion.** Every model where MYC acts alone needs something to disable apoptosis, and the field's answer is always a lesion (Eµ-Myc + p53/ARF loss or BCL-2; β-cell MycER + Bcl-xL, which is the direct ancestor of your rescue — **both citations flagged for checking**). Your claim is that development supplies a transient, mutation-free phenocopy. That's why it's a *window* and not a switch, and it predicts non-stochastic timing.

Also checked: the gland does **not** buffer — Bcl2, Bcl2l1, Mcl1, Bcl2l2, Xiap, Birc2/3/5 all n.s. on the WT timeline. De-prioritisation is the tissue's route; buffering is the tumour's.

**What's in the repo now:** the doc has new §0 (the question), §0.5/0.6/0.7 answering the three, a rewritten ¶3/¶4 of the drafted Introduction, and the §1 frame correction unchanged. `scripts/43_substrate_specificity_and_tradeoff.R` is written and dry-run clean (scratchpad-redirected, `results/` untouched) — every number tagged `[43]` is provisional until you run it at the committed 2000/5000 draws.

**One thing worth doing cheaply:** if respiration is re-engaged once death can't be executed, mitochondria-high METABRIC biclusters should carry higher BCL2/BCL2L1/MCL1 than mitochondria-low ones, independent of proliferative index. That's the human test of the closing claim, in your own cohort, with no new material.

THE TRADE-OFF MODEL. Mitochondrial respiratory capacity is simultaneously the
strongest pro-growth and the strongest pro-death input to a MYC-driven cell, and
which limb is expressed depends on whether death can be executed. The cell arm
shows the sign reversal outright: PGC1a KILLS MYAZ cells; PGC1a + Bcl-xL grows
BETTER than Bcl-xL alone. Three solutions to one trade-off appear in the paper --
development gives the escape away free (the window), selection finds it expensively
(SS and passaged cells lose the asset with the liability), and anti-apoptotic
buffering solves it properly (respiration becomes pure asset). The closing claim:
what changes across progression is not what the tumour NEEDS from its mitochondria
but what it can AFFORD.

PART A -- the alternative hypothesis is that the adult gland's respiratory
withdrawal is just its exit from the pubertal/TEB proliferative state. The
comparator is built to give that hypothesis its best representatives: NUCLEOTIDE
metabolism and the MITORIBOSOME are the two mitochondrial arms most tied to growth,
and PROLIF_* pooled is the proliferative programme itself. The matched null makes
'OXPHOS withdraws more than expected' a percentile; the PAIRED null is the one that
matches the claim, because the claim is comparative.

PART A IS THE LOAD-BEARING ONE FOR THE MODEL. If respiration fell only because
proliferation fell, the two-input model would collapse into 'less proliferation,
less death' and the MYC-ER asymmetry (~80% less death vs ~30% less proliferation)
would have no explanation. A dissociation is what the model needs.

PART A's per-sample wild-type fit is DESCRIPTIVE ONLY. batch = timepoint, so a
surviving tp term is not evidence of a developmental effect; what it can show is
whether the respiratory fall is collinear with the proliferation score.

PART B -- the outcomes are STANDARDISED before fitting, so the myc x axis terms
are comparable ACROSS outcomes. They are NOT comparable with script 42 PART H's
+2.79, which was fitted on the unstandardised ratio; the priming fit is repeated
here on the standardised scale so the head-to-head is internal. redox_ppd is the
NEGATIVE CONTROL and must be null for the positives to be readable (it was null
throughout in script 42 PART H: p 0.72, permutation 51st percentile).

SCOPE. Nothing here separates from timepoint at n=24 -- script 42 PART H already
showed the best term dropping p 0.005 -> 0.088 once tp*myc is in the model. Both
parts are RANKING. The epistemic contract stands: the in-vivo transcriptome
GENERATES the hypothesis, the cell perturbations PROVE it. And the death phenotype
is external (IHC, MYC-ER counts) -- priming is not death.

Proliferation is negative (−3.68/−3.23) with controls shifted the same way but less far, so that's a ranking observation. The defensible claim is therefore a **sign contrast on the one readable outcome**, not a magnitude comparison across five.

One pattern I'd distrust rather than quote: adding `tp*myc` makes the proliferation and composite terms *stronger* (p 0.107→0.031, 0.060→0.011) while making the PUMA term *weaker* (0.005→0.088). Coefficients that grow when a collinear term is added are collinearity; only the PUMA row moves in the honest direction. The doc says not to cite that column.

**And a correction to my own text.** I'd been quoting ~0.42 as the mitoPPS ambient for OXPHOS couplings. That's script 38's *global median across pathways*; the ambient for this axis specifically is **0.493** (q90 0.838), against redox's 0.260. That's precisely the error CLAUDE.md warns about — never borrow one axis's ambient for another. It changes no conclusion, since the permutation null is axis-specific by construction, but the number was wrong and is now right in both the doc and memory.

Net effect on the argument: PART A, which is the load-bearing one, got stronger. PART B is a narrower lead than I first wrote it — one outcome, one working control, a sign contrast. That's still what the trade-off needs from in-vivo data under the epistemic contract, and the MYAZ sign reversal is what proves it.

     expressed <- names(bm)[is.finite(bm) & bm > 0 & is.finite(tn[names(bm)])]
     bin_of <- cut(rank(bm[expressed], ties.method = "first"), breaks = NBIN, labels = FALSE)
     by_bin <- split(expressed, bin_of)
     draw_matched <- function(e) {
       b <- bin_of[match(e, expressed)]; b <- b[!is.na(b)]
       unlist(lapply(split(b, b), function(k)
         sample(by_bin[[as.character(k[1])]], length(k), replace = TRUE)), use.names = FALSE)
     }

       eb <- arm_ens[[p[2]]][arm_ens[[p[2]]] %in% expressed]
       obs <- set_mean(tn, ea) - set_mean(tn, eb)
       nul <- vapply(seq_len(NSET), function(i)
         set_mean(tn, draw_matched(ea)) - set_mean(tn, draw_matched(eb)), numeric(1))
       tibble::tibble(arm_a = p[1], arm_b = p[2], observed_diff = obs,
                      null_median = stats::median(nul),
                      percentile = 100 * mean(nul < obs), p_emp_lower = mean(nul <= obs))

Tested. Your premise doesn't hold, mine was weaker than I stated, and what's left is more interesting than either.

## 1. Why I said "Myc module" — and how strong that actually is

I inferred it from **curated target lists**, not from expression: `MYC_targets ∩ MitoCarta` is enriched for MitoCarta's pro-apoptotic genes (2.7×, p 0.011), `ESRRA∪NRF1∪GABPA ∩ MitoCarta` is not (0.76×, p 0.83). That is a statement about ChEA regulons, and I let it sound like a statement about your mice.

So I tested the expression half tonight. **It fails for both.** On the WT timeline neither group moves: PGC1a-owned payload (Aifm1, Aifm2, Cycs, Endog, Ifi27) **−0.024, 40th percentile**; MYC-owned effectors (Bax, Casp8, Casp9, Diablo, Pmaip1…) **+0.026, 52nd**. Neither is a module in our data. What survives is only the negative: **the PGC1a axis has no privileged claim on the apoptotic genes.** Withdraw the positive half of what I said.

## 2. Your premise, on both rulers

| WT 6→12W | content | vs matched random | **priority (mitoPPS)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| OXPHOS subunits | **−0.255** | **0th pct** | **−0.109** |
| OXPHOS (all) | −0.145 | 0th pct | −0.093 |
| OXPHOS assembly | +0.001 | 50th | −0.002 |
| **Apoptosis-PRO** | **+0.025** | **63rd** | **+0.054** |
| **Apoptosis-ANTI** | **+0.045** | **65th** | **+0.046** |

There is no common de-prioritisation. On the priority ruler they move in **opposite directions** — OXPHOS loses priority, apoptosis gains a little. Gene by gene, of 25 PRO + 7 ANTI on the WT timeline **exactly one is significant: `Bnip3` +0.635 (padj 0.021), and it goes up.** `Bcl2l1` −0.107 (0.79), `Bbc3` +0.062 (0.88), `Bax` −0.145 (0.49).

Where apoptosis *is* de-prioritised is on the **Myc** axis at 6W: −0.210, padj 0.022. That's Myc's doing, not development's.

## 3. The PUMA:Bcl-xL collapse — it has no wild-type definition

| ratio | WT 6→12W | Myc @6W | Myc @12W | retention |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bbc3:Bcl2l1** | **+0.168** | **+0.676** | **−0.044** | **−0.06** |
| Bax:Bcl2l1 | −0.039 | +0.902 | +0.492 | +0.55 |
| Bid:Bcl2l1 | +0.212 | +1.027 | +0.387 | +0.38 |
| Cycs:Bcl2l1 | −0.007 | +0.762 | +0.595 | +0.78 |

The baseline ratio **does not fall — it drifts up.** The entire collapse is in the Myc effect. So transcriptionally it is definable *only as an interaction*, and your intuition needs one word changed: it is **developmental in cause, Myc-dependent in measurement.** The gland changed — MYC-ER proves that, never-exposed animals at equal dose. But what changed is **inducibility, not level**. You need Myc present to see it, because there is nothing to see without him.

## 4. What this does to PGC1a

`CORE_MITO` contains **66% of the OXPHOS subunits** (59/89) — so it is a fair test. The regulon as a whole is **+0.013 on the WT timeline (77th percentile — flat)**, while the OXPHOS-subunit part of it falls −0.255. If PGC1a-axis coactivation were withdrawing, the 300-gene regulon should go with it. It doesn't; **only the respiratory structural genes do.**

That doesn't exclude PGC1a — its output is post-translational and the subunits are its most canonical target — but it excludes the simple version, and `Ppargc1a` transcript is flat-to-up (+0.397, n.s., baseMean 30).

## 5. The reframe — and I think it out-novels the module

Put §2 and §3 together and you get a sharper claim than a co-regulated module:

> **The maturing gland does not dismantle its death machinery. Every pro- and anti-apoptotic transcript is where it was at 6W. What it withdraws is the respiratory state that machinery depends on — and with it, Myc's ability to convert his signal into PUMA priming.**

A module says "these genes move together." This says something stronger and less expected: **they don't move together, and they don't have to** — what is shared is not transcription but **dependence**. That is precisely what your Bcl-xL rescue localises (execution, not induction), and it makes PGC1a co-induction in MYC-ER a clean prediction rather than a hopeful one.

## 6. The one route to a module that would actually work

Define it **by the collapse itself**, genome-wide: among genes with a real 6W Myc effect, compute retention (12W effect ÷ 6W effect) against the ×0.55 global rate and the matched-pair null script 42 already has — then ask what sits in the tail with PUMA. If OXPHOS/apoptosis genes are enriched there, you have an empirically-defined module, in the mouse, built from the phenomenon rather than from a curated list. If they aren't, PUMA is a solo and you should say so.

That is a real analysis, it is novel, and it directly answers "how do we define this transcriptionally."

Script 42 already scanned PUMA's transcriptional inputs (`Atf4, Ddit3, Trib3, Chac1, Foxo1/3/4, Sesn2, Eif2ak3, Nupr1, E2f1, Trp73`) and found none tracking it — but that scan asked "does it *track* PUMA", not "does it *collapse* like PUMA", and ATF4 is translationally regulated so its mRNA is a poor readout. That distinction matters for what follows.

## How PUMA priming could depend on the OXPHOS state

The first move is to separate two questions that "priming" blurs, because **priming is not a transcript — it is an occupancy state at the outer membrane**:

**(ii) Why priming depends on respiratory state even at equal PUMA.** This is where I think the real mechanism is, and tonight's gene lists point straight at it:

- **The payload/trigger split.** `CORE_MITO ∩ APOPTOSIS_PRO` = **Cycs, Aifm1, Aifm2, Endog, Ifi27** — every one a *releasable* IMS protein. The PGC-1a axis owns the **payload** and the respiratory chain; it owns **no BH3-only gene**. MYC's regulon owns Bax, Casp9, Diablo, Pmaip1 — the **trigger**. So: *PGC-1a loads the gun, MYC pulls it.* Development unloads the gun without touching the trigger — which is exactly why every apoptotic transcript is flat while OXPHOS falls −0.255.
- **Cristae and the releasable pool.** ~85% of cyt c sits behind OPA1-dependent cristae junctions. MOMP alone doesn't release it; cristae remodelling does. A de-respiring mitochondrion has fewer, looser cristae — same BAX event, smaller apoptosome yield.
- **Cardiolipin.** Required for tBID recruitment and BAX insertion/oligomerisation, and it anchors the membrane-bound cyt c pool. Made and remodelled in respiring mitochondria (`Crls1`, `Taz`, `Ptpmt1`). Less respiration → less cardiolipin at contact sites → less efficient BAX activation *at identical BH3 levels*.
- **ΔΨm and HTRA2.** Myc's single strongest apoptotic gene here is `Htra2` (+1.49, padj 2.6e-08). HTRA2 import and maturation into the IMS are ΔΨm-dependent — so a low-potential mitochondrion carries less mature HTRA2 to release, and the corpus's odd standout becomes part of the payload story.
- **ROS.** Cardiolipin peroxidation is a required step for cyt c mobilisation; low flux makes less of it.

**(i) Why MYC's PUMA *transcription* depends on it.** Two routes, and both are testable:

- **Metabolite-gated chromatin** — OXPHOS regenerates NAD+ and supports citrate→acetyl-CoA and α-KG for TET/JmjC. This is the route that connects to the finding you already have: `Bbc3` is reachable in `AP_TEB` **and no other context**. Respiratory state and promoter accessibility would then be co-determined, and the collapse is chromatin, not signalling.
- **Retrograde/ISR** — MYC over-driving a high-capacity mitochondrion → OMA1–DELE1–HRI → ATF4/CHOP → PUMA. Script 42's null doesn't exclude this, for the reason above.

**Two things the paper must confront**, both from your own `PUMA-and-its-relationships.md`: the canonical axis has PGC-1a **protective** (it sequesters FOXO3a; losing it frees FOXO3a onto the PUMA promoter) — your model inverts that and should say so explicitly. And §5 of that doc says **FOXO1, not FOXO3**, drives TEB lumen-clearance apoptosis under Wnt control — which fits the TEB story better than FOXO3 does.

Let me write the plan.
